speechtext:
Mr. Jim Fulton (Skeena), seconded by Mr. Caccia moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of preserving and protecting in its natural state at least 12 per cent of each of Canada's ecosystems.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. colleague for seconding the motion. The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of preserving and protecting in its natural state at least 12 per cent of each of Canada's ecosystems.
With the assistance of Kevin McNamee of the Canadian Nature Federation, an amendment will be proposed by my hon. friend, Mr. Martin, to clarify the shared responsibility so that it would read:
- 12 per cent of Canada by working co-operatively with the provincial and territorial governments and assisting them to complete the protected area networks by the year 2000.
It is important that that kind of clarification be made, and I accept it as a good, proper and helpful amendment.
I trust that this amendment is such that the motion will be put to the House and passed today, perhaps by all-party consent. It is crucial that the dormant political process be invigorated by an all-party resolution which will lead to at least protecting 12 per cent of Canada before the end of this century.
Canada's total lands are 9,922,000 square kilometres and our 34 national parks total 182,272 square kilometres. Our provincial and territorial parks, ecological reserves and wilderness areas of which at this moment there are 1,160, total 138,000 square kilometres, substantially less than what is presently in our national parks system.
Of those 1,160 such protected sites at the provincial and territorial level, there are only 43 designated as wilderness areas for a total of 8,680 square kilometres. If you add up all the so-called protected areas, which is 6.3 per cent of Canada or just over 320,000 square kilometres, and take out the national, provincial and territorial parks which allow logging, hunting, mining and other kinds of activities, that total drops to just 254,000 square kilometres or 2.6 per cent of our national land base.
A federal task force many years ago confirmed that an opportunity to set aside lands and complete our national parks system will be gone by the year 2000, due almost entirely to land alienations, roads, electrical transmission lines, hydroelectric facilities, forest harvesting, mining, urban sprawl, and all of those other land uses to which the lands of this huge country are put.
In 1979, some 12 years ago, cabinet approved the goal of setting aside and establishing one park in each of our natural regions. There are 39 terrestrial natural regions and 29 marine natural regions in Canada. The existing 34 national parks represent 21 of the 39 land regions or 182,272 square kilometres which is 1.8 per cent of Canada.
All this area is not protected. For example, logging is going on at this time by Daishowa Canadian Forest Products in Wood Buffalo, Alberta, our largest national park and in the Northwest Territories.
The plans to complete five new national parks by 1995 will leave 13 to be completed in the five years between 1995 and the year 2000. I think I can aptly demonstrate that the government is going to have to allocate more

June 17, 1991
Private Members' Business
substantial person time, and perhaps more substantial capital in order to achieve realistically the completion of our national parks system within the next nine years.
Canada now has 213 endangered species that are either in danger of becoming, or are already extinct. Twenty species were added this year, including some of the most noble creatures that have ever existed on this continent such as the grizzly bear, the polar bear and the Peary caribou. These are now also endangered and up to this moment neither the provinces nor the territories have taken steps to deal directly with recommendations made by biologists in terms of those three species. Clearly these include the establishment of protective zones and a dramatic reduction in pressures on them from both industrial activity and human activity.
Within the green plan we see the promise to, by the year 2000, establish three national marine parks between now and 1995 and three more by the year 2000, including the South Moresby Gwaii-Haanas Marine Park, Saguenay and one other, leaving some 21 marine natural regions unrepresented beyond the year 2000.
Many people ask where the 12 per cent figure comes from. It comes from international scientific consensus, as is found in the 1987 Brundtland report, the World Commission on the Environment and Development. In chapter 6 we find:
Nearly 4 per cent of the earth's land is managed explicitly to conserve species and ecosystems and all but a small handful of countries have national parks.
One then goes on to chapter 6-18, point 72 which points out:
Since 1970, the networks have expanded in extent by more than 80 per cent, around two-thirds of which are in the Third World. But a great deal more remains to be done; a consensus of professional opinion suggests that the total expanse of protected areas needs to be at least tripled if it is to constitute a representative sample of Earth's ecosystems.
So there you have one of the most extensive world wide reports ever done, and done by a United Nations body chaired by Prime Minister Brundtland, which has concluded that at minimum, we should set aside 12 per cent.
This report was endorsed on September 29, 1988 by Canada's present Prime Minister. In his remarks before the United Nations we find in about the middle of his speech, the following:
The world is facing an environmental crisis of unparalleled magnitude. Nature is sending us an urgent message that we ignore at our peril. The signs of this crisis are all around us- shortages of timber, exhausted soil, desertification, depleted fish stocks, seals dying in the North Sea, beluga whales washing ashore in the St. Lawrence river. Some even maintain that we have reached a point where the survival of mankind is at risk.
Prime Minister Brundtland, Chairman of the World Commission on Environment and Development, has said that the threat to our environmental security is "second only to nuclear war".
Those remarks by our present Prime Minister were picked up by the two past and the now present Ministers of Environment. We find in the published green plan, which was released here in Ottawa December 11, 1990, a section called Section 3, Special Spaces and Species, and an allocation of $175 million over the next six years for protecting unique ecological areas. It takes as a goal, and I quote: "To set aside as protected space, 12 per cent of Canada." It goes through some of the points I have been covering, such as the need to establish five new national parks by 1996 and to negotiate agreements for the remaining 13 parks which are required to complete the terrestrial parks system by the year 2000. Many people have asked me and I am sure have asked other members, what does that commitment mean? Is it deliverable? And what are those areas that are still unrepresented? Very few Canadians realize that it is scientifically recognized that there are 13 natural bioregions, 39 natural systems in Canada, and that only 21 of those 39 are presently represented in our national parks system, such as our first park, Banff National Park created in 1885.
I quote from the January 31, 1991, letter from the Minister of the Environment on these very points:
As you know, Environment Canada's recently released Green Plan provides for the establishment of at least five new national parks.by 1996 and for the negotiation of the agreements for the remaining 13 parks by the year 2000. It also provides for the establishment of three new national marine parks by 1996, with an additional three by the year 2000.
It goes on to say:
June 17, 1991

Within the next few months, my department also plans to release a follow-up action plan setting out specific strategies and target dates for establishing national parks within each of the 18 unrepresented natural regions.
That was in January and they have not yet been made public.
Here are the terrestrial regions that are still unrepresented, regions that have active park proposals: Region 15, Bluenose Lake; Region 17, East Arm; Region 27, Churchill; Region 36, Banks Island; and Region 37, Baffin Island.
Regions with currently inactive park proposals are Region 16, Wager Bay; Region 21, Mealey Mountains; Region 24, the Torngat Mountains.
Regions with representative areas that are identified natural areas of Canadian significance, but in which further study is required before a park proposal can be identified are: Region 3, Fraser-Chilcotin Junction area and the Churn Creek area; Region 7, the Spatsizi Plateau and Mount Edziza areas, Kluane/Aishihik area, Yukon River/Ogilvie Mountains area; Region 14, the Long Point area and Little Limestone Lake area; Region 22, the Richmond Gulf area; Region 25, Leaf Bay area and Nastapoka Islands; Region 38, the Bjorne Peninsula area and Bathurst Island.
The regions with regional studies that are not yet complete are: Region 2, the Strait of Georgia Lowlands in British Columbia; Region 20 the Laurentian Boreal Highlands basically running from Ottawa to Quebec City; Region 23 the Whale River region; and Region 28 which is northeast of Churchill, known as Southampton.
Quebec is a particular case that I know you would be interested in, Mr. Speaker, because the Whale River region which is now being studied is the area that is being proposed for flooding by the Great Whale hydroelectric project known to many people as the first part of James Bay II. The flooding from James Bay I and James Bay II is a staggering 25,834 square kilometres, 2 per cent of the entire land base of the province of Quebec. Six times as much land will be flooded by this one project as is protected in all of the federal and provincial parks in that entire province. It is really quite staggering the amount of work to be done on both provincial and national parks strategies, to say nothing of the 12 per cent in our second largest province.
Private Members' Business
The first debate and vote there ever has been on 12 per cent and on the national parks system took place in this House on February 5, 1990, and that motion said the following:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should move to complete the national parks system (land and marine) by the year 2000 and should implement the recommendation of the World Commission on Environment and Development, (Brundtland Report) that Canada protect at least 12 per cent of land and marine zones
Sadly, that was not about to pass through this Chamber. Since that time there have been various suggestions that the wording could have been clarified at least in terms of the 12 per cent. That is going to be done today by Mr. Martin, my friend on environmental matters, to give the House an opportunity to express itself morally on an issue that is truly one of survival.
There are few if any biologists that I have spoken to in the years since Brundtland who disagree that 12 per cent should be the floor-hardly the ceiling but it should be the floor-because we are losing right now about 20,000 species per year that are becoming entirely extinct, entirely related to the activities of humanity. As we lose those species, most of them are being lost in tropical areas because of the proliferation of life in the canopies particularly of jungle areas.
As I said earlier in my remarks, we have lost 20 species in Canada and 20 have been added on to the endangered species list in our country, great creatures such as the grizzly. I mean, how is it possible in a country like ours? There isn't even one area where grizzlies are specifically protected in a sanctuary in the whole of a great country such as this, a country that is massive by the standards of anywhere else in the world. Even the United States has 8.1 per cent of its land base protected, due in large part to states such as Alaska where 37 per cent has been set aside in perpetuity in their national park system.
Even poorer countries in these years leading up to and post-Brundtland have adopted this concept, with a real understanding of the benefits, both in terms of speci-ation and biological diversity. They also realize some of the things that can come with that for poorer countries such as Tanzania, which has set aside 17 per cent of its land base to protect the larger mammals that are resident there such as lions and elephants that people want to see, but also to protect their grasslands and some of the unique species they have there.

Private Members' Business
I am prepared to listen today, hopefully later this morning, to the minister but also to my colleague so that we have an understanding that there is a responsibility for the territories and for the provinces. There is also a very large and leading responsibility for the federal government to get on with the job of isolating those areas, in a land use sense, that are the vital core areas for various species.
We are continuing to see various migratory bird species-we have about 11 right now-that are in real difficulty because of loss of habitat, loss of core feeding areas along their flyways so that as they are coming north or going south, there are huge areas where they are either short of feed or having to operate on reduced feed.
It is very important that all of our biological systems be linked so that travel ways for animals and plants permit them to have an opportunity to continue to migrate within the natural systems, and also that birds and other beings and creatures such as insects have the kind of environment about them that they require in order to get about and to survive on this planet.
There has been ongoing spin as well put to the debate that the federal responsibility may be almost done, that we are at 1.8 per cent, and by the time we get to 3 per cent, that would basically be the federal responsibility. I do not opt into that proposal because, as I pointed out in my remarks, the provincial and territorial systems as they stand are considerably smaller now than the existing federal system. In the only really large national survey, which was done in 1987 by Gallup, 96 per cent of Canadians support strong government action to protect wilderness.
In that year Canadians spent $5.1 billion on wildlife and park-related activities. It has gone up substantially each year since, both among Canadians and among visitors to our country. Canadians when asked a very simple question about environmental issues, certainly to a majority, but to an ever-increasing majority, look to Ottawa, not to the provincial or territorial capitals for leadership in particularly the designation and protection of species and of lands.
So my hope is, through this debate and through the amended wording, to make clear that this is a shared
responsibility. Although the provincial responsibilities are large, they have not been doing them. I use as an example the studies that are going on in the Whale Region by the federal government now that, should James Bay I and II proceed as planned, an area six times as large as everything that is protected in Quebec would be flooded by that one project.
Clearly in terms of the definition within politicians' minds at the provincial and territorial levels, I think the federal government and all the parties in this House have a very big job to do to convince our provincial and territorial colleagues that they must work hard to provide add-on lands and programs that are suitable to dealing with those who live in those areas so that they can in fact find benefits from these kinds of land designations, which are often ballyhooed as being something that causes a loss of jobs. That is hardly the case when one looks at the studies that have been done, not just throughout North America, but in other jurisdictions. Governments have planned properly for those land designations so that aboriginal people, nearby communities and people who had residual occupations tied to those lands, are not unduly or unfairly disrupted in their activities.
In concluding, I hope that today's debate on Motion 330, as amended, will be a successful one and that both the Official Opposition and the government will take the opportunity to endorse what I believe is a much-needed moral voice from this House, that we had better get on with this task. If we were given the option now of setting aside Banff National Park with its size and grandeur, I just wonder whether or not we would have the intellectual and moral girth to do so. I hope that today's debate demonstrates that this House has the foresight to start moving to set aside at least the 12 per cent that future generations need to survive and enjoy this country the way we have.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to a motion that is vital to Canada and to our environment, and I want to congratulate the hon. member for Skeena on the speech he just made. The Liberal Party wholeheartedly supports the campaign to protect threatened spaces and ecosystems. We must complete the national parks network by
June 17, 1991

establishing at least one protected, representative region in each of the 39 terrestrial regions by the year 2000, and in each of the 29 marine regions by the year 2010. Twenty-one land regions are already represented within the national parks system, but to complete the system, an additional 18 parks will be needed.
Even with these additions, Mr. Speaker, only 3 per cent of Canadian territory will be protected, while our target is 12 per cent.

Therefore, we look forward to the government announcing a strategy for promoting protection of the remaining 9 per cent.
This will entail working co-operatively with provincial and territorial governments to ensure that each of Canada's natural regions is protected. If 12 per cent of the lands and waters are to be protected, areas will have to include not only national parks, but provincial parks, territorial parks, conservation areas and heritage rivers.
This will require significant commitments from provincial and territorial governments, as well as the federal government. They may well need financial assistance. The $175 million tagged in the green plan for special spaces and species will have to be released. The short field season means that any delays now suffered in authorizations and promotion translates into much longer delays as far as the identification of new parks and new conservation areas.
If you will forgive a personal note, Mr. Speaker, I am looking forward this summer to tripping the Taft in northern British Columbia and indeed, in the member's riding. I may even have the occasion, after it is all over, to meet some Liberals in the member's riding. If not, I look forward to meeting a number of NDPers who I can convert.
I mention this because the Taft should clearly be designated as a heritage river. Yet British Columbia and Alberta have not joined the Canadian Heritage River System.
One would hope that this and so many other issues, such as the Banks Island National Park proposal could be rectified as soon as possible.
Private Members' Business
The member for Skeena was quite eloquent in talking about the absolute need for protecting by diversity another species.
We in Canada have a tremendous responsibility to the world. Indeed, we have a fiduciary responsibility to the world, not only to protect the vast land mass which we have been so lucky to have inherited, but indeed to show leadership to the rest of the world. How can this country stand up in the international forum and speak of the need for other countries to protect their areas, especially the underdeveloped countries, when we in this country have not taken the decisive steps that are required here.
I regret very much that my time is limited. However, it is with unequivocal pleasure for these and many other reasons that I would move the following amendment:
I move, seconded by Mr. Caccia, the hon. member for Davenport:
That the motion be amended by deleting all of the words after the expression "12 per cent" and by adding the following words:
"of Canada by working co-operatively with the provincial and territorial governments and assisting them to complete their protected area networks by the year 2000".

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in the opportunity to speak to this motion. I think that the subject matter of the motion is very apropos.
All Canadians need to be constantly reminded that this is an issue that has immediate import on their lives and even more so on the lives of their children and grandchildren if we are going to preserve the country and the ecosystems that are so important to us.
I say the subject matter is always pertinent. I think that the motion itself is redundant because the government has already announced its intentions to do exactly what the motion requires or requests the government to do. Second, the government has already taken action to indicate its intention to proceed with what it has already said it was going to do.
I point out to my friend from Skeena that there is no greater evidence than the announcement that was made two or three weeks ago by the Minister of the Environment. He came out to British Columbia to announce the Fraser plan in which the government is assigning $100 million to reclaim the Fraser. Now I know that is not specific to this motion in that it is not setting aside a new park or protecting a new ecosystem, but it is very urgent in the sense that it is an attempt to restore an ecosystem that is in danger. All I can say is that the action taken by the government and the Minister of the Environment indicates the seriousness with which the government takes the green plan and its intention to fulfil the commitment it has made within the programs of the Green Plan. So I say that the subject is never redundant, but the motion itself is.
It is always easy to speak in generalities on a subject like this. Everybody is in favour of protecting the environment and the ecosystems that are so important to us. It is much more difficult to be specific in dealing with these subjects. It is easy for the dowagers in New York City to speak about protecting the marine park in the Queen Charlottes and so forth.
I remember a debate that was held almost exactly a year ago in this House where we were debating the
importance of protecting the environment. The colleague of the member from Skeena, the member for Comox-Alberni, dwelt at length about the environmental issues facing the country and spoke, at length, about Temagami here in Ontario. However, he never once mentioned Carmanah in his own riding. Carmanah is probably the most discussed topic of the environment in British Columbia, but it never occurred to the member for Comox-Alberni that his position on the Carmanah Valley would be very important to the people of Canada, to know whether he really wanted to protect that valley or whether he wanted to see it logged. I am sure he does not want to see the valley logged, but his constituents themselves have asked where the member for Comox- Alberni stands on the subject of the Carmanah Valley. It is easy to speak in generalities. It is much more difficult to be specific about these issues.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I do not mean to break in on the member's time and I will be very brief. I would just like for the record to recognize that the Carmanah is not in the seat of the member for Comox-Alberni. It is in the seat of the member for Nanaimo.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
To be specific, it is the constituents of the member from Alberni who work on the Franklin River project right next door to the Carmanah Valley and I think the member knows that. It is the constituents who are affected, the constituents of the member from Comox-Alberni.
Finally, on this particular topic, I just want to refer to the Brundtland report, the excellent report brought together a few years ago, beginning at chapter 2.
Madam Brundtland says: "Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It contains within it two key concepts, the concept of needs, in particular the essential needs of the world's poor to which over-riding priority should be given and the idea of limitations opposed by the state of technology and the social organization on the environment's ability to meet present and future needs."
Those are very, very important criteria that she establishes. So I concur with the hon. member from Skeena that the government should take a leadership role in this regard. I believe it already has done so. Canada's green plan clearly states that Canada's long-term goal is to set
June 17, 1991

aside as protected space 12 per cent of the country, a goal that must be shared by the provinces, the territories, private stewards and the federal government, as the two speakers who spoke before may have already recognized.
Furthermore, the green plan contains numerous initiatives that the federal government is prepared to take to accelerate progress to meet this goal. The completion of the country's system of national parks, which is one of the oldest and most renowned in the world, by the year 2000 is an example of the one of the green plan's special spaces and species projects which will contribute to meeting the 12 per cent target.
I am also of the opinion that there is some urgency in this matter because Canada's remaining wilderness is slowly but steadily being engulfed. The federal, provincial and territorial governments must act now before opportunities to create new protected areas are foreclosed forever.
Each government owes it to the next project, the most pristine areas within their respective systems of protected areas for the enjoyment and understanding of this and future generations of Canadians.
I might inject, however, that remarks like seemingly unrestrained logging in parks really do not add to the debate when we never define whether those logging activities are designed to deal with infested areas or over mature areas which are becoming a danger.
We need to define actually what we mean by logging in those areas. It is not good enough to say that there is logging going on.
I am pleased to report to this House that real progress is being made by this government. The Minister of the Environment is working hard with his provincial and territorial counterparts to create new national parks. His short list of priority candidates at this time include Banks Island, Baffin Island, Bluenose Lake, the east arm of Great Slave Lake and Wager Bay in the Northwest Territories, Old Crow flats in the Yukon, the Cape Churchill area in Manitoba and the Tomgat Mountains in the Newfoundland and Labrador area.
It would be useful at this time to briefly review the origin of the goal of setting aside 12 per cent of the country. I believe that the 12 per cent figure was
Private Members' Business
extrapolated from sections 1 and 72 in chapter 6 of Our Common Future, the Brundtland report.
This report, which is commonly referred to as the "Brundtland report" proposed a series of actions to halt the extinction of species and the irreversible degradation of ecosystems globally. The report noted that although nearly 4 per cent of the earth's land area was managed explicitly to conserve species and ecosystems, a great deal more remained to be done.
It went on to suggest that the total expanse of protected areas needed to be at least tripled, if it was to constitute a representative sample of the earth's ecosystems. The application of this goal to the Canadian context was pioneered by the World Wildlife Fund (Canada), one of the country's most prestigious non-government conservation organizations when it launched its 1989 "Endangered Spaces: The Future of Canada's Wilderness" campaign.
This 10-year campaign urges governments, industries, environmental groups and individual Canadians to take action on two key points; first, to integrate conservation practices or sustainable development into the management of lands and waters used for resource production; second, to protect a representative sample of the country's undisturbed natural areas so that a minimum 12 per cent of the country's area will be protected as wilderness.
The proposition that at least 12 per cent of the country be protected has generated considerable debate among government agencies, industry and conservation organizations. Many have made the point that there is no agreed upon formula or percentage for determining that a sufficient amount of natural heritage resources has been protected.
For example, whereas the Brundtland report recommends a target of 12 per cent, the UICN, the world conservation union notes in its report, From Strategy to Action of 1989 that if only 10 per cent of the earth's surface was devoted to protection, the trend for species and ecosystem depletion would be stemmed globally.
There are varying opinions about what the percentage figure ought to be. I simply want to underscore the fact that while this subject is always pertinent and never redundant, the motion is redundant because the government is committed to it, and the target should not be a specific percentage. The target should be what is necessary to preserve those ecosystems.

Private Members' Business

Mr. Speaker, I also would like to congratulate the most distinguished member for Skeena for his motion and my colleague for LaSalle-Emard for his amendment.
I cannot say the same about the member for Surrey-White Rock-South Langley. He twice declared the motion redundant, but found it nevertheless possible and necessary to speak for 10 minutes, thus demonstrating that the essence of the motion is not redundant at all.
Considering the record of the government to which he belongs, there is no motion that is redundant in the field of the environment and conservation.
I bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, a paragraph from the Brundtland report which reads as follows: "The challenge facing nations today is no longer deciding whether conservation is a good idea, but rather how it can be implemented in the national interests and within the means available to each country." The member for Surrey-White Rock questions the desirability of a percentage and we should not invest too many energies on that question. Certainly it would be desirable to be very flexible on this subject in certain circumstances. But considering the pressures from development and the pressures from population growth, it seems essential that a percentage be set as a goal as a guideline and a percentage below which we should not go. Therefore the percentage becomes a very important policy guideline without which we would have a variety of different standards by continent and by nation, and we would in the end not achieve the goal put forward by the Brundtland report.
Mr. Speaker, in the green plan there is a commitment to 12 percent. The green plan states that 6.9 per cent of Canada's land is currently protected. There is a controversy though on that 6.9 and it has to be put on the record. The World Wildlife Fund in Canada has concluded that roughly 3.4 per cent of the Canadian land meets the required criteria. Therefore the statement made in the green plan by the government does not seem to be supported and verified by the World Wildlife Fund, which is perhaps the non-governmental organization most active in this particular field of conservation.
The debate offers an opportunity to raise some questions in relation to the present government activities and intentions. For instance, will the government, to which the member for Surrey-White Rock-South Langley belongs, announce a target date for completing the national marine park system? Will the system of national parks be completed by the year 2000, which will then allow us to reach at least 3 per cent of Canada's land area
When will the government announce a strategy for promoting the protection of the remaining 9 per cent?
Another point that ought to be raised in this connection is, when will the federal government provide the financial support that is needed in the territorial governments to assist them in establishing territorial parks so that the achievement of the 12 per cent goal is facilitated. For instance, regional development funds, will the government to which the hon. member belongs encourage provincial jurisdiction to contribute to the 12 per cent goal by contributing funds from regional development funds themselves?
There is also the question of Canadian heritage river systems, which is a phenomenal, positive program, initiated a long time ago and to which unfortunately British Columbia and Alberta do not belong. This is an opportunity to raise the question which goes beyond our jurisdiction as to when will British Columbia and Alberta enter this Canadian heritage river system. The federal government has a certain leverage to achieve that goal.
One also has to bring to the attention of the House the fact that there is in the green plan a commitment to $175 million for our special spaces and species. When will this fund be released? Obviously there will be competition for the use of this fund, and the sooner it is made available the better. We will know also how we can achieve the goal that the hon. member for Skeena and all of us have in mind.
Then there is the unfinished business of the Banks Island National Park proposal. The Park Service has been working on that agreement for some time, actually since 1978. Most if not all of the issues have been settled and what is missing at this stage is only cabinet approval.
June 17, 1991

Private Members' Business
When will cabinet find the time and the will to do that? As you can see from the case of this particular site, the Banks Island National Park, it takes years to create a national park. It is not a process that takes place overnight. Actually I would venture to say that since 1984 each and every national park that has been declared by the present government is the result of painstaking and intense work of the preceding government. So here is the opportunity to bring to a conclusion something that was initiated in 1978.
In connection with this motion, we have to make reference to the necessity of including in the National Parks Act the Canadian Landmarks Program. When we debated the act the last time, unfortunately the program was resisted and despite efforts at second reading in the House, it was turned down. Therefore, we are still facing the necessity of raising this point because the Canadian Landmarks Program is not included in the new revised parks policy that is presently being developed.
We would urge the government instead to include the landmarks program because it helps in a variety of ways. It is a way of promoting federal-provincial co-operation; it is a way of stimulating public participation. It is also a very important way of developing public education on the importance and the essence of our publicly owned land, national parks, and the role that they play for the recreation and the enjoyment of Canadians, and for the preservation of course of species and valuable land.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that we have here a unique opportunity that the government should seize today by not talking out this bill but by recognizing that the motion by the member for Skeena, as amended, is an expression of public opinion and reflects extremely well a priority in the minds of Canadians from sea to sea to sea. It is one that the government ought to take very seriously and respect, because what we are talking about here, as preceding speakers have already said, is spaces for future generations and a policy decision that has to be made now while it is possible to make it. There are certain continents where this kind of implementation of 12 per cent of a land mass cannot be made any longer. In Canada we still have that opportunity, and we hope that there is enough enlightenment on the government side and that no one will have the talking out of this motion on June 17, 1991, on his or her conscience.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to speak to a veiy important motion presented by the hon. member for Skeena who is to be commended for having tabled this motion in the House. This motion is useful because it gives us an opportunity to address one of the goals we as a government have included in the Green Plan. Among the Plan's various objectives, Section III mentions the target of preserving 12 per cent of our natural heritage by the year 2000. In fact, the hon. member for Davenport mentioned the budget for this project which totals $175 million. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 1991 budget sets out a plan for economic recovery, a strong solid recovery that would not only put the recession behind us but lead us forward to continuing growth and renewed prosperity. The plan demands that Canadians work more effectively in a partnership for prosperity.
For decades, the federal government has provided large and growing financial support to the provinces. This year alone total federal transfers, including both cash and tax transfers, will reach almost $37 billion. Just the cash portion of the transfers accounts for one-fifth of all federal program spending. These transfers are simply too large to exempt from the expenditure re-

Government Orders
straint program. The deficit is a national program problem and it demands a national solution.
Most importantly, it should be understood that in slowing growth of transfer payments, the federal government is seeking to encourage all levels of government to realistically live within their means, just as the federal government is doing with its other programs.
Both levels of government will benefit from the budget's initiatives, which will translate into lower interest rates, economic recovery and enhance long-term economic competitiveness. It is therefore in the interests of both levels of government to co-operate.
It should be noted that the 1991 budget had no effect on transfers in the current fiscal year. The 1991-92 transfers were made on the basis of the budget a year ago in February, 1990, which provinces had already factored into their planning.
What this year's budget did was to announce that the two-year expenditure management measures affecting transfers that were put in place in February, 1990 will be extended, unchanged, for a further three years to 1994-95. This gives more than a year's notice to provinces and reasonable time to adjust.
Federal transfers to provincial governments account for 23 per cent of our program spending. They will again total over $37 billion.
They are simply too large to be exempted from efforts to control our deficit. In 1989, Ottawa moved timidly to reduce the growth of federal transfers for Established Program Financing by reducing it to 1 per cent or $200 million beginning in 1990-91. In hindsight, this was far too little.
In cash and tax equivalents, Ottawa pours $20 billion a year into that one program, presumably to support provincial financing of medicare and post-secondary education. Since the transfers are in the form of unconditional block grants, some of the funds may find their way into provincial places unrelated to health and education.
What is far more grating to federal budget makers wrestling with the huge fiscal and political dilemma is the seeming disregard of some provinces for spending money generally, and federal transfer funds in particular.
Some provinces, such as Alberta and Saskatchewan, have come close to matching the federal level of program spending restraint. But Ontario, our richest province and the one largely fueling our inflationary situation, has been increasing its spending over 10 per cent a year and that simply is not fair.
Since taking office in 1984, federal program spending has been held to an average annual increase of 3.7 per cent a year. By comparison, spending by the provincial governments increased on average by 7.2 per cent each year over the same period. Annual provincial spending has ranged from over 10 per cent in one province-and into that you can read Ontario-to just about 3 per cent in some western provinces. Despite requests to the provinces to help out in deficit reduction, federal transfers have continued to increase at an annual rate of 6.5 per cent, nearly twice the rate of spending Ottawa has allowed itself.
The message that was communicated to the finance minister during the period leading up to the budget was that Canadians expect government to bear its share of restraint. In a budget that is tough on governments at all levels, the finance minister has declared war on the deficit. The budget included an array of measures to control government spending, including the passing of a law to place a ceiling on how much politicians can spend; another measure to apply the GST to the deficit instead of new programs, and the establishment of inflation targets, so that the public understands what price stability means.
Also, by saying the deficit is a national problem which needs a national solution, the finance minister is not asking more of the provinces than it is doing itself. Federal and provincial governments have to start co-operating and stop pointing fingers.
The message in the budget is that governments must stop spending more than Canadians can afford. Given the importance of deficit reduction, and as the largest single employer in Canada, the government is introducing a three-year program of wage restraint in the federal Public Service. In taking this step, the government wishes to stress that federal employees are not being singled out for restraint. All Canadians face difficulty during the present period. Every one of us knows individuals who have lost their jobs or are now on lay-off.

In the current situation, the government must also cut back. Pay restraint is particularly important at the provincial and the municipal levels, including education and health services.

speechtext:
Wage and salaries in these sectors account for 45 per cent of all expenditures. Wage settlements in these sectors have been running ahead of inflation and our ability to pay. Some provinces already have introduced programs in their budgets to limit the pay increases for their provinces. My colleague reminds me that Ontario was negligent in its recent budget by not doing that.
This government will introduce unprecedented legislation this year to strictly limit spending increases in all federal programs. A new law will ensure Canadians that higher taxes cannot be used to pay for additional spending. Canadians do not want taxes to pay for more spending. They are telling governments to keep spending under control. Based on comments received from constituents, many Canadians do not believe that government can control its spending. I feel legislative controls are a way to instil confidence that Ottawa will maintain a firm control on its budget.
This law will bring in a major change in the way government manages its spending. New programs will have to be funded within the total legislative ceiling. The government will not be able to raise taxes to pay for new programs. Legal limits on program spending will be imposed for five years. With few exceptions, program spending growth will be limited to 3 per cent a year. This 3 per cent ceiling on spending growth is based on savings anticipated for specific cuts already announced in the budget so that no further cuts will be needed to meet these legislative targets.
Another important budget announcement was the establishment of the Debt Service Reduction Fund which responds directly to public concerns that revenues from the GST could be used to fund new spending rather than reducing the deficit. All GST revenues will go into the new fund and be used exclusively for lowering the deficit and bringing the public debt under control.
According to the budget documents, the GST will produce $16.4 billion for the government in the next fiscal year and $18.3 billion in the following year. It is expected to climb substantially in 1992-93 because of the
Government Orders
one time cost associated with moving from the old manufacturers' sales tax, that the parties on the opposite side wanted to keep in place and that the GST replaced.
One time costs include the transitional grant to small businesses. Canadian businesses will receive approximately $2.3 billion to offset the federal sales tax that existed in their inventories. The entire $16.4 billion will be put forward to the annual $42 billion cost of servicing the debt in the current fiscal year. The remainder will come from general revenues.
Again, one message communicated from local correspondents is the concern that the revenues from GST might be used to finance new spending programs instead of to help reduce the deficit. But the decision to legislate spending limits and the decision to earmark all the GST revenues for deficit reduction should ease concerns about wasting that money on new programs.
In a bold move aimed at pulling down Canada's inflation rate to a 20-year low and one of the lowest in the industrial world, the federal government and the Bank of Canada have announced targets designed to reduce inflation to 2 per cent by 1995.
The government said the target is to get the year over year increase in the Consumer Price Index down to 3 per cent by the end of 1992, 2.5 per cent by the middle of 1994 and 2 per cent by the end of 1995.
In the budget the message was that inflation targets are one of the key steps on the path to price stability. They should give Canadian consumers, Canadian business, labour and investors a better understanding of how quickly price stability can and will be achieved. This should reduce the resistance to lowering inflation thus bringing the benefits more quickly and more easily.
There is no denying the direct link between inflation and interest rates. Our economic history proves it. During the 1950s and 1960s when inflation was low, averaging less than 3 per cent a year, interest rates were low. When inflation surged in the 1970s interest rates soared also. Unless Canadians are told what price stability means and what the result is likely to be, they will inevitably be reluctant to begin adjusting their behaviour accordingly. But if the country was presented with a target of 2.5 per cent for two years from now, Canadian investors, business managers, consumers and employees can begin planning now.

Government Orders
If Canada were to abandon now the objectives of price stability and lower inflation the country would be locking itself into an inflationary future, and would probably isolate itself as a high inflation country in a low inflation world. Even if the rest of the world were not moving towards low inflation economies, Canada could and should adopt price stability as an independent objective.
If we were to target, as a nation, 6 per cent as our target inflation rate, a $100 purchase 12 years from today would cost $200. It would double in price in 12 years, and 12 years after that, it would cost $400.
If we were to achieve a 3 per cent inflation target, the $100 good today would take 24 years to reach a price of $200. Therein lies the importance of inflation targets. If we do not start on it today, the question that will be talked about in this House 25 years today will be: Why have prices quadrupled in Canada but maybe in the United States or in the rest of the world, they have only doubled? If we do not do that, certainly this country will be in major difficulty.
Inflation also creates real problems for wage negotiations. Employers and employees often have quite different expectations of inflation, and this makes it harder to agree on a fair settlement. It is not surprising then that periods of high inflation in Canada are matched by an increase in days of work lost due to strikes.
Let us review an example of the impact of inflation and wages on a settlement. A company expects its revenues will only increase 3 per cent next year. If it raises prices any higher, it may lose sales to lower price competition, so it offers its workers a 3 per cent wage increase.
The workers are sitting back and they expect that the consumer inflation will be 5 per cent. In fairness, they want at least this amount so they can maintain their standard of living. This puts the company between a rock and a hard place. If it gives the 5 per cent wage hike, it could become less profitable and even go out of business. If it does not give the workers what they expect, the result could be a strike which could then mean lost sales and lay-offs.
That is an example of why nobody is a winner with high inflation. It should be acknowledged that there are numerous problems with setting targets. Using the Consumer Price Index as an indicator of inflation is certainly open for debate. There are unexpected price shocks such as an oil price explosion and that could throw inflation off the target set by the government and the Bank of Canada. These are weak reasons for avoiding explicit inflationary and monetary policy objectives.
If we want this economy to be lasting, we need to do a better job of fighting inflation pressures. Our national goal must not be just to control inflation, but to get it down dramatically and then keep it down. In other words, our goal must be to achieve price stability.
The economic and social benefits of price stability are enormous. Lower interest rates are one example of one benefit in achieving that stability. Price stability is vital for Canadian consumers and Canadian companies to compete and succeed in today's global workplace.
I would like to conclude with a statement that a former British Prime Minister of the Labour Party gave in September 1976. James Callaghan said:
We used to think you could just spend your way out of a recession, and increase employment, by cutting taxes and boosting government spending. I tell you in all candour that option no longer exists, and in so far as it ever did exist, it worked by injecting inflation into the economy. And each time that happened, the average level of unemployment has risen. Higher inflation, followed by higher unemployment. That is the history of the last 20 years.
I close with those comments from the Labour Party back in 1976. Before I sit down, I move:
That this question be now put.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could speak on this bill for several hours, and I am going to find it very difficult to restrict myself to the 20 minutes I
have.
In the limited time I have, I want to talk about two or three significant things that this bill does. First of all, I want to talk about the whole question of debt because the Conservative approach to debt and deficit reduction is to off-load that responsibility on to other levels of government. They have not curtailed their own expenditures, they have simply said: "We will not honour historic agreements in Canada for transfer of payments."

June 17, 1991

The Conservatives make a lot about the question of the Ontario deficit, but they do not say that $3 billion of that deficit is because of loss of revenue from the federal government.
The UI increases in Bill C-20 amount to $150 per worker for a worker who is earning only $27,000 a year. That has a significant impact. It is a tax increase on working people, particularly affecting those on low incomes or fixed incomes. It is also a tax increase on small business. Small business has difficulty meeting its increased costs under UIC.
In the meantime, the federal government has withdrawn from its historic responsibility in unemployment insurance.
I will just talk briefly about the effects this is having on my own local community of Surrey. What does this mean? The UIC changes mean that the Surrey municipalities must raise $300,000 more for unemployment insurance premiums this year. That means that the taxes on people's homes have to be raised, and that certainly is not fair to Surrey residents. It means that the school board has to take $1 million out of educational dollars and put it into unemployment insurance that has been the responsibility of the federal government. What does that mean? It means they have had to cut teachers. They have had to cut back on special programs to assist children with learning disabilities. That is not fair to my local community.
What about the Surrey Memorial Hospital? The cutbacks to UIC mean that they have to come up with $350,000 more for UIC premiums. We already have had long waiting lists at the Memorial Hospital. These are now going to get longer because staff have had to be cut and services have had to be reduced. So it has a health impact on people at the local level, and communities like Surrey are forced to bear the brunt.
All the federal government has done is take its responsibility and put it down on the local taxpayer and the local government. Because of its fiscal mismanagement and its fiscal incompetence, it has said: "We can no longer deal with it, we are just going to throw the whole mess to the local government and hope that they or the provinces can."
The curtailment of the Canada Assistance Plan for the three big provinces simply means that those provinces either have to slash money for child welfare, child
Government Orders
protection, services to single parents who are on welfare, or they have to pick up the cost.
I think this whole way that the federal government has decided to deal with its deficit problem is going to result in not only a curtailment of services right across the country, but in extreme difficulties at the local level.
I want to spend most of my time talking about health care because in Canada health care has been a source of national pride. It is one of the areas and one of the fundamental ways that Canadians define Canada, particularly as distinct from the United States.
In Canada there are no financial barriers to people seeking medical treatment. The system is relatively efficient and is widely supported. Canadians move within Canada on business, holidays and to seek employment with the knowledge that similar health care standards are met in all provinces and territories. This promotes a national identity and national unity.
Any changes that would result in the erosion of our national programs are not supported by the Canadian public, but what we have seen is a consistent attack on national medicare. This is not a recent attack. This did not start in 1984. This started under the previous Liberal government in 1975.
It put a ceiling on its transfer of payments to the provinces for medicare, the same as the Tories have done now. It arbitrarily put a ceiling on the transfer payments. Then in 1977 it forced the provinces into block funding. The only party who opposed block funding was the New Democratic Party.
In 1982 the Liberals brought in legislation to do away with the revenue guarantee which cost the provinces $4 billion over the next five years and loss of income for medicare. Under the Liberals the share of federal costs or expenditures for medicare went from 50 per cent to 43 per cent and of course, under the Tories it has gone from 43 per cent down to 37 per cent, with projections now in the last week coming out to say that by the end of the five years it will be down to 32 per cent.
The Liberals set the platform. They set the means and the agenda for the attack on medicare, and of course, the Tories were excellent learners. They were even more than good. They learned very quickly and the first thing they did was to start limiting the projected increases under established programs.

Government Orders
Let's look at what the Established Program Financing was. It was based on the increase in gross domestic productivity. In other words, if the economy went up, the transfers went up. If the economy did not expand, the transfers did not expand. In spite of the fact that there was an expanding economy the Tories brought in arbitrary and unilateral legislation to limit transfer payments.
In 1986 when it was brought in, it was to be 2 per cent less than the GDP. In 1989 it was raised to 3 per cent. Last year in 1990 the government froze it for two years and now in this bill it is freezing it for a total of five years. The loss of revenue to the provinces in terms of what they should have received and anticipated receiving for medicare is dramatic.
Provinces like my home province of British Columbia will receive $3.5 billion less for medicare by 1995. Ontario will receive $10.58 billion less.
By the year 2000 there will have been $62 billion taken out of medicare by this federal government. That is not counting the money that was taken out by the Liberals that also affected the base line and has been estimated to probably be in the neighbourhood of $1 to $1.2 billion a year.
What we have is a dramatic erosion of medicare by the federal government. These estimations on the loss of revenue for the provinces have been repeatedly documented by organizations like the National Council on Welfare. The Parliamentary Library has documented it as has the Association of Universities and Colleges. Yet the government pretends that it is not so.
By 1995-1996 there will be no more cash payments to Quebec, and a few years after that to any other province. This means that we will no longer have a national medicare program that can be enforced. We will be going into an Americanized system.
We should be very careful about how we approach this. If you look at the American system, it spends 10.63 per cent of its GNP on health care compared to Canada at 8.62 per cent. They say down there that 37 million people have no health insurance, and another 20 million have inadequate health insurance. That is what is going to happen if we proceed down the path set by this government for national medicare.
I want to spend a few minutes looking at the impact of the cuts on medicare first of all and what the cuts in the transfer payments mean at the service delivery level. The impact is dramatically different on the wealthy provinces as opposed to the poorer provinces. The wealthy provinces still have some financial capability to absorb some of the fiscal cuts from the federal government without dramatic reduction of services. That is not true in the weaker provinces.
In provinces such as Newfoundland, 10 per cent of the nursing staff had to be laid off because of the reduction in money from the federal government. They had no choice. That is a province that is already spending 9 per cent of its GNP on health care. Prince Edward Island is spending 9 per cent. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are spending 7.5 per cent. They are already spending a large percentage of their GNP on health care, much more than the wealthier provinces, which the minister must know. Ontario spends only 5.5 per cent of its GNP on health care. Alberta spends 5.8 per cent, and B.C. spends 6 per cent.
The provinces that are in the weakest financial shape and are already putting out the highest percentage of their GNP on health care have no alternative but to slash medical services in their provinces and close hospitals.

Just looking at the whole issue of the cutbacks, I think the government has tried to play tricks with the Canadian public. There was a formula in place that said there would be an increase in payments, and all the government has done is they have said: "We are not going to honour that formula; we are not going to honour the formula that had been agreed to, and we are not going to pass on the increases".
It is the same as if you had a wage contract that called for percentage increases over the next several years, and one day the employer came along and said: "We are not going to honour it".
In the workers' pockets there is that much less money, and they can play around all they want but in the provinces' pockets there is going to be $62.4 billion less by the year 2000. That is going to have a tremendous impact on our health care in this country.
I have talked briefly about the impact on the ability of the provinces to deliver health care services. There is a whole range of things that the provinces have started to do. They have cut back on things like eye examinations, on general health examinations; they have laid off staff; they have closed hospitals; they have also started to talk about the introduction of user fees and extra billing. In fact Quebec has a bill before its assembly to do just that for hospital emergency wards.
There have been many finance ministers in the provinces who are starting to say: "Look if you are not going to give us the money, if you are going to continue to cut back on our anticipated transfer payments, then we want the ability to manage our health care systems as we see fit".
The minister of health in this House last week confirmed that by 1996-97 Quebec will be able to manage its health care system as it sees fit because he will no longer be in a position to enforce standards.
This issue of national standards is one with which the government is trying to play games. It says that it can cut back the money and still insist that the provinces meet national standards. These are the standards that Canadians have learned to accept in our health care: universality, accessibility, non-profit administration, comprehensiveness, portability. Once the federal government's ability to enforce these standards on a national basis is lost, what we will have is not a national medicare program, but we will have 12 different jurisdictions all with 12 different sets of standards and 12 different goals,

Government Orders
including such things as the introduction of user fees and extra billing.
The federal government is saying that it does not believe this is going to happen, that it can cut the dollars and still insist on the provinces meeting its standards.
I think that is a little bit naive on the federal government's part. This bill says that it will attach other transfer payments. I say to the federal government that at this point in time, in the sensitivity of our relationships across Canada, it is inconceivable that either politically or legally it can sustain the position that it will be able to attach the kinds of dollars from other programs that it is cutting if it is not transferring cash payments under medicare.
The Canadian Council on Welfare I think summed that up clearly in a report that it released last year. It says: "Under the budget proposal, Ottawa apparently intends to withhold federal payments other than payments for health care from the provinces and territories which do not respect the principles of the Canada Health Act once cash portions of EPF run out."
The National Council on Welfare cannot imagine the provinces and territories letting this proposal go unchallenged. The delivery of health care services is within provincial jurisdiction under the Constitution. It is only the federal spending power that allows the federal involvement in this area. It is difficult to imagine how Ottawa could continue to maintain its presence once the money for medicare dries up.
In any event, it is obvious that the final word on the proposed legislation will come from the Supreme Court of Canada rather than the Parliament. We would much prefer to see the federal government reconsider its course of action and make such legislation unnecessary.
One of the things that we have already found out is that the province of British Columbia, joined by other provinces, has initiated court action when the federal government tried to curtail Canada Assistance Plan payments. That is where the federal government simply had to give a year's notice and it failed to do so.
So I do not see how, in a time when national unity is very, very fragile in this country, when we need the co-operation and the goodwill of all of these provinces, how the federal government can, on the one hand, say it is going to cut the money that it is transferring, but it is going to continue to tty to tell the provinces what they can do in an area that it does not have any constitutional authority in.
I think we have already seen the indication from the provinces-

Mr. Speaker, I do not rise on debate. There was an inaccuracy when the member said that we tell the provinces- and we will tell the provinces-what to do. He is wrong. They have all the flexibility even to put the user fee on if they want.
In other words, I want to correct my friend and say that we do not have the power to tell the provinces what they should do. The provinces have all that flexibility.

Again, the minister is attempting to mislead Canadians. It is true that technically you cannot order them what to do, but you can impose a financial penalty on them to the point that it becomes impossible for them to do it.
For every dollar they would save or collect by doing something like putting in user fees or extra billing, you take $1 away from them. It is by financial incentive that you force them to do things or not to do things.
It is true, they can commit suicide. They can go ahead and try to introduce user fees. You would simply take the money back. It is technically true that you cannot legislate. There are other sections in the Canada Health Act which indicate that you could make it mandatory. You could impose other penalties on a province over and above the dollar for dollar take-back of money.
It is true that the federal government does have other powers under the Canada Health Act to enforce the standards that it wants the provinces to follow. I notice that my time is up.

Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, I would like to correct all the inaccuracies in what my friend has said, but I will not have enough time in 10 minutes.
I will just make a short comment and ask questions of my friend. My comment is that Canadians, as it is quite obvious, know that the poor provinces get more money from the federal level than the rich provinces, and he knows that very well. It is based on a per capita basis.
For example, Newfoundland receives about $2,500 a year per person while there is about $965 per person for Ontario. In other words, we treat the poor provinces differently in light of the capacity they have to pay for what is considered the best health system in the world.
My friend knows that very well. He looked, as I did, last weekend at what was said in the United States about the Canada Health Act. It did not say that it will not be good tomorrow. It said: "It is the best in the world today." We have had it for seven years, which means that we did something for it.
The growth in the poor provinces increased faster than in the rich provinces. It is 4 per cent, as opposed to 3 per cent. I could continue with figures for a while, but I want to give my friend a chance to explain to me something he said about the fact that we pay 38 per cent and the provinces pay an average of 62 per cent rather than 50-50 in terms of the cost of the health care system in the country.
I would like my friend to explain to me exactly how and why it has been changed. Maybe I am wrong, but he seemed to say that it was changed by the former government in 1977. How was it before and why is it the way it is today?

Mr. Speaker, I would be delighted to respond to the minister's questions.
First of all, let us make no mistake. All you had to do was watch the last several provincial budgets to know that the poor provinces had no alternative but to dramatically slash their health care services because of the cutbacks in EPF payments. They anticipated receiving payments from the federal government but they did not receive them.
There is no way you can wiggle around and use words. There is $62.4 billion less going into our health care system under your government by the year 2000.
Government Orders
You are correct that the erosion of medicare started under the Liberals. Prior to 1975 it was a 50-50 program. It was shared 50 per cent by the provinces and 50 per cent by the federal government. Then there was a cap put on the federal government's share unilaterally.
As a result of that the EPF was put in place. It was a block funding mechanism which limited the amount of money the federal government would transfer. The minister knows this very well. I am sure he is probably even more familiar with it than I am. It limited the amount of money the federal government would transfer to the provinces by a formula based on expenditures in the previous years, the increase in population and the growth in GNP or GDP.
That formula has been in place except for the time it was tinkered with by the Liberals in the early 1980s and has been totally demolished by the minister's government starting in 1986. The formula was there to transfer moneys to provinces based on growth in the economy. The economy grew and the federal government unilaterally, without consultation and without any concern about the impact that would have on the ability of provinces to deliver health care, changed the formula. Initially it went to 2 per cent less than GDP, 3 per cent less than GDP and then frozen for two years and now frozen for five years.
I am sure next Wednesday, when the minister meets with his counterparts from the provincial health ministries, they will all say to you that the actions of this government have severely hurt their ability to deliver effective, efficient and accessible health care in their provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform my friend that his explanation of the way it worked in 1977 is not exactly correct.
It is not my role to explain what a former government did, but it was not the federal government that decided. It decided to change the formula because it was requested by the provinces. They wanted more flexibility. They wanted to determine exactly what type of care they would provide to their constituents.
In other words, if a province makes the decision to pay the ambulance from Vancouver to the hospital, it can do that. It is within its flexibility. It is not what we consider, as agreed by the provinces, a medical service given by a

Government Orders
doctor or a hospital and therefore it could be done by the provinces but the provinces will pay alone.
We transfer two tax points which were used by Quebec, in Ontario to a lesser extent, and in other provinces. In other words, when you say 38 per cent, you should tell Canadians that it was requested by the provinces because they wanted to manage their own systems. They asked for more flexibility. We do not have the right, as we do for the social services, to ask for 50-50. It is quite different and it has to be explained because it is the reason we have good service. We have big principles. Services have to be provided by doctors or in a hospital. They are the only constraints. The provinces can do what they want. It is quite different.

I would like to congratulate the minister for being in the House while this important debate is going on. We do not normally have the opportunity to get into a discussion with the ministers on these kinds of issues.
On the whole question about the changes in the formula and the flexibility under block funding, it did allow the provinces more flexibility but they requested it based on the fact that they had a formula in place which they thought guaranteed them moneys in the future. They thought, mistakenly, that we would accept this idea of better management and more flexibility of our health care dollars on the understanding that we know now, next year, five years from now and ten years from now what the transfers we will receive from the provinces will be. That was what the EPF was all about.
They took on the role of managing the health care dollar better. They took on the role of flexibility and then they were totally double crossed on the formula because both the Liberals and the Tories, particularly the Tories since 1986, have unilaterally scrapped the formula. That is what has happened with health care in Canada.
The provinces bought into it on the basis that they had a formula that would give them a guarantee. All of a sudden, that guarantee has been worth absolutely nothing.

Mr. Speaker, my question to my hon. colleague has to do with unemployment insurance. He has spoken about the increases both to the employer and the employee.
Under Bill C-21, a bill that was passed by this House and sent to the Senate, we would be looking at longer hours to qualify for unemployment. If I remember correctly, my hon. colleague did not agree that we should make it longer hours to qualify.
It was passed by the House and went to the Senate. The Senate did not approve it. Was the hon. member in agreement with not extending the hours and therefore costing both the employer and the employee additional funds? Does he feel that unemployment is a way of life, and not an interim measure when people are unemployed?

Mr. Speaker, if we get many more Tory governments, unemployment insurance is going to be a way of life for people if the way of life is not welfare. We have seen that dramatically in the last year or two. That is a way of life.
I did not agree nor did my party agree with the cutbacks in the UIC plan whereby the people had to work longer for less benefits.
Furthermore, we did not agree with the fact that the federal government again unilaterally pulled out of its historic responsibility to contribute to the unemployment insurance fund. It simply dumped it on to the employees and the employers, which hurt small business, municipalities, hospitals and school boards in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to debate today Bill C-20, an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in Parliament on February 26 of this year.
What is it really? This bill covers a lot of issues that will adversely affect Canadians, but there is one issue on which I would like to focus in light of my responsibility as critic for health and welfare.
Before I get to that, I would just like to indicate for the record that I recognize that this bill will address amendments to the Parliament of Canada Act, Public Utilities Income Tkx Transfer Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act.
June 17, 1991

In so far as the Unemployment Insurance Act is concerned-I was listening to some of the questions posed earlier by the government side-I would like to remind the House that during debate of Bill C-21, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the government made some assurances that though direct contributions would cease, the government would nevertheless be there to help finance the program in difficult times.
We are in difficult times. We are still in a recession. If I would quote Mr. Wilson as he indicated in his budget papers of 1989, he said: "The government will continue to contribute to the financing of the program in difficult economic times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums and prudent to allow deficits to build in the unemployment insurance account."
He went on to say on October 22, 1980 through a government senator: "The other place was assured that Mr. Wilson, during a lengthy crisis, would provide money to supplement the UI account."
That has not been seen and I would just like it to be recorded.
I would like to focus, as I said earlier, on what this bill is in so far as the future of medicare is concerned. For me, that future is the end of medicare.
Last night I was in my office past midnight sorting out sheets of newspaper clippings-and I have a lot here-set out before me. There were dozens of stories from newspapers all across this country along with reports, press releases and all the speeches of mine. They all said the same thing. Medicare is dying. Who holds the knife? The government does hold the knife. The knife is a bill like C-20 before us.
In my mind I retraced the steps of this death sentence on medicare from Bill C-69 through two budgets of this government and they rank with the bile of heartlessness. I thought, "How can the government expect to succeed if it destroys medicare?" How can the government expect to save this country if it destroys our sacred national institution?
I believe I found the answer in a reply from the Prime Minister during Question Period on June 4, and the records of Hansard can be checked. When the Prime Minister was questioned about reductions in transfer payments, his reply was a lifeline for a sinking government. His reply hinged on an ability to make the
Government Orders
Canadian people accept blame for the inabilities of his government. I quote his response:
We are all in favour of the most advanced and most modem medicare system and the most generous in the world. But we're going to have to find the money to pay for it. These funds come from taxpayers.
He went on to say that lower taxes and improved services, and I quote:
Both can't work together simultaneously.
The Prime Minister is trying to convince Canadians that they expect too much and pay too little. There must be a sacrifice and loss, payment for living a lifestyle beyond our means. As two elections will show, Canadians believed in the Conservative government's financial vision and that is sad because the Tory caucus trademark since coming into government has been a social policy by stealth. This is not an original analysis. This is an analysis done by Mr. Gratton Gray in an excellent article published recently in Policy Options.
In other words, this government has carefully disguised as sound fiscal management changes that serve to destroy our social system including medicare.
Recall 32 tax increases in six years. That has been phenomenal. Safety nets so low you fall further before reaching them. Children of poverty-over a million. Free trade, its debacle effect on loss of jobs. Now we are seeing cross-border shopping and hospitals barely able to cope, but everything is the fault of the Canadian public, so the Prime Minister would like us to believe; at the Canadian public have lived beyond their means and expected too much. Now is the time to pay for the misdeeds of decades.
I say it is untrue. There is nothing seriously flawed about our federal health care system. In fact it is one of the best and most efficient in the world. The minister of health earlier this morning during debate has alluded to that. If it is really as good as he said it is, then why is he trying to dismantle it? It does not make common sense.
I should say that the medicare system was recently lauded by the Comptroller-General of the United States who when speaking before a U.S. congressional committee said, and I would like to quote:
In 1987, Canada's per capita spending on insurance administration was one-fifth that of the United States. Canada spends less because its publicly financed, single-payer system eliminates the costs associated with marketing competitive health insurance policies, billing for and collecting premiums and evaluating risks.

Government Orders
