For physician services, Canada spent 34 per cent less per person in 1987 than did the United States. This difference is largely the result of Canada's controls on physician fees. In addition, the Canadian physicians have lower practice expenses for billing and malpractice premiums.
For hospital services, Canada spent 18 per cent less per person in 1987 than the United States.
The same Congressional Committee heard testimony from an American family with a young daughter whose illness was so expensive to treat that they could no longer find a company to insure them. This family was considering fleeing to Canada to become "health refugees". And we want to destroy our medical system, Mr. Speaker?
This is what happens when private insurance agencies control medicare. In the United States there are almost 1,500 insurance companies. The bureaucracy of dealing with these companies-for billing, for payments and communication-consumes much of the time of doctors and their staff.
The Canadian model is cost and people efficient, freeing our health care professionals to do the jobs they have been trained to do.
Yes, medicare is valued, and it is a right of Canadian citizenship, but it is more than that. Medicare is a necessity. It is a national necessity.
If your citizens are not healthy, then your country is not healthy. In the United States there are over 31 million people who have no health insurance and many more who are under-insured. Their lives are mired in fear for their own futures, afraid they will become ill, a fate which often destroys them financially.
Last week in Prince Edward Island the federal finance minister shrugged his shoulders when his provincial counterpart requested more money for services. I would like to quote. "We are doing the best we can", were the comforting words he gave them to take home to health care systems in crisis. "We simply cannot afford the type of escalation we have had in the past."
Well, I would like to put on record that the forthcoming report of the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare, which I believe will be tabled in Parliament
before the end of the week, shows the funding for national health care has been more or less stable since 1975 as a percentage of the gross national product. And the gross national product ought to be looked at by Canadians as a measure of our ability to pay. So we must be careful when this government tries to scare Canadians and say we have over-spent.
Sure, we need reforms, but the way to reform is not to kill medicare. The way to treat a patient is not to kill the patient but to truly provide the necessary remedies of genuine reforms.
In real dollars the cost of transfers per capita in 1978-79 was $705 while today the amount is $805. In another three years that figure will drop to $689, according to the National Council on Welfare.
A much more sobering thought is the Council's prediction that transfer payments will stop altogether by the year 2010. That year is really within clear reality, it is soon to come. Others say that is a generous timetable, giving the system fewer years to crash. Meanwhile, if the transfer payment schedule continues as now is proposed by this government, the federal government will save at least $97.6 billion in the next nine years. When we speak of saving $97.6 billion, it sounds terrific.
But the government is not telling us that this is not a true saving for Canadians. The load of this expense will be transferred to the backs of the provinces. Who will pay the taxes? The Canadian people will.
Mr. Speaker, this is political trickery in a real sense. This money will need to be replaced by the provinces if they are to ensure that the quality of health care will be there.
The government accuses the opposition of scaremon-gering when we say the government is driving Canada towards a two-tier health care system. Those who are watching the government see bills like C-69 now law, and C-20, the bill before us. They see transfer payments being cut and frozen, and what are they to believe? They see this everywhere in newspaper reports. Should we shut our eyes and pretend nothing is wrong? Should we pretend that our hospitals are not closing beds and that our nurses and doctors are not stressed to the limit; that there are not queues for every type of surgery, including surgery in life threatening situations?
June 17, 1991

Funding for Established Program Financing must increase at the same rate as the Gross National Product, not GNP minus 3 per cent. It is of little help to many provinces, particularly the have-not provinces if tax points are increased while cash transfers diminish. The government does not deny that this is happening, but what it is continuing to deny is that the reality will happen, that medicare will die. I would like to shake this government to come to consciousness to save our sacred Canadian institution.
Listen to one finance minister from Prince Edward Island again. I find it "excellent" to discuss the gloomy situation for medicare. "Every time the federal government cuts money to the provinces it puts us in a bind."
Or take the case of New Brunswick's finance minister, and I quote:
Federal funding is clearly on the decline and every indication is it's going to continue in that direction. We're having considerable difficulty continuing to live up to the standards required under the Canada Health Act.
Mr. Speaker, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland already spend 11 per cent of their Gross Domestic Product on health care and higher education, even when receiving equalization payments. This compares to six per cent for Ontario, a have province. How can these have-not provinces be expected to find more money to make up for federal government lapses, I ask?
Without enough money, how can the Canada Health Act be maintained?
In the last federal budget, the government promised to introduce legislation to protect national standards. I thought: well, at least the government is thinking of protecting medicare. In keeping its promise, the government has introduced Bill C-20. Now this is a hollow promise because why should we believe that Bill C-20 will protect medicare? I tell you, when you look at Bill C-20 you will see and recognize the application of financial penalties under the Canada Health Act, to other federal payments to provinces in the event of a breach by a province of the national health standards set out in the Canada Health Act. What it is telling us is that it will even penalize other programs. It will penalize such programs as the equalization payments, territorial financing, grants in lieu of taxes, public utilities income tax transfers, statutory subsidies, the Canada Assistance Plan, the Crop Insurance contributions, the miscellaneous Health and Welfare transfers, the Young Offenders Services, Justice transfers and transportation transfers.
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, at least over a dozen areas will be even more adversely affected with this Bill C-20. Who really believes the government anymore? They are just buying time. They are cutting away at our social safety net, piece by piece, at their leisure. If the government truly believes in health care, truly believes in protecting medicare, we already have the leverage in the Canada Health Act of today. All it has to do is provide that leverage, that financial contribution that ought to be adequate for its needs. That would be the guideline that ought to be the criterion that Canadians will accept.
Medicare is under the knife and so too is funding for education. The Canada Assistance Plan, unemployment insurance benefits and tax points in return for cash transfers are of little help to the have-not provinces.
In the remaining time I would like to indicate that every day our health care is being whittled away and, to believe the words of the government, "is a luxury" I and other Canadians can afford. Trust is a dear commodity these days, especially trust in light of the government's past actions.
I am an opposition member. This kind of distrust of the government perhaps is expected of me. But let me say that because we are in opposition does not mean that we are opposing this only because we are in opposition. We are opposing this bill because we are reflecting the sentiments of Canadians, as expressed by the National Council on Welfare in its recent publication Danger Looming. Because of time, I cannot quote at length, but the National Council on Welfare is truly concerned.
Cuts are not only hurting medicare. They are directly affecting our children. The situation is so bad that last week, while participating in the largest day care conference in Canada, the Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association issued a press release indicating that it calls on the federal government to remove the cap on the Canadian Assistance Program.
In conclusion, I would like to say that Bill C-20 must be defeated. The government must negotiate with the provinces and restore adequate funding for medicare. The government already has the leverage to protect the Canada Health Act. Our medicare system has been enshrined as a Canadian institution to guarantee that all Canadians, irrespective of income, and particularly the poor, have access to health services. It must protect Canadians when they become ill from becoming poor or poorer.

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
I submit that these are difficult times in our country. The forces of disunity are all around us. Let medicare be the national glue that maintains us as Canadians from coast to coast to coast.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great care and attention to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North. I have a question for him.
Where can I get one of these wonderful credit cards that the Liberals have, where you can spend and spend and spend and the interest accumulates and the interest accumulates, but you never have to pay the bill?
My hon. friend talks about scare tactics with respect to medicare. I remember 1988,1 remember the scare tactics that terrorized senior citizens in my area, about how medicare was going to be destroyed by the free trade agreement. Now what is happening? The Americans are coming up here to study our medicare system because it is so good. Why is it good? It is good because we can pay for it.
This debate is about whether or not we are going to have medicare in the future. If the spending of this government had continued in the uncontrolled manner of its predecessor which left office with a $38 billion deficit, today it would be $99 billion.
My hon. friend talks about unemployment insurance. He decries the increase in unemployment insurance. My understanding of an insurance program is that the premiums are supposed to pay for the program, so that if the pay-out goes up, so do the premiums. In the case of this one there is no question. With Bill C-21, it was the intent of the government to set the premium for three years, but we have had a recession in this country. We all know we have had a recession in this country that has been milder than it would have been had it not been for the measures implemented by this government.
The fact of the matter is the government has a responsibility to manage the UI account. If there had been no change in those premiums, we would be looking at a $6 billion deficit in unemployment insurance by the
end of 1992. That is unacceptable. That would be irresponsible on the part of the government. Even with an increase to $280 we are going to be looking at a $500 million deficit which will be made up by the government, as the government committed itself to doing when it introduced Bill C-21 a year or so ago. The truth of the matter is that the rate increase will coincide with the recovery so that the impact will not be as great as my hon. friend suggests.
Does my hon. friend not think it incumbent upon government to spend within its resources or does he believe the way to prosperity in the future is to allow deficits to accumulate, accumulate, accumulate?

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to respond to those comments.
Do we believe that we have to continue to spend endlessly? No. Do we believe that we should spend efficiently for the health care system? I said yes. The premise to the question that he makes is expenditure for medicare. That is the topic before us.
Let me go to his question on the unemployment insurance for a moment. Perhaps the member was not listening quite carefully to what I said on that point. The former finance minister Mr. Wilson, indicated in 1989 with the support of the government and Senate in 1990, and I quote again:"The government will continue to contribute to the financing of the program in difficult times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums and prudent to allow deficits to build in the unemployment account." Mr. Wilson said again in 1990 through Senator Simard: "Money will be made available to supplement the unemployment insurance account so that the premiums paid by the employers and the employees are not unduly high."
The former finance minister himself recognized that fact. This member refuses to recognize the proclamation of his own former finance minister.
I am really at a loss as to the logic of this government.
I believe premiums would increase if there were a necessity for the Unemployment insurance program benefits to increase, but what is lacking, and he fails to
June 17, 1991

recognize this, is the support from government. The unemployment insurance program is not an ordinary, private insurance program in the country, it is a government program administered by the government and the government must continue to be responsible and play its role if it is going to put its money where its mouth is.
We care about the deficit, and of course we are worried about the deficit, but we are as worried if not more worried about the deficit of lives as a consequence of the dismantling of our medicare system.
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member from Winnipeg North.
Pretty tough to listen to was it not?

No, I think it was an excellent speech. I think he had a lot of good comments. It is too bad that the members on the other side of the House would not put some of them into effect.
It is certainly true what he says about the federal government just trying to pass on part of the debt that it has created.
Now the hon. member discussed how he sees the reduction in transfer payments will affect the health system. I wonder if he would take a few minutes and briefly outline how he sees the reduction in these payments affecting the education system. I know in my own province of Prince Edward Island that students now are or will be faced next year with tuition increases of 15 per cent. The student loan programs have not increased since 1984. There is now a 3 per cent fee on student loans, plus the students are feeling the effects of the GST. They even have to pay the GST on books.
I know that in my riding office I have many students coming and looking for summer jobs, jobs they cannot get because of policies that this government has followed which have created a recession in this country.
I would like to hear the hon. member give his thoughts as to how he sees our education system being affected.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for her excellent question. To indicate for the record before I go to her question, the western provinces
Government Orders
alone stands to suffer $8.5 billion over the next three years as a consequence of cuts in transfer payments.
Before I touch on the matter of education I should say I was prefacing my earlier comment on the physical and mental health of Canadians that stand to suffer as a consequence of cuts to health care funding. My colleague has identified a health equally important and that is the educational health of Canadians. No doubt in Manitoba alone tuition fees have been increased as a consequence. Scholarship programs have become fewer and universities are truly under the crunch as a consequence of cuts to transfer payments.
The end result will be the lack of necessary economic provisions for the youth of our country. If we are to be truly competitive, as has been indicated in an excellent speech entitled "Do Canadians Really Want to Compete?", we have to be competitive. To cut transfer payments at this time and reduce necessary funding for education there is no doubt that the youth of our country, the strength of the future, the leaders of the future, will stand to suffer.
I beg of this government for that additional reason to withdraw this Bill C-20.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the opportunity to rise today and participate in the debate on Bill C-20, the act which will among other things freeze the per capita Established Programs Financing transfers, or EPF as it is known, and cut the Canada Assistance Plan, known as CAP, to the richer provinces thereby effectively crippling and possibly destroying our high standards of the education and medicare systems. At the very time when our neighbour is looking at our excellent medicare system and wishing to adopt it, this government wants to destroy it.
It is both my duty and privilege to reflect the views of my constituents in Parkdale-High Park and bring them to the floor of this House. They have elected me to express concerns on federal matters and I would like to begin by answering a question posed by one of my constituents. He asked me: "Jesse, don't you ever get frustrated in the House of Commons knowing that no matter what you say the government will bring in all its members and push through whatever legislation it wants to push through?"

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
He went on to remind me that there had been debate on the free trade agreement but all attempts by us to amend the bill were blocked. He reminded me that Canadians did not want the GST, but despite the debate in this House and hearings right across Canada, despite the thousands and thousands of petitions tabled in this House and in the other place, and despite the fact that many senators were listening and were ready to block the GST, this government appointed eight new senators and the will of the government over-rode the will of the people.
People in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe have been fighting that for 50 years, and what are we doing? We are going back to what the Soviet Union and the east European countries are throwing out in their political system.
Essentially my constituent was asking me why I just did not give up and let the government run roughshod over any opposition. He implied that Canada had a worse dictatorship than the one he left behind in eastern Europe. He thought it was worse because in eastern Europe under communism at least the people knew they had no hope of changing the minds of their leaders. He came to Canada thinking that the will of the people would be expressed by our parliamentary democracy and had found that it was not always so.
If the new Minister of Finance, a parliamentarian who has shown over the years he takes democracy seriously- I got to know him when we worked together on the transport committee and that is why I say that with all sincerity-takes a good look at this legislation which was drafted by the former minister and if he takes the time to listen to what we on this side of the House bring to this debate, he will do what is best for the majority of Canadians. He will do the honourable thing and withdraw Bill C-20.
There is still time to restore the fate of my constituent in our democracy. There is still time to ensure that high standards in health services and education which Canadians currently enjoy will be maintained.
This bill will reduce the amount of cash transfers to the provinces for post-secondary education and health. If the reductions continue as this government proposes, according to a statement issued by the National Council
of Welfare: "Federal cash payments to the provinces for medicare and higher education will end by 1997."
It also feels this is an estimate based on the best case scenario if the recession comes to an end soon. How can Canadians accept this? Our medicare and education systems are the envy of the world. Our standards of equality of service for all Canadians guarantee that a child bom into poverty has the same right to medical care and education as a child bom into wealth.
It means that every Canadian has the opportunity to live a healthy life and get a level of education which will enable them to have a good job and a good standard of living.
By reducing the transfer payments, this government is guaranteeing that children in the less affluent provinces will be stuck in a cycle of poverty. Their inability to afford an education will mean they get low-paying jobs or go on welfare. The reduction of federal money for medicare will mean the individual provinces control the health system.
They will inevitably lead to variations in the quality of service available to Canadians. Again, to quote the National Council of Welfare: "We could wind up with 12 vastly different provincial and territorial medicare systems." People in the poorer provinces would have to make do with health care services which are inferior to the services enjoyed by Canadians who happen to live in richer provinces.
Will this mean extra billing and user fees? I think it will. Will it mean that you better not have a premature baby in the maritimes because the incubators are not there? If you have a heart attack in Toronto, will there be a bed for you or not?
Scare tactics.

The hon. member says scare tactics. A friend of mine is now waiting for a bed in Toronto for a heart by-pass. If he does not get one soon, he will have to be flown to Saskatchewan and if he does not get an operation there, he will have to be flown to the United States, and that hon. member says: "Scare tactics."
Will Canadians in the north lose their airlifts to large hospitals? This could mean a lot of changes, but the change I am most afraid of is cash and carry medical care.
June 17, 1991

Canadians who have a post-secondary education and a job will be able to afford medical care. Canadians with grade 12 education or lower and the low paying jobs will not. Cash and carry medical care is not acceptable. I do not want to have to show my credit card before I can get into the emergency unit at St. Joseph's Health Centre in my constituency which is one of the best health care centres probably in the world, but it will not be if this government puts through this bill, Bill C-20.
I do not want to find that one of my constituents is denied medical attention because he or she is poor. I have many of these lining up in the food banks which are getting longer under this government. I want them to have first-rate health care when they need it.
Post-secondary education for the rich and grade 12 education for the poor is not acceptable. Education is an investment in our future, but tuition costs are so high already that it is a struggle for many families to send their sons and daughters to university and community college.
How will they be able to afford a higher education if the federal government cuts funding and tuition skyrockets? They will not. It is plain and simple.
Mr. Speaker, I know my time is up. I would just like to end by appealing to the government, please withdraw Bill C-20.
It being two o'clock, the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Mr. Speaker, last week the many chiefs of Canada chose their new national chief, Mr. Ovide Mercredi. We wish him the very best.
Yesterday, another important election was held.

The Federation des communautes francophones et aca-diennes du Canada, formely known as the FFHQ, elected Mr. Raymond Bisson as its new president. Mr. Bisson, the current president of the Societe franco-manitobaine, is becoming the leader of some one million francophones outside Quebec. He works really hard for francophones and is their best advocate, while recognizing Canada's other realities: the majority, the native people and Canadians of other ethnic backgrounds or origins.
I am convinced that Mr. Bisson will do a lot for the development of the French-speaking communities, while at the same time respecting the others. We wish him every success.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has just won a major trade victory regarding pork exports to the United States. For the first time since the Free Trade Agreement was implemented, in January 1989, Canada has won over the US in a final round concerning one of the trade areas subject to the most heated debate between the two countries, namely shipments of fresh chilled and frozen pork.
This decision by an Extraordinary challenge committee will have positive effects for Canadian pork producers. Indeed, since the countervailing duty levy order will be repealed and the collection of duties stopped, approximately $20 million will be reimbursed to Canadian pork producers. This ruling by the committee reaffirms the benefits of the review system by a FTA binational panel on disputes regarding anti-dumpiong and countervailling duties. A great victory indeed Mr. Speaker, for the 4,300 Quebec pork producers and slaughterhouses, many of which reside in my riding.

Mr. Speaker, can Canadians have any confidence in the ability of health and welfare to regulate medical devices effectively?
On the evidence, the answer is an empathic "no". An extraordinary change to health and welfare regulations in 1989 concerning contraceptive sponges has meant that

spermicidal products can be sold on the Canadian market without any testing or checks to ensure safety or effectiveness.
We now learn that claims that these contraceptives are 90 per cent effective are far closer to 70 per cent, or worse than any other method of birth control.
Like the Meme breast implant, these faulty products are now on the market because health and welfare overruled its own competent scientists.
Now Canada, according to the World Health Organization, may be the only developed country which does not test or review spermicidal products.
Surely it is time for an immediately public enquiry into licensing and marketing of medical devices in Canada. Anything less betrays the trust that Canadians, particularly women, must have in medical products in the marketplace.

Mr. Speaker, resolution 541 of the Security Council of the United Nations condemns the division of the island of Cyprus and the formation of a Turkish Cypriot state. The de-occupation of the northern part of Cyprus and the withdrawal of Thrkish troops must be respected and enforced.
Turkey, which received strong international and economic support during the Persian Gulf crisis, should demonstrate its good will by moving toward the termination of the Cyprus problem.
I believe the time has come for the embarkation of a sincere and serious dialogue among Greece, Turkey and Cyprus so as to build a new climate of trust and understanding which would lead to concrete and lasting results.
The war in the gulf has shown that respect by all countries for the basic principles of international law and avoidance of the rise of violence in international relations are of vital importance for security in the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, six weeks ago the Nova Scotia Clam Company closed its doors and 250 people were thrown out of work.
Yesterday I attended a rally on their behalf at the clam plant site at Auld's Cove. Their message to the company, to the unions and to the federal and provincial governments was simple: "We want our jobs back now".
I hope this call will be heard. We cannot afford to lose 250 more jobs in Highlands-Canso and this company, with the proper support, has a bright future in Auld's Cove.
There is in Japan a promising new export market for its product. The hard lessons of developing this market have been learned. Most important, the workers are there. They are hard working. They are responsible and they take pride in their work. This is not the time for the company or the government to abandon them.
Two things are needed. One is a financial package that will enable the company to continue. This, I understand, is within reach. The other is assured access to the resource to process clams in Auld's Cove.
This is the minister of fisheries' job. He must not dissipate this access and these jobs by approving new licences to process these clams elsewhere, to flood the Japanese market, to foster destructive competition and to snuff out this young enterprise.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I had the pleasure to attend the ceremonies for the Seventh Annual Ismaili 10K Run for Charity. Over 1,300 runners participated.
I want to thank the Ismaili youth who has been planning this event for over six months and the leadership shown by President Nizar Kanji and many other community leaders, many of whom are from Markham.
June 17, 1991

The net proceeds of the run, which should exceed $50,000, will go to the North York General Hospital's Capital Campaign. The proceeds from previous runs have gone to such worthy causes as the Cancer Society, the Alzheimer Society, and the Heart and Stroke Foundation.
A special thanks to Apotex Inc., the Canadian owned pharmaceutical company that made a contribution of $20,000.
As I said in my remarks at the event, the Ismaili Muslim community deserves the congratulations of all Canadians for its Outreach programs to all communities. Its sincere caring and sharing is a model for all Canadians to emulate.

Mr. Speaker, in 1986, five years ago, a special all-party committee unanimously urged the federal government to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, discrimination based on whether a person was a lesbian or a gay man.
The amendment was supported by all parties and the government at the time. This government said that it would introduce such an amendment to the Human Rights Act. The government has shamefully refused to act to this day.
The amendment goes beyond the charter and would guarantee protection against discrimination in the federal private sector and in the federal public sector. There are over 1.2 million Canadians in that group who would be covered by the amendment. There are 100,000 gay men and women in Canada. This is an important protection for those men and women which all parties have agreed they are entitled to and need. The time has come for this government to act.

Mr. Speaker, today's Montreal Gazette publishes a story headlined "Backbench Upheaval-Tory MPs speaking out against the Government".
The story mentions me and several of my caucus colleagues as if we were some kind of rebels. It also quotes a member of the opposition saying he believes
Tory caucus members such as myself must have been hauled over the carpet by the political gods of the Conservative Party.
I have news for the opposition. Freedom and independence for MPs is a goal of this government. It was mentioned in the throne speech, and members of the caucus have taken that as a further encouragement to do exactly what those people who voted for us want us to do.
Canadians want MPs who are neither sheep nor cheerleaders. They do not want blind partisanship. They want instead common sense on the floor of the House of Commons. There is no revolt; just a bunch of members of Parliament over here doing their job.

Mr. Speaker, over the past weekend 135 residents of the province of Quebec were hosted by the people of Gananoque, a town on the shores of the St. Lawrence River here in eastern Ontario.
The weekend was a good will gesture sponsored by the common people of Gananoque and was dubbed "Between Neighbours". The people of Gananoque who initiated this project have every reason to feel very proud today for proving to Canadians everywhere that the best way to promote unity and understanding among Canadians is by reaching out to each other.
Congratulations, Gananoque, and may the good will which you project between neighbours become a model for all Canadians to emulate throughout the country.
Yes, Canadians do want to remain united, and the best proof we have is seen in projects such as the one demonstrated by the people of Gananoque and their 135 visitors from the province of Quebec over the past weekend.

Mr. Speaker, the people of Abitibi and I wish to congratulate and thank you for your courageous decision to cancel the annual reception at your residence in Kingsmere, which costs approximately $15,000.

June 17, 1991
This goes to show that our government means what it says, now that we are in a recession. In fact, I urge all federal departments, the Governor General of Canada and the Senate to charge a "user fee" for this summer's festivities. Another alternative would be to immediately cancel summer parties held at taxpayers' expense.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you on behalf of all Canadians.
is attributed to the higher level of taxation imposed by our federal and provincial governments.
A major survey done by Ernst and Young found that 72 per cent of those surveyed had gone shopping in the U.S. in the last 30 days. Gasoline accounted for 36 per cent of the total dollars spent by customers. Of those, 68 per cent said that if gas prices were comparable they would not shop in the U.S.

The fact of the matter is that lower gas prices are luring Canadian consumers south and once there they are buying other retail goods.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are hearing speculation that the Department of National Defence may be returning to a tri-service set-up with three separate basic training facilities.
CFB Cornwallis presently trains recruits for all branches of the military. This avoids the cost of duplication that would arise if each branch had to carry out its own basic training.
Canada has today two streams for new basic recruit training: English at Cornwallis and French at St. Jean, Quebec.
In 1990, Canada graduated only 5,600 new recruits- one-third from St. Jean and two-thirds from Cornwallis-at a cost of $3,200 per trainee at Cornwallis and $5,300 per graduate at St. Jean.
If the cabinet is serious about saving money, it had better look at the $12.8 billion rather than look at the basic training which barely trains enough recruits in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a significant motivator in cross-border shopping is gasoline. High taxes on gasoline are having a deleterious effect and are driving consumers southward.
Our retailers in border communities sell gasoline at 56 per cent more per litre than their American counterparts. Approximately 76 per cent of the price difference
In order for us to remain competitive, our federal and provincial governments must take a serious look at taxation of gasoline. A graduated tax approach, an across-the-board tax reduction possibly financed by GST revenue from the underground economy or some other approach all should be seriously considered to help address the whole cross-border shopping issue.

Mr. Speaker, the belated Japanese apology to the Canadian survivors of Japanese prisoner of war camps is not enough.
No group of Canadian POWs in any conflict involving Canada has endured more pain and brutality in the most hideous and unacceptable circumstances. This four-year legacy of cruel and harsh treatment continues to haunt many and their families today.
The Hong Kong Veterans Association has been pursuing a claim for just and reasonable compensation before the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva for the slave labour they performed at gun-point.
The Prime Minister has told them this is a futile claim and that they should seek redress from their own government, and he is right. However, he is dead wrong when he says there is no money for them.
Their circumstances are special and justify compensation. They and their families should get it now from their own country for which they suffered so much but served so bravely.
June 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, this weekend I was questioned by individuals in two branches of the Royal Canadian Legion wanting to know if and when Canada was going to recognize our Korean war veterans.
I am sure that these two veterans and all members of this House are pleased with today's announcement that a Canadian volunteer service medal will be presented to our veterans of the Korean war.
Today's announcement was timely as these same veterans will be observing Korea Day at the National War Memorial and cenotaphs across the country on Sunday.
We can look with pride at the Canadians who volunteered to serve with the United Nations, and we must never forget the supreme sacrifice made by the 516 Canadians who died in defence of South Korea.
For 40 years our veterans wanted their volunteer service recognized by their own country. Today's announcement is a well deserved and overdue recognition.

Mr. Speaker, this government found money for a war but nothing for Canadian children.
In 1984 the Prime Minister promised a national child care program as a top priority. In 1986 a child care task force travelled Canada. We were told repeatedly that over a million pre-school children urgently needed licensed care and many were at risk.
The government responded with a token $200 for mothers at home, nothing for day care centres.
In 1990 the Prime Minister chaired a world summit on children urging nations to give every child a better future. Then he came home and cut child care funds by limiting the Canada Assistance Plan.
Today, another generation of one million kids needs child care-87 per cent of these are in unlicensed arrangements or have no child care at all while working mothers are frantic.
Oral Questions
When will this government learn, as most European countries have, that child care is an essential service and a social investment?
Let's turf the Tories out and get on with it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
During his trip to Germany the Prime Minister said that he was planning to cut back our forces in Europe, but he would not say by how much.
I would have thought that the proper way to do this would be to withdraw the old policy first and then announce a new one, not to do it bit by bit before we know where we stand.
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister why the policy was announced in Europe to withdraw from there when the government is not ready to tell Canadians what the new defence policy is.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I think we should be very clear about the fact that Canada believes in NATO, that it participates in NATO and that it believes its participation in NATO plays a key role in its defence policy.
Second, the geostrategic situation in Europe has been profoundly changed by the dismantling of the Warsaw Pact and the reunification of the two Germany's. As a result, all our allies, including NATO, are reviewing their defence policy in Europe. The government already announced it was withdrawing 1,400 members of the Canadian forces in its 1990 budget. This exercise is now in progress. Furthermore, the government, like practically all its allies, is reviewing its defence policy, and once it has been discussed and accepted by cabinet, it will be made public. The government, the Minister of Defence and several other ministers have made it clear within the last few weeks that Canada will reduce its presence in Europe.

June 17, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, agree it is time for a new defence policy, because the 1987 policy was based on the Cold War concept, and at the time, we already knew the Cold War was over. It makes perfectly good sense to have another policy. However, we would like to hear from the minister why the government announced a defence policy in Europe without having a new one in Canada, without asking Canadians what they think about the matter. And I would like to ask the minister if and when Canadians will be consulted, before these policies are announced piecemeal as was the case on the weekend.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize the Leader of the Opposition should be informed of a number of situations in this country, but I may remind him that I had to answer the same question several times since the beginning of May. I have repeatedly made it clear, as I did in papers released to the public, that Canada would reduce its presence in Europe while remaining a participant in NATO strategy. This is not new. Anyone who wanted to know about these issues was in a position to do so. On the other hand, since Canada is part of an alliance, it is advisable for us to consult our principal allies before defining, in concrete and practical terms, the position of our allies for submission to Cabinet, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my next question is directed to General Masse- I beg your pardon, to the Minister of National Defence and Marshal Foch-
My question for the Minister of National Defence is simply this: In statements made on the weekend, the Prime Minister indicated that the government intended to close a number of military bases in Canada. I want to the ask the minister whether this time the government will take certain precautions and, if it has to close military bases in Canada, it will ensure it has economic strategies to cope with the problems the communities in question will be faced with once these closings have been announced, and that they will not wait until the deed is done to try and find economic remedies.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can inform the Captain of the Liberal Party that that is exactly what I intend to do.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister made a major policy statement on defence regarding our military posture in NATO last Friday. He made the statement after consultation and after having been, I think the term he used was swayed and impressed by the German chancellor.
After three years without a defence policy, can the Deputy Prime Minister tell this House when he will have public consultations and be swayed and impressed with Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as soon as discussions with my colleagues are finished and a decision has been made, it will be made public.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the Minister of National Defence.
Can the minister give us the assurance that before announcing that certain military bases will be closed, economic impact studies will be conducted, their findings published and viable economic alternatives submitted?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian bases and their infrastructure must first of all meet the requirements of the Canadian Forces as set forth in a defence policy. That is the primary objective of a base.
Obviously, these bases also have an economic impact on the region, but their primary objective is to serve the Canadian Forces.
Third, it is no secret that there are too many bases in Canada, considering the requirements of our Canadian Forces. Obviously, their number will be reduced, Mr. Speaker.
June 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs.
When the Spicer commission was first struck, Canadians were told that it was a commission which would listen to them and would report back directly to them, not a reported vetted by the government. Yet today we understand, it is reported, that members of the government have received portions or all of that report before the report has been given to Canadians.
Will the minister responsible immediately table any portions of that report that his government has, or all of that report if the government has it, so that we can keep the faith with Canadians and say that the report of the Spicer commission will go to Canadians first and not vetted by the government?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to give that assurance. I have not seen the report or any portions of it. Certainly I have no intention to vet it.
I think that this kind of public participation by Canadians is exactly the kind of innovation that we need to achieve, working in close concert with the parliamentary system that has served this country so well for so long.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
I would understand from that that the minister says his government has not seen any of the copies of that report. I would again ask him, if that is not the case, if he would table those reports that he has seen.
Today, on another matter, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, along with the vast majority of Canadians, presented the idea once again of having a more open constitutional process. Yet we see the government again creating a parliamentary committee with 10 unelected senators and the same old style that has gone on before.
Will the minister listen to groups like the National Action Committee and many others across this country and Canadians who are saying that this time there must be a more open constitutional process? Will he withdraw his proposal and bring back a proposal that includes Canadians?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to withdraw our proposal. I have seen the proposal of the National Action Committee. I was struck that what it was talking about was a constituent assembly for the rest of Canada, something which by definition Quebec would be excluded from.
I could not help but notice the article in The Globe and Mail of Saturday by Lysiane Gagnon reporting on the hon. member's convention in Halifax. It says:
The NDP held a convention and Quebec didn't come.
I do not want to be in a situation where this country holds a constitutional discussion and Quebec does not come.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows full well that there can be representatives from Quebec. There will be representatives on his parliamentary committee, I assume. Those same members could also be on a constituent assembly.

I would like to touch on another subject, Mr. Speaker. The government kept the door shut this morning and refused to meet with the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. Yet, 52 percent of the population, women, live in fear. Violence against women is still rampant. What does the government intend to do to make this violence socially unacceptable and promote zero tolerance, as we say? Will this government finally realize that what is required is a combination of shelters, public education programs and anti-racist training throughout the whole justice system?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that the issue of violence against women is uppermost on the agenda of this government, including many ministers, many whom you saw rising. It is not only the minister of health and welfare who announced the $136 million family balance initiative. It was my colleagues the Secretary of State, the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice, all of whom are involved in bringing forward initiatives including of course the most impor-

Oral Questions
tant one which will be the national inquiry announced in the Speech from the Throne.
I have been discussing it with my colleagues on both sides of the House. We really hope it will help us as a country come to grips with this issue and find real solutions and plans of action which will involve women and the provinces and ourselves to finally solve this problem for all of Canada.
*
*

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the minister of the Environment. Tbesday, in this House, the minister said he was waiting to see what Quebec will decide about the Great Whale project. Quebec made its decision known the very same day: the roads and the project will be treated separately. For a year now the federal government has been making excuses and looking for reasons not to take on its responsibility. Now, it has ran out of excuses. There is no way out. My question is this: In view of Quebec's final decision, will the minister immediately set up a single comprehensive federal environmental assessment on the project as a whole, by that I mean not a split study, Mr. Speaker?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before going any further in our approach to the environmental assessment of the Great Whale project, we will sound out all interested parties, including the Quebec government as well as the Inuit and the Cree. The hon. member should know that the Quebec decision came precisely after a meeting where Inuit, Crees and the federal and provincial governments all sat around the same table to review the approach to the environmental assessment for the Great Whale project. We said, and so did the Quebec environment minister, that we would prefer doing one single environmental assessment for the whole project. Now, it seems that they maintained their original position. We will see what approach we can take regarding this project, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, all of the soundings have been held. The minister's colleague, the minister of Indian affairs, expressed some puzzlement this morning as to the government's position in terms of James Bay.
Some weeks ago, Quebec's minister of the environment begged Ottawa to support the environmental cause. He said:
We need the federal government to do its job. I'm puzzled about
the absence of the federal government on matters of federal
jurisdiction.
That was Quebec's minister of the environment. He is not the only one who is puzzled. The minister of Indian affairs is puzzled. The Canadian people are puzzled.
Will the minister state unequivocally here and now that not only in the case of James Bay but never will the government allow a major project to go ahead anywhere in the country within its jurisdiction without a full public environmental review completed before a shovel hits the ground?
Before this minister or the Prime Minister lecture the Germans about the environment, they had better make darned sure they have clean hands at home.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member says that some people are puzzled. I must admit that I am also puzzled by the attitude of the member for LaSalle-Emard who would want us to go in there without talking to the Government of Quebec. Only two weeks ago he was on his feet here in the House of Commons saying that this government was intruding into the provincial government's area of jurisdiction in the area of regional economic development. His party was saying that here in the House. He felt that the way of doing productive business in this country was to talk to the other level of government.
We propose to do that business in a way that respects the jurisdictions of every level of government. Our approach in this specific case of Grande-Baleine is based on our environmental concerns and on doing an environmental assessment that is comprehensive. We intend to follow that up, and the member should help us with executing that mandate.
June 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board.
Will the minister stand in this House today and assure the women of Canada that there will be no further substantive cuts both to funding for women's programs and to funding for women's groups?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Secretary of State of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to reiterate what I told the women's groups that I met last week. There are no further funding cuts to women's programs in this country this year.
The amount, as a matter of fact, is going to rise. Every group has received, if you like, an advance payment of 25 per cent of what they had received last year. The final allocations will be made public to every group before the end of this month.

Mr. Speaker, in light of that seemingly good news, and in light of today's emphasis on women's groups through the NAC lobby with some caucuses in this Chamber, I would like to ask the minister if he would therefore stand and make a further commitment to restore the funding to women's programs and to women's groups to its pre-1988 levels and to index such funding.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Secretary of State of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned a few minutes ago, I made that commitment. I met with the president and some members of the executive of NAC last Wednesday. I met with the whole group last Friday. We talked about this.
The commitment is really simple and it can be found in a rather usual place. Look at Part III of the estimates. It is very clear. The funding is there. It will be continued, and I can say that the priorities are also listed.
The priorities are the following. We are very concerned about violence, violence toward women, family violence. We are concerned about those women who are doubly disadvantaged. Obviously some programs in that area will be enhanced. We are also very concerned about the efforts we are making and have been making to
Oral Questions
achieve over-all equality for women and full participation and access to Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, today women from across Canada expressed their outrage that the epidemic of violence against women continues to destroy their lives.
Government members claim to be committed to changing that. They point continually to their recent announcement of a $136 million program to fight family violence, but this announcement is merely a smoke screen for the real actions of this government.
In reality, only one-third of this money will be spent before the next election. Over the same period, programs which support women and children at risk will lose $155 million through the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan.
In the name of ending violence against women, will the Deputy Prime Minister remove the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan and spend the money for the family violence initiative program before the next election?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement made by my predecessor last February about the $126 million over four years for the family violence program will be respected. There has never been a question that we will not spend that money.
At the same time, we are working on a strategy dealing with children in light of the commitment made by the Prime Minister at a convention last September. However as good managers we do not spend the money before. We spend the money after it has been decided to spend the money, not before.

Mr. Speaker, the minister of health gives us these vague kinds of responses. The fact of the matter is that according to their own figures they are cutting $155 million to families and women through the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan.

June 17, 1991
Oral Questions
Will the minister of health stand today in the House and make a real commitment to ending violence against women in our society and announce an end to the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is not a Canadian in this country who does not want to stop violence against women. It is not just ministers, not just members of Parliament; every Canadian wants to stop that kind of disaster against women.
It is more than saying what you want. We put in $126 million. We gave a billion dollars in transfer payments to the provinces.
As minister of health I want to continue to work with the provinces. It is what we do and will continue to do. I will meet my counterparts this week in Toronto, and we will look at the problems with the CAP.
However, I will return the question to my friend: Are you ready to help me fight against violence against women?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for Housing.
At the present time, 17,000 families in Toronto are on a waiting list for public housing. Refugees have also been added to this list as potential clients.
I would like to ask the Minister what he intends to do to address the housing issue in the city of Toronto?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a meeting scheduled with the minister of housing for the province of Ontario. My colleague opposite knows that we have only so many resources available for this, but we are prepared to make any commitment that we can to improve the lot of these people. I can assure him of our commitment to do whatever is possible under the circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, in addition to the 17,000 families there are 5,000 seniors and over 2,000 people with special needs.
Does the minister think that the answer he just gave is adequate to provide a roof for this large number of people waiting in the larger metropolitan Ibronto area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague knows that since 1986 our policy has been to target resources to those most in need, and there have been considerable resources put aside in our housing policy for seniors, for those who have special needs, and we will continue to do this.
However, he knows as well that there is only so much that can be done by the federal government. We seek partnerships with public, private and other groups to assist us in this regard. We will continue to try to show leadership.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister?
When the green plan was announced last December, $250 million was set aside for the Department of Indian Affairs to produce a plan of action for dealing with water and sewage in Canada's poorest communities, the reserves throughout Canada.
Does the minister know that subsequently the Department of Indian Affairs has ruled that hook-ups are the responsibility of individual home dwellers?
In other words the poorest of Canadians, where two out of three homeowners are unemployed and where the average income is $9,000, are expected to pay $10,000 to hook up the sewage system. How does the ministry expect these people come up with the $10,000 to provide clean water and a sewage system for their homes?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is quite right. There was quite a substantial amount of money provided specifically for water and sewer to aboriginal peoples.
There have been ongoing discussions with those groups, and particularly in his province of Manitoba. Considering that the base budgets of Indian affairs are 60 per cent administered by the bands, those discussions are ongoing. I think it is that sort of approach that will lead to a resolution of the problem the hon. member raises.
June 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
Although discussions are ongoing, the minister does not seem to realize that Indian affairs has taken what seemed to be a nice public relations scheme giving a lot of money to these communities and has carried on as under the old plan, that is to say forcing individual residents to pay for these connections.
The construction season is almost half over. I want assurances from the minister that every effort will be made to increase the construction program so that work begins this summer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, particularly in Manitoba there have been meetings, discussions between the department and a subcommittee of the Manitoba chiefs. There is scheduled before the end of the month another meeting to discuss exactly the best way to proceed.
I like him look forward to a good resolution to the problem based on the co-operation between the government and the bands.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board.
The government is currently at the bargaining table with the Public Service Alliance. We know that the government has offered zero per cent in the first year and three per cent in each of the second and third years.
Is the minister aware that half the alliance members are women, most are at the lower end of the pay scale, and a freeze on wages in the first year means that these women, already living close to the poverty line, will be taking a cut in real wages? Will the minister tell us what this says about the government's commitment to pay equity?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to reassure the hon. member that pay equity stays there, I mean will be implemented. During the course of the last budget we had to make very difficult decisions in a number of fields, including freezing the wage budget which affects all public servants.
I am fully aware that this impacts particularly on employees with lower wages. Also it could in the course of the PS 2000 reform possibly be a threat to our women employees. We have given very strict instructions to our managers to be very attentive to this so that employment equity and pay equity are preserved throughout this exercise.

Mr. Speaker, I hope when the minister says that "pay equity stays there", he does not mean stays there on the shelf.
The minister is expected to table PS 2000 legislation tomorrow. Will the minister assure women working in the public sector that they will not find themselves, under this legislation, faced with a strategic rewards management approach which will really mean: if the boss likes you, you will get the goodies; if he or she does not like you, look out. Will the minister assure women that will not be in his legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the progress we have made during the course of the mandate of this government speaks for itself.
I would like to remind the hon. member of the situation we were in when we came of office as far as management positions were concerned. We only had two women ambassadors; we now have 13 women ambassadors. We had seven deputy ministers; we now have 22 deputy ministers. We had 16 members of boards; we now have 31. We could go on and on.
This government is attentive. We are also the government in the area of pay equity which has set aside $76 million each year to improve on that. We have also paid, something the Liberals never did, $317 million to help improve this. These are real facts.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
It is clear that the California Public Utilities Commission and the U.S. Senate energy committee are making a co-ordinated attack on Canada's gas industry.
Using the Dominici Wirth amendment-and there are other demands which would prevent Canadian gas producers from getting the same price in California as their American counterparts and which would extend U. S. power over Canadian pipelines-they are trying to break the sanctity of contracts and the commitments in the free trade agreement.
The Alberta government is taking steps to stop this. What is our government prepared to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two points.
First of all, the California Public Utilities Commission has been holding hearings in an attempt to reopen contracts that exist between Alberta and California shippers and suppliers.
Alberta primarily, but western Canada has been a very good supplier of natural gas to California back to 1961. The Dominici Wirth amendment to the national energy strategy which was proposed by the Senate committee is written in such a way that it is targeted directly, we feel, to Canadian pipelines.
We have made representations directly to the U.S. government. I have made them personally to the Secretary of Energy, Admiral Watkins. Our embassy in Washington has been very fully informed and is constantly advising both the executive as well as Congress of our objections.
We feel that this is a violation not only of the contractual obligations of both parties, but is also not in the spirit of the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Forty thousand members from the Khalsa Dabar Sikh Temple in Mississauga, Ontario have had to resort to court action in an attempt to secure for their priests the same rights that a directive from the Quebec region immigration office guarantees to all priests: specifically, that their immigration request for a credible basis refugee claim be presented without an interview or hearing.
Since the minister, in referring to those priests, said "They are at the end of the process; they should just get out", will he tell this House if he read their files before he decided to interfere in an ongoing case?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member pointed out, this case is before the courts and it would be improper for me to comment on it at this stage.

Mr. Speaker, he has already commented on it.
The correspondence between the Ontario region office and the lawyers for the priests indicate that neither the national headquarters nor the regional headquarters had an awareness of the files before the minister decided to make his statements public. Moreover, those priests have at their disposal at least 12 more administrative procedures before refugee hearings.
How can this minister now expect that any of them will get a fair hearing anywhere in Canada or elsewhere when he makes judicial pronouncements without jurisdiction and without ever having seen the files?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the member who held a press conference. I noted in his press conference on that very topic before the action was started six most glaring misstatements which he made to the people of the community in question.
All I can tell the hon. member is that the cases he is referring to were refugee applicants. We have a refugee determination system that is probably the most generous in the world. That process is one at arm's length from the minister and is following its proper course.
If he wants me to interfere politically in a system that is at arm's length from the minister, my answer is: Thanks, but no thanks.
June 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance and is with regard to a meeting that he had last week with his provincial counterparts in Prince Edward Island.
At that meeting they brought in a process aimed at giving the provinces the power to set their own income tax levels independently of Ottawa.
My question is in relation to this.
The minister has stated that he does not have a problem with a system that maintains a degree of simplicity and does not complicate the present system, but he has also reportedly said that if this new system or new method, if we do move to it, is just a question of optics where it creates the impression that provinces have greater tax autonomy.
Are we looking at real change for the right reasons, or are we looking at change merely for the sake of change which will or could add some confusion to the already confusing mess the taxpayer presently faces?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was no such power granted as the hon. member suggests. What we did was decide to deal with this issue through the release of a discussion paper.
As the hon. member knows, since 1962 there have been federal-provincial tax agreements which have provided for a great degree of harmonization and co-ordination. It is clearly the objective of both levels of government to ensure that there will be that continuance of harmonization and co-ordination.
Oral Questions
The provinces want to have more flexibility in terms of personal income tax. It is for that reason they have asked the federal government to engage in discussions about new tax agreements that could be in place consistent with the policy of co-ordination, harmonization, transparency and simplicity.
It is with that spirit that we will engage in a public dialogue to see whether in fact we can improve the system.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
Some organisations, like the Federation des commu-nautes francophones et acadiennes du Canada, formerly known as FFHQ, have serious concerns about changes that could be made to official languages.
Could the Deputy Prime Minister give a commitment to this House and to the Canadian people that no constitutional changes will be made by this government which might compromise the language rights of our minorities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Secretary of State of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I can answer by outlining what this government and our Prime Minister, Mr. Mulroney, have done over the years to protect language rights. We have promoted the linguistic duality of this country by consistently standing for the rights of linguistic minorities outside and inside Quebec.
What we have done since 1984, is a good indication of our position in the future.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
In view of the acrimony, the bitterness, the conflict, and in fact the discontent caused by legislation such as Bill 178, Quebec's sign law, as well as Saskatchewan's and Alberta's legislative decisions which reduce the status of French in their respective provinces, will the minister confirm that his government has no intentions of making provinces or territories responsible for minority language policy or its implementation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Secretary of State of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat for the hon. member in English what I just said in French.
We have always been very staunch defenders of minority language rights: French outside Quebec and

June 17, 1991
Oral Questions
English in Quebec. That is a commitment we took a long time ago. We have acted on that commitment. It is a commitment that we maintain and it is a commitment that we will respect in years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister.
At this morning's meeting of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women concerns were expressed at the erosion of our national health care system, yet last week the Group of 22 asked for the abandonment of national health care.
Further, the minister of health said in response to a question that in regard to medicare Quebec will by 1996 "be able to manage as it pleases" .
Can the Deputy Prime Minister tell the House whether his government supports the position of the Group of 22 and the minister of health, or will he assure this House that there will continue to be a nationally financed medicare system with national standards?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have answered outside the House questions with regard to the very useful deliberations by the Group of 22, prominent Canadians such as Allan Blakeney and others among them.
I think it would be premature for any of us now to comment in detail upon the particular proposals that were brought forward by this wide ranging group of constitutional experts.
I think it is entirely helpful that serious, concerned, informed Canadians representing a broad cross-section of youths are turning their attention to ways in which we can reform this federation. There will be opportunities for members of this House and of the other place to do that more actively and consistently in the fall if the House agrees to establish a joint committee of this House and the other place, which is the means by which we have an opportunity to respect the parliamentary traditions of the country in a way that would allow the province of Quebec to take part in those discussions.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister of health. I am not surprised after that response that the women of Canada are worried out their health care system.
Will the minister of health assure us that at the federal-provincial meeting of health ministers on Wednesday in Toronto he will make no federal constitutional proposals that health become exclusive provincial responsibility? Will he ensure the ministers of health that the federal government will restore federal cash payments so that we can once again have a medicare system from coast to coast to coast that meets national standards?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that my friend asked a question about the health care system in Canada. He knows very well that even the Americans consider that we have the best system in the world. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General.
For several months now our Correctional Service prison guards across the country have been threatening to strike this summer over low wages, reduced staff levels and insufficient training.
Can the minister tell this House what his department intends to do if prison guards do strike? How will he ensure that public safety is not jeopardized and when will he begin to address these concerns of prison staff?
