speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I was on my feet prior to Question Period I was debating Bill C-20 whose title reads: "Budget Implementation Act, 1991, Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act." It would be more appropriate if it were entitled: "The Destruction of Canada Act", another one of the government's bills which is destroying the very fabric of this country.
I have the honour and the pleasure of representing Parkdale-High Park, which is representative of our beautiful country. In this riding I have the more fortunate Canadians who live in homes with swimming pools, three cars in the driveway, ravine lots, you name it. I also have the less fortunate Canadians who are paying most of their income for rent and have very little money left for clothing and food. Some of these people, to make ends meet from month to month, do have to line up in food banks to get additional food for the children. I then have all of the other constituents on that spectrum.
Whoever created us or got us on this earth built into the life span of everyone an equalizer. That equalizer is death. Unfortunately, prior to death many of us do require some kind of medicare or hospital care. I think in everyone's opinion, that kind of care and that service should be equal to everyone.
Before Question Period we heard from a Conservative minister from Quebec, stating that he does not care if an
Government Orders
ambulance drives a patient from Quebec to Vancouver, that is the province's choice. Well, when my constituents have to be driven one mile to the hospital by ambulance,
I want that ambulance service to be there. I do not want it reduced or cut because this government is reducing its transfer payments.
My constituents have a fairly good health care service. In the west end of Toronto we have the Runnymede Hospital chronic care which looks after people well into their 80s, 90s and 100 years. I have the honour of going in and celebrating people's 100th birthdays thanks to the care they are getting in this hospital.
I have the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in my riding which provides first-class care for the handicapped who are able to lead their lives in a very dignified and respectful way.
Last Friday I had the honour of going to my riding to help open the Frank O'Leary Health Clinic for citizens 55 years and over, a community health centre where people can drop in in a relaxed manner. Not in the riding but serving Parkdale, we also have the Parkdale Community Health Centre, a drop-in centre. Centres such as these help take the pressure off the emergency wards of health centres and hospitals and that is as it should be.
Last Sunday I participated in a fund raising event in High Park to help raise funds for St. Joseph's Health Centre in my riding. What pleased me was that people came from Parkdale, High Park, Baby Point and there was no distinction between rich and poor. There was no distinction between the people who have the swimming pools and the people who can barely make ends meet month to month. They were all out there as a family helping to raise funds for St. Joseph's Health Centre because the federal government is cutting further and further and, as a result, the provinces are giving less and less to the health centres and to the hospitals.
St. Joseph's Health Centre has a community health case clinic. It has a community mental health clinic. There is an emergency ward. There is a family life program. There is a family medicine centre. There is a pre-natal screening program. There is the women's health centre. There is also our Lady of Mercy chronic

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
health care where I spend every July 1 helping these shut-ins celebrate Canada Day.
That is why I say that the constituents in my riding are fairly well looked after, but they are getting very concerned because they already see cutbacks as a result of reduced transfer payments.
I mentioned the shut-ins because sometimes we forget about them on Canada Day and since we are leading up to Canada Day weekend. On this weekend I visit the hospitals, the senior citizen homes and I visit all of the people who cannot come out to the parks or the streets for celebrations. So I go to their bedside and I present them with a Canadian flag and I wish them a happy Canada Day.
Hopefully, our health services will be such that these people will be able to celebrate more and more Canada Days with us.
With your permission, Madam Speaker, I would like to wish all the shut-ins across this country from coast to coast to coast a happy Canada Day, especially those who will not be able to get out on July 1 weekend.
In the government's obsession to reduce the deficit, it has threatened our entire way of life. By reasoning that if it spends less and less money, it will be able to take what is saved and apply it to the deficit, this government has ground our economy to a halt.
Imagine a situation where the Minister of Finance would say to the Prime Minister: "Mr. Prime Minister, when you fly to Hong Kong, instead of chartering a plane for $100,000, could you please wait two hours and fly on a regular flight?" One hundred thousand real dollars would have been saved.
This is real money which could be applied to the debt, but it is not hospital money, nor education money. Bill C-20 is not going to save money, not real money. By reducing the amount of money transferred to the provinces for post-secondary education, tuition will go up.
When tuition goes up, the chances of the average person getting an education, a job and paying their own way goes way down. This government is putting into motion a cycle of poverty and lack of education which terrifies me.
Before coming to this House, I spent 28 years in education, as a teacher, vice-principal, principal, supervising principal and as co-ordinator of special education of students with handicaps. I worked with adolescents, in psychiatric treatment facilities, in hospitals and so on, so I know just how important it is to get an education.
Education is not a luxury. It is a necessity. Money spent ensuring Canadians get a post-secondary education is the best possible investment we can make for the future of this country.
The federal government has a duty to take the money it collects from taxpayers and invest it wisely. Investing in equality of opportunity, the opportunity to get an education and the opportunity to get medical care, is a good investment.
I urge this government to reconsider this bill. I urge the minister to take a good look down the road. I am a little disappointed that so few Conservative members are taking part in this debate, but I think they know if they stand up to defend this bill they will lose the next election. They know it and that is why they are sitting quiet on their hands, refusing to debate this damaging bill.
Projections to the year 2000 show $100 billion in federal support will be taken out of the provincial medicare and education systems. As the flow of federal cash is taken out, the federal influence over both areas is reduced. When that day comes universal medicare will be dead. Access to education will be beyond the reach of all but a few.
If changes must be made, they must be as a result of federal-provincial negotiations. They must not be imposed unilaterally by the federal government with no thought of the consequences for the provinces and the people I described earlier. Minimum standards must be maintained in all provinces and territories, and only the federal government can ensure that that is done.
If the government backs away from the leading role it has played for so many years, in the beginning it will be at the expense of the poorest people in the poorest regions. It will not take long, however, for all regions to begin to suffer and for all Canadians to feel the consequences.
This is not my Canada. My country is one of equality of opportunity where every person has the same basic rights. There is time to change. There is time to get off
June 17, 1991

this destructive path and get back to being a country with one of the highest standards of living in the world.
There is still time to preserve our post-secondary education and medicare systems, and I urge the minister to listen to Canadians and do the right thing: withdraw Bill C-20.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with pleasure today to participate in debate on this bill. I realize the previous speaker, the member for Parkdale- High Park, questioned why there were so few Tories getting up to speak in defence of this bill. There is one Tory standing right here who has absolutely no trouble defending this bill, and I am in fact proud to do so. Not only am I proud to do so this year. I was here last year when Bill C-69 was put through the House, a bill that further restrained spending a year ago, and I do not have any hesitation in standing up and supporting government restraint.
For too long in this country, for too long in this city, for too long in this Parliament when Liberals were in office, no member of the Liberal Party stood up and said to the government: "Restrain your spending, cut it back, stop it from increasing, don't spend it here, don't spent it there". In fact, one particular case comes to mind to show the foolishness of Liberal governments of the past. Where were the members opposite? Why didn't they stand up and speak?
There was a trucking company that went out of business because it was bankrupt, potentially bankrupt, and what did the Liberals believe? The Liberals believed that if this small trucking company was allowed to fold nothing would move between Toronto and Montreal because there would be no way of transporting the goods between the two cities. In total absence of any comments from the members opposite while they were in government, the Government of Canada gave $29 million to a trucking company only to see it go bankrupt anyway. It is that kind of nonsense that preceded us and causes us now to bring forward this particular bill, which of course is a further restraint on spending that we had last year.
What is all in this bill and in just what direction is it going? Before I get to that I would like to talk about some of the things we did last year. There are some very serious steps we took last year which we are continuing this year. Certainly one of the things we did in last year's
Government Orders
budget, which I think was a very positive step, was the tax back provision of various government programs to high income Canadians, whether they be family allowance or Old Age Security recipients.
Another thing that does not get an awful lot of press nowadays, because I guess it is something the opposition does not want to give us credit for, is the special tax we placed on large corporations. Various large financial institutions and banks cannot use the tax system to avoid paying a minimum amount of income tax. This was in last year's particular bill that I am mentioning.
Of course, the other thing we did was to stop or slow down the growth in transfers to the provinces. I find that a very positive move.
I sat here today during Question Period, an hour ago, and listened to members of the opposition talk about what I perceived to be their restraint on spending, their thoughts on this year's budget and where they would be going if they had their way.
There were demands that the government increase funding to the Canada Assistance Plan, open-ended funding, versus restraint to three provinces, one of which I happen to be a member of Parliament for. Yet opposition members say: "give them all the money in the world, all they ask for". That was one of their questions.
Another question rather facetiously asked was about why we were spending $126 million over the next four years on violence to women? Why didn't we bring it forward and spend it over two years so that we would have it all spent by the time the next election rolled along?
Of course, the reason we did not do that is because we do not spend money based on next election programs. The other fact of course is that if we did they would be saying: "the only reason you are spending it over two years is because there is an election coming and you are trying to get it in in advance of the election". That is not the way we operate.
They also demanded more money for housing. Even though we have substantially increased funding over the six years devoted to social housing, there they were demanding more money for housing. They were complaining about the defence spending cuts that we are presently undertaking in Europe. They were looking for

more funding for Indian bands even though we have substantially increased funding for Indian bands over the last number of years. Of course they were objecting to the restraint on wages we put on the Public Service. Then they asked for unlimited funding for health care programs. It was attitudes like that, Madam Speaker, that if their spending patterns had carried on from 1984, we would now have a $96 billion or $98 billion deficit instead of the one we have.
That is the attitude that Liberals and NDPers bring to debate. It is amazing that after six years of looking at the serious financial problem we have, there has been no change in their outlook. Their cure to all of the problems of this country is simply to spend money. Well, I am one who is proud to stand in this House and say I do not agree with that cure; in fact, some of the cure might be better achieved if we didn't spend quite so much money.
What have we done? In the February 26 budget we asked we asked many Canadians to share further in the fiscal restraint that the government started on.
We know, and I certainly hear it from many of my constituents, that there are already Canadians who have made some very important sacrifices in the name of restraint. We also know that there will be a reluctance on the part of many of those to accept further requests for If we took no steps to deal with this worsening debt and fiscal situation that we have in Canada, the deficit would be much higher than forecast over the next five years. In fact, it would be so much higher that an additional $215 billion would be added to the public debt-$215 billion that my constituents cannot afford, $215 billion that the children and future children of my constituents cannot afford, and I would hazard to say that is the case for all Canadians.
What have we got? We have come up with a bill that does some very specific things. I can use some words which I think probably reflect what we are trying to do here, words of Mr. McKenna in a speech that he gave back on February 21 of this year. I would like to quote from an article in The Globe and Mail of February 28. It says: "Each government would be required to produce a
four-year balanced budget. No leader could buy popularity today with the dollars of tomorrow. The leaders of the sixties and seventies have placed a first mortgage on the future of Canada. The leaders of the eighties and nineties are placing a second mortgage on the same asset. There is no equity left. We must once and for all put an end to the suffocating debt load we are placing on the backs of our children."
I like what Mr. McKenna had to say and I think that this particular bill goes in the right direction, to stop today's government and future governments from simply spending money for the sake of it.
What is in this particular bill that has the opposition so terribly concerned? Certainly one of the things is restraint on federal transfers to the provinces, and yes, they are being restrained. I find it interesting that here in the province of Ontario that with our new provincial government is spending money like drunken sailors. I would like to share with you just what the Government of Canada is proposing for the health care system and the various other things.
When the Government of Ontario brought down its budget a couple of months back, it indicated that the reason it had a $9.8 billion deficit was because the Government of Canada was reducing its payments to the province by some $3.4 billion. That is rather far from the truth, Madam Speaker. What has basically happened is that over the last she years, since 1984, the Government of Canada has increased the transfers to the province of Ontario by some $3.2 billion, which on an annualized basis meant that the increases were running at about 7.5 per cent per year, year over year increase.
The province of Ontario is saying: "Well, yes, but you should have given us more. If you take their number, we should have given them, according to this, twice as much". Can you imagine trying to justify to my constituents why we are increasing the transfers to my province at the rate of 15 per cent a year? When we are living with a 5 per cent inflationary environment, my constituents would certainly not accept us increasing transfers and thereby allowing other governments to increase their spending at a rate of 15 per cent a year.

Now, if they don't agree with the fact that it should have been done over the last six years and say it should have been done all in the last year, you have to understand that what the province of Ontario is suggesting is that the Government of Canada should increase its transfers to the province this year by some 45 per cent. I do not know in whose mind 45 per cent would be an acceptable number.

I guess the socialists might. Unfortunately for us, we have a socialist government in Ontario. But fortunately for Canada we have a Conservative government in Ottawa because they are not getting 45 per cent more from us this year or any year while I am here, I hope, so that it is very clear.
What have we done this year? We are increasing transfers to the province of Ontario, contrary to all that rhetoric that comes from Queen's Park and from some of the opposition seats. We are increasing transfers to the province this year by about 2 per cent.

speechtext:
About $220 million, not some small sum. That is a rather significant sum. When in fact we in Ottawa are holding our spending quite successfully, we see no reason why other provinces and other levels of government should not do the same.
I stand here to say that in this particular bill that is in front of us, we are restricting the rate of increase in our transfers to the province. However, I say quite clearly that I support that restriction without any hesitation. Canadians across this country are calling on all governments to improve efficiency, to tighten up the rules under which government money is spent, and I think this is exactly what we are doing with this bill.
Now, some will argue on the opposite side-I heard it on Friday, I heard it today-that because of this restriction in the transfers that we are giving to the provinces, the federal government will lose its clout; that it will lose its ability to enforce the Canada Health Act, to enforce the rules and regulations under which the services will be delivered because there is no money that it can use, shall
Government Orders
we say, in a sense to attach penalties to provinces if it is not transferring any money to them.
Of course you know that the second part of this bill very clearly deals with some revisions which give the Government of Canada power to attach financial penalties to transfers other than those that would be attached to health care transfers, so that we could use any sort of financial transfer that we have to a province to in fact penalize the province if it set out to restrict the government's ability to have proper services provided by the various funds that we are transferring.
There is another item that is in here which personally I might suggest does not go far enough, particularly when it deals with MPs. We can maybe discuss it in the context of the wages that MPs and senators are going to receive.
As you are aware, the Government of Canada has announced-and this bill goes further to implement it-that members of Parliament salaries will be fixed too. As you are aware, there are already two bases under which this is fixed. One is 1 per cent less than the consumer price index, and the other I believe is 1 per cent less than the industrial average wage in Canada. Now there is going to be a third restriction, and that basically will say that MPs cannot receive more of an increase than we grant to the civil service.
As you are aware, based on some of the news reports that are going on right now, the civil service is negotiating a salary increase but the government has said that for this year there is no additional money. It appears that they will get 0 per cent this year, 3 per cent next year and 3 per cent the year after that. So this bill basically says that MPs and senators will receive that amount of money or less if the Consumer Price Index is lower.
I think you will find that Canadians have been calling on members of Parliament and senators to participate in this restraint measure, and you can see very clearly by this particular item in the legislation that we are doing that.
I might suggest that there are some Canadians who would support the idea of looking at the tax-free portion of the allowance that members of Parliament and all politicians across this country receive. That might be an interesting subject for a private member's bill.

Government Orders
I would suggest that clearly members of Parliament and senators are participating in the restraint that we have been asking the rest of the civil service here in Ottawa and across Canada to participate in.
Having said that, I do have some concern about the civil service salaries. Yes, they are being restrained, and they have been restrained for the past four or five years. If I listen to many of the federal civil servants who live in my riding-and I have had a chance, particularly this weekend, to talk to a number of them-I can sympathize with their point. They are being asked in a period of 4 and 5 per cent inflation to accept a 0 per cent increase this year, when for example last year they got less than the provincial civil service, or in fact probably less than the civil service in my municipalities. There are a lot of civil servants who are saying: "For the last four or five years, we federal civil servants have been asked to bite the bullet much more severely than any other level of civil service". From my observation that is correct. I wish we had more money to give them. They probably work harder or work as efficiently as any civil servants, but the fact of the matter is we do not have any money. There is a choice in the matter, and that is to be laid off so that we have money to give more to those other civil servants who still have jobs.
I am not sure that is necessarily the appropriate step. I do not think we should simply be slashing staff for the sake of slashing staff. I do not think we should be slashing staff so that we can say to other staff: "Well, we got you a salary increase". What we are saying in this circumstance-and it is a very appropriate circumstance-is that the federal government has a problem: "We all have to tighten our belts. Your contribution to this will be an absolute restraint on your wage increase'1. I support that, even though I understand how difficult it may be for many of those people who are caught by that.
Further in this bill there are a number of other items that are affected. The Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act is being affected. There are many public utilities across Canada that would pay income tax and that tax is transferred to the provinces. What we are doing with this particular piece of legislation is capping the transfer of that tax to the provinces. Principally, it is Ontario and Alberta that pay the bill on this.
It is coincidental that in Alberta they passed a piece of legislation that in fact stopped that transfer from going all the way through to the municipalities. They certainly agree with the gist of what we are proposing with this kind of legislation. They have implemented steps that are much more severe than that which we are proposing.
Also in this particular bill are changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. When the present Government of Canada came to office in 1984, the Unemployment Insurance Act was operating with a tremendous deficit in that we were paying out substantially more in the way of benefits to the unemployed than we were collecting in the way of premiums from those who were employed.
It is an insurance scheme and the Government of Canada said: "Just a minute, if you are going to have this kind of a scheme, and if you are going to have this kind of a plan, it certainly has to be self-financing". Over the last number of years we implemented a program to make the unemployment insurance fund totally self-financing. As you are aware, now the Unemployment Insurance Act has again become non-self-funding. Of course as many members of the opposition would echo, unfortunately it is not paying its way because there are many unemployed people now who are unable to make their contribution.
What we are doing with this particular bill is increasing the premiums being paid by the worker from $2.25 per $100 of insurable earnings to $2.80. On the part of the employer we are increasing it from $3.15 to $3.92. The intent of that is to make the plan self-funding. It will not all be done in the immediate step, but over a period of about a year it should make it self-funding.
What does that do? It stops it from going into a deficit. It stops future contributors to the unemployment insurance fund from having to pay interest on the debt that the unemployment insurance fund has. That kind of step is appropriate because, unfortunately, if previous Liberal governments had not spent their way out of office, we would not have the problem today of trying to raise all kinds of money simply to pay interest. On the unemployment insurance fund, we are saying that we are not going to allow a debt to be accumulated, and therefore future contributors will not have to tiy to earn first the interest to pay that fund before we carry on any further.

Those are some of the highlights of what is in the legislation and they are certainly very positive steps.
Just so that it is understood that there is some light at the end of the tunnel, I thought I would quote from an article from The Ottawa Citizen, which appeared on June 13, a column written by Marjorie Nichols.
I would like to read a couple of paragraphs from her column. The first paragraph reads:
The budgetary deficit numbers actually distort the fiscal truth. In
fiscal 1984-85, the Liberal budget deficit was $38.3 billion, of which
$16 billion went to pay for "groceries"- federal programs and
salaries.
In fiscal 1991-92, by contrast, the Conservative deficit will be
$30.5 billion, all of which is interest charges on the national debt.
Members would be happy to know that at least 85 per cent of that interest is on debt which was there when they were in office.
So I hope I have shared some important aspects of this particular bill. I am proud to stand here and say that I support this bill in spite of all the catcalls from the other side.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me dubious pleasure to speak to Bill C-20. Ten or 20 minutes is not near enough time to denigrate the actions or the policies of this government.
I am going to, from time to time, quote from Premier Bob Rae's speech in Halifax because I know my colleagues in the Liberal caucus from northern Ontario are very interested in what Premier Rae has to say. I know the members opposite, and even the Japanese, are very interested in Premier Rae.
I want to quote from his speech in Halifax because I think it was a great inspirational speech for, not only New Democrats, but for Canadians had they heard it, so I want to be sure to cite several quotes from Premier Rae. He said: "Let's build something together. Let's build something positive together instead of this absolutely futile cut and cut, cut and slash, cut and withdraw and cut and then express surprise that the country seems
ill at ease. Why the hell wouldn't it be ill at ease with that kind of leadership and that kind of approach".
The present Minister of Finance says: "We are staying the course. We set a course in 1984 and we are staying that course".
What a circuitous course that has been, especially since 1988. It is difficult to stay a course when at first you practice to deceive. There is a sudden rebirth or change on behalf of the government. We need only look at 1988 when the course was very, very different from the present course of this government.
I take a look at the Tory-I will not call them promises because they certainly were not promises, I am not sure what they were. The Tories were talking about $12 to $16 billion that they would be able to spend across this country. All of this money was within the budget. It was already in the estimates. It was taken care of.
Some of those promises included: "Free trade will mean lower prices for Canadian consumers, better jobs and greater opportunities". The Prime Minister said in Prince Edward Island, as late as October 1988, that: "In the future Canada will be doing more, not less, for all of you. As long as I am Prime Minister social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished by our government which is committed to social justice and fairness for Canadians." We know that turned out not to be true.
He then said: "We will continue to pursue policies to make equality of opportunity a reality for all Canadians by expanding the training and skills, upgrading programs of the Canadian Jobs Strategy". That was in 1988. In 1991 we cut $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
He continued: "Social programs will be strengthened. We will have more millions of dollars to fight illiteracy and combat drug abuse. We are prepared to subject every federal undertaking and every undertaking on federal lands to a full environmental impact study". Another promise certainly broken.
The issue here is not broken promises, but the suggestion that this is a course that we are staying.
The course has changed very dramatically since November 1988. There is a new course being followed by this government, which suddenly has been converted by
June 17, 1991

Reverend Ike, James Baker or whomever. The government has said: "This is the course on which we are going to stay now. It is all about deficits".
We say in Ontario, and federally, that there are two ways of dealing with a recession. I can talk about the anatomy of my own constituency. The Ontario government says: "We would rather fight than switch. We do not want this Operation Desert Storm with the province of Ontario, the country of Canada or the constituency of Sault Ste. Marie".
Transfer payments have been cut. They have been capped at the worst possible time, and I cite statistics from one of the hospitals in my community. The provincial government has given a 6 per cent increase across the board to hospitals. It is conceivable that they could receive as much as 11 per cent depending on the services. Yet, the hospitals tell us: "That is not enough".
Inflation is 6.4 per cent in hospital services. As a result, even with this increase by the provincial government, there are still beds being cut in the hospitals in my community. I am sure there are cuts across this country in hospitals.
We say: "We cannot increase the transfer payments to the provinces". The province of Ontario has tried, and even with that attempt, there are still dramatic cuts in the medical system of this country.
This government is not transferring payments. It is transferring responsibility, and there is the major difference. It is squeezing what it can out of the provincial government, which has no recourse. All the other governments in this country have chosen to swim with the stream as opposed to swimming against the current.
It is the only government with the fortitude to swim against the tide and attempt to help people when they most desperately need it. That is now in the midst of a recession.
We talk about UI and the increased payments for employees and employers. The suggestion is that this is a safety net. When you most need the UI system, as my community did in a 16-week labour dispute, just try to get what you think is rightfully yours from the UI system. Even when you think you have won a settlement or an appeal or even when you have won a Federal Court ruling there is a possibility that this government will take
Government Orders
you to court over a ruling, that it will go to the Supreme Court of Canada to ensure that you will not get UI.
It was the audacity of this government to add insult to injury in the midst of a strike or labour dispute when the workers received vacation pay which they so desperately needed. The government continued to say: "We are going to continue to take UI premiums from your vacation pay even though you cannot collect UI". This was ironic at worst and tragic at best.
The UI system is fraught with inconsistencies. It is nigh on impossible to extract old moneys from the very upper levels. I have no quarrels at all with local UI offices. However, the higher you go the more difficult it is to extract any funds that workers, after having worked for 25 or 26 years and never having collected a red cent from a system they thought was there to protect them, thought they deserved to get.
This process of appeal goes on and on. Six and eight months later we are still proceeding with appeals.
There are communities at stake and quite naturally I speak for my own. This government says we have to cut the deficit, and that is good. We have to cut expenditures, and that is good. We have to cut transfer payments, and that is good. We have to cut eligibility for UI, and that is good. We have to cut VIA Rail, and that is good too. We are cutting inflation, and that is good too. We have to wrestle inflation to the ground. We have to maintain a high Canadian dollar, beyond the belief of everybody, including the allies of the government.
Nobody believes this high dollar policy is sensible or practical or makes any sense economically, fiscally, or any way. It is literally draining the lifeblood of the manufacturing base of this country. The Algoma Steel Corporation in my community talks about if the dollar was lowered we would have a chance. We would have a chance to sell some steel in the U.S. markets. But in the very next breath they say that even with a lower Canadian dollar the free trade agreement precludes us from selling steel into the United States.
The present penetration of U.S. steel into Canada is now about 15 or 17 per cent. That is five times what it was before the free trade agreement. A lower Canadian dollar would help, but it is not the sole solution to a major problem.

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
Cut all of these things. Cut the deficit, cut expenditures, cut transfer payments, cut eligibility, cut VIA Rail, cut inflation. But is it good when you cut a community off at its knees, bring a country to its knees? Does it profit a government to do all of these things if, in the end, there is nothing left to cut? There is no industry, there are fewer businesses, there are fewer employed, there is less tax to be collected. Even if the government's policy was sound, we are doomed to destruction. Everything is great, all of these things are wonderful, but if there is nothing at the end of it, what good have you done? You have wreaked economic disaster upon the country.
When the final cut is in, and that is all this has been, everything that comes forward is a litany of cut, cut and cut, and very little has escaped the swath of the cut.
So what then? What about a year from now if its policies have worked, and there is nothing. There is a vacuum in many constituencies, not only Sault Ste. Marie. It may have won a battle over inflation, but it has won a war over the people of many communities in this country.
If I could digress for just a moment to mention the GST. The revenue minister says Canadians are overtaxed. The finance minister said no, they are not overtaxed. Many of the backbenchers on the government side say yes, they are overtaxed. The revenue-neutral GST collected $400 million more than anticipated in the first three months of 1991. Canadians say: "Thank God it is a recession. The amount would have been doubled if there were good times". There is some suggestion by many members from the government that we are over-taxed. Well, give everybody a break. What better time than in a time of recession? Give them a break. Say: "We are going to cut this down to 5 per cent, and we can still get ahead with our preoccupation with deficit reduction". You could cut it to 5 per cent and make some people happy. Be positive. That's all Canadians are looking for. A little bit of positive initiative from this government.
It may denigrate what the Ontario government has done, and it suggests, before the budget, when are the New Democrats going to come forward with their promises? They are not carrying through with any of those promises. So when they brought forward the budget and
came through with some of the promises and some of the spending, it said they are spending too much. Well, you can't have it both ways.
What does the government want? Does it want the promises or does it not want the promises?
My community is very, very thankful and grateful for the initiatives that have come forward from the Ontario government. Twenty-five million dollars has come into our community and they are happy. And the only people who are unhappy in Toronto are the folks on Bay Street who finally got an opportunity to demonstrate, and we are happy for them. They got out of their offices, where they have been cooped up for all those years, and said: "We are going to demonstrate". And it was great to see them.
And how about "Fax Floyd"? "We are going to fax Floyd and tell him we don't like the budget". Well, I think the Treasurer of Ontario had a great answer, he is more concerned about the people who don't have fax machines.
So we are happy that some people are upset. And just this past weekend I read where some of the folks who don't like the budget have rented an office in downtown Toronto, no doubt a very expensive office, and said: " We are going to stay here and fight that Ontario budget until the New Democrats are gone". Again, that points out the illegitimacy of what these people are saying. Certainly the poor people of this province couldn't rent a room in downtown Toronto and try to turf out this government, because they couldn't afford it. They would have to meet in somebody's basement somewhere, which is probably better, at any rate.
Of course, I had mentioned when the Prime Minister went to Japan that he got into a cab and the first thing the cab driver said in Tokyo was: "What about that Ontario budget? Isn't that terrible!" He didn't mention anything about the federal budget but he was preoccupied with Bob Rae's provincial budget. Surprise, surprise. It seems that everybody is preoccupied but I am not so sure the people of the province are that preoccupied. I know the people in my constituency are not that concerned. And if they were concerned I am sure they would be calling my office, as they do with many other complaints, but one of them has not been the Ontario budget or the deficit.
June 17, 1991

It has created work in the community and in the province. We appreciate, we really do appreciate, that the deficit is a problem. But we cannot fight that deficit right now, we cannot afford cuts in transfer payments. When hospital beds are being closed, cut out of hospitals, when there are layoffs, fairly substantial layoffs in education, despite the increase of transfers from the province to the municipalities, one just cannot afford it, it is impossible. Because, as the finance minister said, there is only one taxpayer. And if the federal government continues to squeeze at the federal level, it comes out at the other end, if we want to try to maintain services. There is only so far you can go with a cut-and-run mentality.
I suggest that Canadians are willing to pay their share, even more than their fair share, when the time is right. The time is not right at present. This kind of budget is the wrong budget at the wrong time. We have a couple of choices; cut and run, as this government is doing and taking away federal presence across the country.
I had the privilege the other night of speaking to the At and East, a topic about which I knew very, very little, until I stayed here for three or four hours and listened to other speakers and found out the illegitimacy, the illogical reasoning behind it, that it would cut out $35 million in subsidy and preclude $40 million in revenue.
Somebody just made the decision and said: "Well, we have to cut somewhere. Let us take a look at this At and East, it has been round since 1966. There is a good one to cut".
So the choice is, cut and run, or stay and fight. I think this government has cut and run and has removed federal presences across this country. The Ontario New Democratic Party has chosen a different path and I believe it is the appropriate path.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to my hon. friend for Sault Ste. Marie. I must say he leaves me somewhat bewildered by some of his remarks.
Before I raise a couple of questions-and I will be brief-I just want to correct something he said. He quoted the Minister of National Revenue as saying that Canadians are overtaxed or taxed too much. Perhaps he
Government Orders
was not in the House when the minister corrected the record.
The remarks the minister made were with respect to the gasoline tax. He felt that Canadians were over-taxed or "taxed to the limit", I believe is what he actually said. He did not say that in general. He made it perfectly clear in the House. If my hon. friend was not here to have the record set straight, I do it for his benefit now.
I could comment on so many things that my hon. friend said. I think he had the same speech writer as the hon. member for Surrey North earlier. They should be jointly put up for the Governor General's award for fiction for some of the things they had to say.
One of the two questions I specifically want to ask him has to do with the Canadian Jobs Strategy. He laments the cut in this budget of $100 million related to the Canadian Jobs Strategy. I recall over a year ago touring this country with some of his colleagues on the C-21 committee when time and again, day after day as we went from city to city, I heard them say that the Canadian Jobs Strategy was a waste of money. They said that the training provided was a waste of time and energy and it did not contribute to people at all. Madam Speaker, the debate today reminds me of an occasion a couple of weeks ago when I was out speaking to a group of people who had immigrated to Canada in the last six or seven years. They were from all over the world. They were from Iran, Ethiopia, Nicaragua, El Salvador, Cambodia, Vietnam, and they were telling me they were having a hard time understanding why we have a government that keeps destroying things instead of building
Government Orders
things. That certainly is the most appropriate way of describing this bill. Fiscally, socially and culturally, this bill continues the program of destroying much of what is good about this country, much of what we are proud of about Canada, much of what makes us the envy of the world.
I am reminded as well of Lucy and the football. You know, we see the cartoon every fall in Peanuts where Lucy holds the football. Charlie Brown is supposed to kick it. She promises him every year that she is not going to pull the football away. He is not going to fall flat on his face or his back. And every year he falls for it and every year she pulls the football away. It seems to me that is the kind of promises we have had out of this government for the last seven years. It seems to me that with every budget we have had more intense rhetoric about the deficit and the debt, while the deficit and the debt continue mounting, despite relatively prosperous economic times for the last half dozen years.
In every budget, every throne speech, we have promises about getting rid of the deficit and debt. We all have to handle a little bit of pain so that that can happen, and in the end things are going to be better for our children.
Madam Speaker, it never seems to happen. The deficit does not seem to go down and the debt keeps going up. And yet we still have to handle a little bit more pain, a few more cuts, to the point where we are losing some extremely valuable programs in this country. We are also losing our ability to be strong and competitive in the coming decade and in the coming century, and to be a prosperous, healthy, fairly egalitarian and just society.
Canadians have said very clearly that what they want is strong national programs, national standards across Canada from sea to sea to sea, because after all, that is what this country was built on. Let us have a nation from sea to sea to sea, where people enjoy common standards, common benefits, equality regardless of where they live in the country and where they are socioeconomically.
We have to ask the question: with all this pain is the government saving money? No, it is not, it is just transferring government spending to other levels of government. I have sat at the other end of that spectrum. I have sat at a municipal council. It is happening all over the country right now where the pain and the hurt of your people becomes evident. So even if the senior levels

Government Orders
of government are cutting back on health care and social services, deinstitutionalizing to save money, it is the community which ultimately ends up with people sleeping in the streets and sleeping in garages overnight. The community ends up providing the food banks, the emergency shelters and the extra little bit of money to help people make it through to the end of the month without starving. So we do not save money, we simply transfer it to a level of government that is least able in fact to carry out these programs.
Cuts in transfer payments and federal revenue sharing are changing a structure of the country, changing a structure of the Canadian federation through the back door. More of the spending obligations are being transferred to provinces and municipalities where the ability to pay for programs is less than it is at the federal level. The national ability to set standards and criteria is being diminished entirely.
Medicare payments, social service payments and the ability of local communities and provinces to deliver child care are being cut because the government is not meeting its contract. It is not meeting its obligation to share those costs and all we are doing is hurting the poorest, the most disadvantaged and the poorest regions of our country. We are not hurting governments, we are not hurting politicians, we are not hurting bureaucrats. It is people who are being hurt; it is the one million children living in poverty in this country, the same children who, when they are poor, suffer twice as many deaths from accidents, traffic accidents, homicides and suicides as do children of wealthier families. These are also children who drop out of school at four times the rate.
This bill before us, cutting the federal government's share of our social obligations across Canada, is going to make those statistics desperately worse. Children are going to be poorer, women are going to be poorer and people with disabilities are going to be poorer. The poorest parts of our country are going to be poorer because they are the ones that can least afford to provide the services that people need.
We talk about medicare. Americans are up here looking at our medicare system. I heard one speaking on television just last week saying: "We are up here to find out what you are doing because you are able to deliver
medical services to all your people better than we are and cheaper than we are." They are paying far more for medical services in the United States and there are 30 million Americans who have no medical coverage whatsoever.
Unemployment insurance. Well, we are told we have to bear some of these difficulties because we are fighting inflation. Then what the heck is the government doing increasing the unemployment insurance rates by over one-third since the beginning of last year, if it wants to fight inflation? Why is it telling the same people who are being told they are not going to get any salary increase this year that they will have to pay $204 more if they are earning approximately between $35,000 and $40,000. They will be paying $204 a year more for unemployment insurance. They will not get an increase in their salary but they will be expected to pay more to the government for unemployment insurance.
This is entirely contrary to promises made by the Minister of Finance when he said that the government will continue to contribute to the financing of the program in difficult economic times. Well if this is not difficult economic times I do not know what is.
We had 1988 election promises that benefits would go up and premiums would come down and exactly the opposite has happened.
An earlier speaker this afternoon said that none of us in this House had addressed the question of restraint on member of Parliament salaries. I do not think there is one of us who does not agree that if there is restraint we should start with restraint on ourselves. But that is not what the government has done. Those people it has appointed to very highly paid positions, sometimes over $500,000, are still getting their increases while women and other people earning under $20,000, and most earning under $20,000 happen to be women, are getting no increase from this government this year.
In this bill, the government very carefully did not make its own salaries subject to the wage freeze this year, the freeze that it is imposing on the other quarter of a million people who work for the people of Canada. It will come in next year when it is talking about a 3 per cent increase, not this year when it is talking about a wage freeze.

The government veiy nicely protected itself from the same restraint it is imposing on everybody else.
I want to close with one thought. Perhaps what the government should think about is getting people back to work. What would happen if those 1.5 million people who are unemployed were not drawing unemployment insurance or social services in their local communities but were working and paying taxes. What would even a 1 per cent drop in the unemployment rate do for our deficit in this country?
Instead of restraining spending like this, destroying medicare, destroying unemployment insurance, destroying our social programs, what this government should be doing is concentrating on getting people back to work and contributing financially to the debt and the deficit reduction.
Perhaps then we would see some solutions to our problems instead of continually exacerbating and expanding problems for the majority of Canadians, such as the continuing growth of disparity between those who are rich and those who are poor to the point where some who have will be able to get good medical care and some who have not, will not.
This is a disastrous bill that touches all those things that link and hold this country together in a sense of common purpose. It is a disaster for Canada, and the results will be in effect long after this Parliament is not.

We do not build the strength of this country and our ability to be economically strong by diminishing the health of Canadians, by diminishing the opportunity of children to have a good education so that they can prosper and contribute to this society in the long term. We do not do that by letting children go hungry, by letting people go homeless and by letting people have health care only when they can afford to pay for it.
The member opposite has obviously forgotten that there was a time in this country when people had to decide whether they could afford to take their child to a doctor, whether they could afford to have an operation that was needed to save their lives. Those were the days before medicare. Those are the days I remember when I was a child and those are not days that I want to see in this country for my grandchildren.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before the fat cat from South Shore made his phony intervention my colleague from Ottawa West was completing in a very thoughtful manner her analysis of this bill which reads: an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in Parliament on February 26, 1991.
Behind these harmless looking words there is some very dangerous substance that ought to be put forward and explained to the Canadian people.
This bill, I submit to you, reveals the real cruel agenda of the Progressive Conservative Party with respect to its long-term intentions in this country and, in particular, with its intention on medicare and post-secondary education.
To make it worse, it has the ability through the budget speech of last February to couch its language in a small l liberal manner so as to make it appear actually what it is not, to make it appear as something liberal and progressive. However, when given the chance to analyze this bill more closely, one can see that it hides something profoundly regressive and something that no backbencher of the Progressive Conservative Party would dare to defend on the hustings at the next election.
It is so well put that it has to be put on record once again what the well-known Canadian writer, Gratton Gray, wrote in Policy Option very recently when he spoke of this government's social policy by stealth. He said:
The social policy by stealth relies heavily on technical
amendments to taxes and transfers that are as difficult to explain as
they are to understand and thus largely escape media scrutiny and public attention. It camouflages regressive changes in the rhetoric of equity in an attempt to convince Canadians that tax increases are tax cuts and that benefit cuts are benefit increases. By further complicating an already complex labyrinth of taxes and social programs, the stealth style of policy-making confuses the electorate and so insulates itself from criticism. The Conservatives record on social and tax policy constitutes a variation of Newton's third law of motion. For every positive action there is an equal and opposite negative change. As a result the goal of a fairer, simpler and more rational system of taxes and transfers remains as distant as ever.
It could not have been put better in describing the bill before us, Bill C-20.
Who is hit by the measures proposed in this bill? Who will suffer under it? Obviously, it will be the people who are least able to defend themselves, those working at minimum wages, the family led by one parent, those who are on low fixed incomes, all the people whose well-being depends on the capacity of having access to adequate health care. They may not be affected today, nor perhaps next year as the charts would reveal, but just give it a little time, two, three, four, five years from now. What kind of Canada will emerge as a result of these measures when they are fully implemented downstream?
It will be a patchwork of Canadian health and post-secondary educational services whereby the provinces which can afford it perhaps will be able to maintain certain standards and others will gradually fall behind.
Who will benefit, as the member for Ottawa West has pointed out so well? Those who will benefit will be the fat cats in our society, the rich people who will be able to insulate themselves from the impact of this measure. In other words, it is a classical example of Progressive Conservative policies put into place and disguised behind fancy language, using actually Liberal language. That is what is so annoying about this particular approach.
I would like to draw the following to your attention. Between now and the year 2000 as a result of this bill, $97.6 billion in federal support will be vanishing, putting a squeeze on both medicare and post-secondary education. This is almost $100 billion. To be more specific, the forecasts that have been carried out show that the last federal cash payment for medicare and post-secondary education, when it will still be available in certain have-not provinces in the year 2008, will be $238,000 to the Yukon. In the following year not one cent of federal cash would go to any province or territory.

In the case of Quebec, the cash payment will disappear by the fiscal year 1996-1997. Madam Speaker, you may want to remember that on the hustings during the next election campaign.
Cash payments to the province of Ontario will be gone by the fiscal year 2002-2003.
As for the rest of the provinces and territories, they will lose all federal cash for medicare and for post-secondary education a few years after Ontario. That is the picture that emerges when this measure will be in place a few years downstream.
Therefore, the question is to imagine how Ottawa could maintain its legislative presence with the five principles of medicare once federal funds for medicare have dried out. What will happen is that Canada will become a hodge-podge of provincial and territorial programs with different medicare systems, and everybody unto himself.
The changes proposed in this bill have the potential to undermine the full range of federal transfer payment programs. To this point I have dealt with post-secondary education and medicare.
The federal government, as a result of this bill, if and when it wants, will be able to withhold transfer payments from equalization payments to territorial financing, to grants in lieu of taxes, to public utilities income tax transfers, to statutory subsidies, to the Canada Assistance Plan, to crop insurance; to payments in education with respect to official languages, to miscellaneous health and welfare programs, to young offenders services, to justice and to transportation.
It is impossible, even in the limited time available, not to make reference to the fact that in the budget speech the Minister of Finance announced that he was soaking employers and employees by an amount of an additional $2 billion by way of increased premiums, this at a time when unemployment is in the area of one and a half million. In that budget document we were not able to find one reference to measures to relieve unemployment, to deal with unemployment, to establish policies to create jobs. Would you not expect, at a time when one and a half million people in Canada are unemployed,
Government Orders
that the budget speech would address the situation of the unemployed, that it would attempt to kick-start the economy in the badly hit regions so as to provide relief?
That is not what has happened. Unfortunately, Madam Speaker, you are indicating to me that my time is over. I will therefore have to restrain myself from indicating how the Government of Canada is squandering taxpayers' money with its ill-conceived defence policies, particularly by insisting on maintaining its troops' presence in Europe at the present time. That will be for another occasion.

That fund was, up until this period of time in the history of Canada, the responsibility of the government. It is a responsibility which the other side of the House has chosen to ignore. June 17, 1991
Government Orders
I would like to address another very critical issue that this legislation is bringing forward and how it affects the national health program in Canada.
We are all involved today with the constitutional debate and the unity debate. We all know that section 92 of the Constitution Act gives the responsibility for the delivery of health care to each province in this country. As in education and in other areas, the responsibility for health and the delivery of a system of health care within Canada is strictly on the provinces. Through transfer payments in this House, we take federal tax money and give it to the provinces. As a result of giving these funds to each province in this country, we can then set conditions on the availability of those funds. As a result we in effect have usurped the responsibility for the delivery of health care in Canada from the provinces and because of the restrictions we place on the transfer payments, we have taken over responsibility, but not complete responsibility.
If a province chooses not to accept those funds, as we saw a few years ago, then it can carry on with its own delivery of health care. With this method of transfer payments we could very well establish within this country several types of health care delivery systems. This is contrary to the very essence of what we in Canada have come to understand and accept as a universal plan for medical care for every Canadian who lives in Canada.
I am amazed, as I listen to this debate, that we have not yet addressed one of the key problems that will be created as we diminish and lessen the amount of transfer payments to each province. The people who built this country are going to be affected. I would like to speak about how it is going to affect the senior citizens of our country.
There are some of us in this House who are gradually approaching that age when we will become senior citizens. I do not refer to you, Madam Speaker. I refer to some of my colleagues who circle around us.
I want to talk about how it will affect seniors. What right has this government or any government-whether it is this government in power today or any future government, which I assume very much will be a Liberal government, or any provincial government in this country-to interfere with the fundamental right of all
citizens? It is a right that has not been given but one that every citizen in this country through their dedication-some who have come to this country by choice and some who have worked in excess of 40 years-has earned. It is not a privilege. It is an inalienable right of every citizen in this country to expect a universal health delivery system that is not subject to any restriction.
Let me rephrase that. It is the inalienable right of every citizen in Canada to be able to accept and expect a universal health care system that is not subject to any restrictions whatsoever. I think it is the responsibility of a federal government to ensure that this federal system of health delivery maintains that important aspect.
Now the people who are put in jeopardy, as my friend from Toronto just said, are the people who can least afford to pay for that service, the poor of the country. I want to talk about, in my remarks today, the elderly, the senior citizens of this country. We should not even be discussing the fact that in the future, they may be responsible for the payment of what is called a "user fee" to pay for the costs of health care within this country.
In 1988 and 1989, there was $23.9 billion spent in Canada by the provincial governments for health care. Tax transfer-and that is a subject for debate today and the subject that this government is trying to cap-was $6.6 billion, federal cash outlays were $8.2 billion, municipal spending was $0.6 billion, and private spending was $14.8 billion. That all totals up to the tremendous amount of $54.1 billion spent on the delivery of health care in this country. I think the federal government has a responsibility to ensure that this money is not only spent wisely, but spent frugally, with care for the responsibility of every citizen in this country.
I get very upset when I hear that money in health care is being wasted-and I think about the $500,000 that just recently went to some United States agency for one individual. The federal government should show leadership in health care, especially for our senior citizens. It should ensure that funding for a health care program in this country be spent with some wisdom. It should ensure that within this country of 10 provinces and two territories Canadians are not subjected to a user fee or hospital fee and that money that is collected is spent for the best interest of every Canadian.

Madam Speaker, as did my Liberal colleague, I want to limit myself in my participation in this debate to a specific area, and that has to do with transfers to the provinces. I will not concern myself with the changes that are going to affect medicare or general social programs through cuts in Established Programs Financing, as well as the Canada Assistance Plan. I would like to make a few observations on the issue of Established Programs financing as it affects post-secondary education.
I am sure you will recall that when this government first came into office our concern at that time was that the provinces were not delivering their fair share of funding to the universities as compared to what the federal government was doing. At that time they were arguing that we should have assured levels of financing for the universities, that there should be a guarantee of provincial participation and that some effort at negotiations should be entered into in order to bring that about.
The issue has become dramatically more important, as others are beginning to recognize. Almost everybody now is beginning to recognize that the real creation of wealth comes from the mind, from creativity and from innovation. In that context there are two significant components to economic development as all recognize now; education and training on the one hand, and science and technology on the other.
We are at a stage where it is perfectly clear that we must enhance our national literacy, our national education and our national training in order to bring about the
Government Orders
kind of economic development that will put Canada into the 21st century.
Unfortunately, as we look at what has been happening since, we cannot be encouraged. At this stage of the game we observe that the changes in the funding mechanisms that were brought about in 1977 with the Established Programs Financing let loose the provinces from their responsibilities of paying a fair share, then estimated at 50 per cent for post-secondary education. The Liberal government at the time not only changed that formulation releasing the provinces from their obligation, but as a result of changes which were described as the six and five per cent change and other changes brought about by the Liberal government, some $5.7 billion was not delivered to the post-secondary system. Even when this government came into office, the university system was feeling the pressures already from under-funding.
What has happened since? In 1986 this government passed Bill C-96. This was the first attack by the Conservatives after vigorous attacks by the Liberals which set the escalator of the Established Programs Financing at the change in the Gross National Product, minus 2 per cent. That cost the system a considerable bundle of funds, but to make matters worse, in 1985 Bill C-69 was passed. This bill increased the deduction from the rise in the Gross National Product that would be delivered to Established Programs Financing so that we would have the change in the GNP minus 3 per cent. Not only that but with Bill C-69 the Established Programs Financing was frozen for two years. Now we have Bill C-20 which escalates the attack on the university system. Bill C-20 freezes the Established Programs Financing for another three years.
The effect of this is $13.8 billion in accumulated loss which has been brought about by legislation and budgetary action by this government at a time when almost everybody says that education is of immense importance. The government in the throne speech described a number of educational goals, not the least of which was to double the number of graduates in science and engineering. It said it was going to increase by four-fold the number of workers who were trained. It said it was

Government Orders
going to abolish illiteracy. It said it was going to increase the number of graduates from high school.
The government uttered all these platitudes about how important education was and the Prime Minister said he was going to make eveiy effort to make it possible for eveiy young person in this country to have the educational weapons necessary for economic survival.
Yet time after time after time since his government has been in office, just as did the government before, it has cut its commitment to post-secondary education. This in spite of the fact that people have become convinced of the importance of education, including post-secondary education, to the extent that 93 per cent of Canadians agree that the federal government should maintain and not cut its role in the financing of post-secondary institutions.
Two-thirds of those polled supported increased funding for post-secondary education. Yet this government persists in substituting words for actions and causing severe damage to the system.
All one has to do is look at Memorial University. It is cutting programs and cutting staff. You can look at the University of Calgary and the University of Alberta where they are cutting staff and programs. You can look at Mount Royal College in Alberta. My God, because of the increased costs of tuition and living, there is a food bank for students. All over the country libraries are deteriorating and students are lacking access to the system. A special program for access to engineering at the University of Manitoba is going to be cut because of under-funding. Ihitions are being increased by 10 per cent, 15 per cent, 20 per cent per year to the extent that students are now constantly paying out increasing proportions of the cost of post-secondary education while the contribution of this federal government decreases steadily.
This is supposed to be a government that understands the importance of knowledge to our future economic growth. This is a government in which a member can stand up and say: "Oh my God, I talked to some young people and told them they are going to have a $15,000 debt which they are going to have to pay when they grow up because of the actions of their parents." What the member did not say last week was that those young people to whom he was talking are unlikely to be able to
afford that $15,000 because there will be no jobs. It means that the deficit is going to increase.
The deficit increases for a number of reasons, but not the least of the reasons is the failure for adequate economic growth. If you do not have people who are earning an income and you have to pay social costs, then you are going to have an increasing deficit because you are not going to have the revenue from the wage earners or the corporations. After all, in this modem, economic context, the Canadian situation is such that if we do not change things pretty quickly, the deficit is going to grow and grow because nobody is making any income or many profits to pay those taxes.
The reason for this is that this government has not understood that you have to do something to control the deficit, but you had better mobilize the resources, the human capabilities and the opportunities that people need for learning in order to make the economy grow so that you can eliminate that deficit.
Bill C-20, as with so many actions of this government, takes the wrong path. If this government continues in power we are doomed to more and more words while more and more damage is done to a post-secondary system which will be unable to meet the challenge because this government has failed not only that system, but our people and certainly our children.
