Madam Speaker, I guess the minister has forgotten about the Draconian, undemocratic process you have instituted in this House which does not even allow us to talk at any great length about the serious issues that face this nation. We just all have to talk in very superficial terms.
While it is a privilege to rise in this House and talk on behalf of my constituents of Mount Royal and on behalf of a lot of people across this land, I do so today with a great deal of concern and regret for a government action which is so regressive and found in this Bill C-20, a bill to implement the 1991 budget. It is a bill which is trying to remove this government from its area of traditional jurisdiction and traditional responsibility and, in particular, increasing the pressure on our already strained
June 17, 1991

higher education, health situation and health education and programs under unemployment insurance.
Certainly, I meant to include the medicare system of our country. It is doing so by limiting provincial transfers until 1995-96. This is a very tricky, hidden way to to impose a social structure that is totally against the Canadian way of life. The debate goes to the very heart of what this government is doing wrong as it undermines the fundamental social contract of this land. It abandons our goal for a much more just society in the name of the deficit, which is important.
The choice of action this government has taken ignores the principles of the Canadian approach of pursuing the twin pillars of economic opportunity and social justice that have always been the hallmarks of Canada and the Canadian way of life.
The Canada that has been so renowned around the world is being struck. This is why Americans are now studying our health care system, which is far less costly than theirs and serves all our people, while their system does not even serve 37 million of their total population. Yet this government seems bent on demolishing this fundamental fact of Canadian life.
We see every day in the streets of my Mount Royal riding, in the community centres, in the food banks, the images of hunger, the images of great social needs going unmet, of middle and upper income executives who no longer have a job, whose self image has been destroyed, whose sense of self-worth has gone down the tubes because of this government's unenlightened approach of dealing with this deficit. Yet, this government goes merrily along and introduces bills and takes steps like today's saying: "We cannot do any more. Our hands are tied. The deficit is far too important. We would love to help, we just cannot afford it". I say the question has now become: "We just cannot afford not to help". This government does not understand that it takes economic measures as well to make the deficit shrink.
Noel Alexander, the president of the Jamaica Association in my riding, brought to my attention that 67 per cent of the unemployed Jamaicans in Montreal are young people between the ages of 18 and 25, a figure that disturbs me no end.
Government Orders
Thousands of jobs have been lost in my riding since the free trade agreement was signed with the United States, in textiles, in clothing, and in food processing. The high dollar and the high interest rates have closed many, many more plants. This government goes right ahead at this time of great recession without any care. It has destabilized this whole population.
It has introduced a goods and services tax. The Department of Finance now tells us the Minister of Finance did not have a clue as to what he was doing. He has indicated that the GST has collected in the last fiscal quarter $400 million more revenue than was estimated. That is $400 million on a base of $1.8 billion, which this government has collected. That is 25 per cent more money than was anticipated out of the pockets of Canadians. No wonder they are having problems. No wonder they are going to cross-border shopping. No wonder they have no money to buy food and have the normal lifestyle we expect as Canadians.
All during this time, new Canadians have been coming into our riding, new Canadians have been coming in across this country, notwithstanding the fact that there are long waiting lists, and Al-Mashat got in first. Like any other people, they want desperately to work and earn their fair share of the Canadian dream. However, the recession has erased the few jobs that were left and the students entering the summer job market are in a very sad way. The government has cut over 15 per cent of the funding in my own riding that was to help people find summer jobs.
Look at what is going to happen to tuition fees, taxes on books, all kinds of costs that are inherent in having an educated population.
The story of poverty in my riding I am sure would shock many members of this House but it is repeated right across this country. There are literally thousands and thousands of people living below the poverty line, either the working poor or those on social assistance; thousands and thousands of people, I would add, who have no sign of hope from this government: single mothers who number in the thousands, seniors who rely on sponsored in-home health care or just plain meals because their needs exceed their means.
Food banks are serving many more people than they used to serve in Montreal, in my riding and across this country. Children are increasingly having to go to school

Government Orders
hungry and rely on food programs at school for meals. No, this is not the 1930s.
The message today is that this government is so set on using the back door approach of technical bills like this that rarely set off alarm bells or newspaper headlines to severely undermine the kinds of social policy principles from health care to education that have always been the cornerstone of this country's social contract.
That is really what concerns us, that is why we will not be supporting this bill and that is why the government should not be cutting the debate short. The population out there can start putting some pressure on those dinosaurs across the way so we can get some things done.
We are talking about a federal government that is making these very Draconian cuts, but worse it is making them now in a very familiar, sneaky, smoke and mirrors, hidden way. As my friend from Winnipeg North Centre, who made an outstanding speech in this House, said: "The language is there that makes it look good. The language of fairness, the language of concern and the language of good management. The government knows the language".
It knows it so well after seven years of practice but it is too bad it does not start to live up to the language that it uses. The substance is just not there. The real programs and the real dollars are not behind the words.
Canadians should know what this government is doing. We are debating here very dry, very unexciting, very technical changes. It makes closer inspection of government's rosery rhetoric all the more important.
I could give all kinds of figures which would blow our minds. They would certainly upset the population just as much as Bill C-69 did. In that case the government also did not allow enough conversation or enough exchange.
Here we are seeking to undermine the Canada Assistance Plan, extending the capping on day care, on matching funds, on disability payment and on welfare payments. This is actually an attack on poverty. That is what we have out there. We are undermining equalization programs, our medicare system and our post-secondary educational system. Add to that the increase in unemployment insurance payments for employers and employees and the government not accepting its part of the responsibility.
This government is moving out of its traditional domain. It is doing the wrong thing at the wrong time,
particularly at this very sensitive time with the constitutional uncertainty that is going on out there.
As we travelled across this world in our duties to learn about other countries and to exchange what can be done as the world becomes a little village, the question I am constantly being asked is: "What is wrong with you out there? You are destroying yourselves. You are destroying this country that millions and millions of people want to come to. You are structurally changing this country, fiscally, socially and culturally. You are destroying it. You are destroying the dream of millions of people".
I was in Hong Kong at the refugee camps that the Prime Minister so glibly talked about. There are tens of thousands of people in those camps who are anxious to get into Canada. They are sleeping in a bed that is the size of a queen size bed stacked three rows high. Yet, here we are tearing down everything that these people want to come to.
What is the matter with this government? It needs its goals re-examined. It needs to understand this country. I would like to take government members and dump them in central and eastern Europe, in Asia and India. They might come home, count their blessings and kiss the soil which this land is all about.
Bill C-20 is cutting provincial transfer payments on health and education. It is taking $338 million of federal money from health and education programs in 1992 and 1993 and a massive $2.3 billion out of our hospitals, medical clinics and post-secondary institutions over the next five years.
Anyone who has a brain, who has gone out there and opened their eyes knows that the country has two weights, if they look at the demographic studies. We are bringing in immigrants because our people are not repopulating this society. As a result we have a youth bulge coming up. At the top we have an aged bulge. The aged need health care delivered from the home, all kinds of housing needs and all kinds of support needs. What are we doing? Cutting back hospital care.
I would say that the tax increases this government is trying to tell us are tax cuts, what it is trying to dump on the provinces, are totally unacceptable. It has used the back door, squeezing the provincial coffers and, as I said, it is trying to sell us on the fact that tax increases are tax cuts and that the benefit cuts are benefit increases. It tries to confuse the population and insulate itself from the criticism that it justly deserves.
June 17, 1991

Government Orders
We are saying: "Look". We are saying to the media: "Start talking about what is going on out there, get the population up and angry, and let these people know what is going on. The programs it is cutting are totally unacceptable".
I will finish in one minute. I would just like to end up by saying that we are asking the government to protect medicare, to protect the ability of those with little means to attend to their education. Don't add to the line-ups waiting at hospitals, don't make people have to travel to look after their health, don't penalize the disabled or victims of violent crime. That is part of what is in this bill, if one really reads it carefully. It is totally unacceptable.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in this debate, although the subject is a painful one. To those of us who listen to Canadians, it is clear the question is not just what will happen as a result of the legislation introduced by the government, it is a matter of attitude, and for the vast majority of Canadians, a matter for concern.
I spent the weekend in my riding, and people asked me whether unemployment insurance funds would be able to respond to the needs of a society that in certain regions of our country is experiencing unemployment rates of more than 30 per cent. Who can guarantee this, Madam Speaker, now that the government has decided employers and employees will have to pay the bill?
When we visit the elderly, they, like those of us who are getting on in years, say they want a health care system like the one we have had for decades in this country. It is very hard to answer these questions, Madam Speaker, because if it only depended on government financing, the ability of the Government of Canada to pay the bills, perhaps we could say: Well, even if times are hard across the country, there is a serious commitment on the part of this government to ensure that in the future, every effort will be made to provide the same security Canadians have known for the last thirty, forty or even fifty years.

When people ask whether the Canada Pension Plan is going bankrupt, whether or not unemployment insurance is going to remain as a fundamental protection for Canadian men and women in the work place, when people discuss what they see happening in a number of provinces with nurses and doctors, with hospital administrators concerned about the future of medicare, it is very difficult for a member of Parliament or anyone who is sensitive to these issues to be very reassuring.
I wonder if at some point as we progress in the consideration of legislation, not just this particular piece of legislation but other legislation that is being brought forward by the government, if we could have a new statement on the intent of the government. What is its ideology?
Many people in this country voted for the government on an early issue in the 1984 election of jobs, jobs, jobs. Now we are faced with the loss of jobs, jobs, jobs. In 1988 many people voted for this government because they were convinced that, as the government put it, its people were the best managers, it had the people who could best deal with the very, very onerous task of trying to govern this country, to find sufficient funds to maintain fundamental programs and to maintain some balance between debt and income.
Deficits are not at an all-time high; they are staying at $30 billion. Our debt is at $400 billion.
I believe Canadian people have a right now to hear from the government as to what is its vision of this country in the 21st century with respect to an aging population. What assurances is the government prepared to give now similar to what Canadians were told to expect in 1988, that some of the social programs were sacred trusts?
Very few people in Canada remain naive about the problems of trying to finance the operations of federal, provincial and municipal governments. That being said, if this government is to continue on its program of changing very dramatically what Canada is all about and how Canadians can feel secure in their country, not just in terms of the Constitution but in terms of their health, loss of employment and their retirement, there is something dramatically the matter.

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
We have heard about competitiveness. We are talking about changes in the economic system and our trading partnerships with Canada and the United States. We know what is happening in Europe. We recognize the emerging giants coming out of Asia. There is a great deal of effort being put forward by the government in convincing Canadians that we can no longer afford the kinds of programs we used to have and that people felt secure about in terms of unemployment insurance, medicare and the Canada Pension Plan. If that is the case, then I believe it is incumbent upon this government to demonstrate its courage and its conviction that it does have a plan to deal with these kinds of programs moving into the 21st century.
I would like to issue a plea today on behalf of Canadians that the government come forward and tell Canadians what they can expect. For many years it was gospel in this country that if one was sick one received medical services. If one was out of a job, one received unemployment insurance. If one grew old one was not only eligible for the old age pension per se but also, for those who had participated in the work force, the Canada Pension Plan. Those were tenets, principles of Canadian life and part of what makes us different from most other nations in the world.
Surely all of us in this place have a responsibility to tell Canadians where we are going and what kind of a Canada we are going to have for the sick, the elderly and people who have made their contribution to our society.

Madam Speaker, the time has come to review the Unemployment Insurance Program, for instance. The government and the ministers responsible for introducing legislation on unemployment insurance last year gave Canadians, including workers, the assurance that substantial programs would be provided for training and retraining.
With the advent of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, we were promised adjustment programs, and if those programs had been in place, there would certainly be a very substantial number of Canadians who would be eligible for those programs. Whether we are talking about Toronto or my own riding of Acadie-Bathurst or Western Canada, there are men and women
who wonder where they should go to take advantage of training and retraining programs. Where do they go to find a job or prepare for finding a job, when they were laid off because a plant or business closed down?
The current constitutional crisis, Madam Speaker, is probably a matter of concern to the vast majority of Canadians as far as national issues go, but on the strictly personal level, there is no doubt that Canadians are worried about a rapidly changing situation. And that is why, Madam Speaker, I would not be surprised that pretty soon-in fact I was expecting to hear in the Throne Speech some echos of a Conservative vision of what Canada would be like at the end of the twentieth century and at the beginning of the twenty-first.
However, if that is not to be, I hope that we will not waste all our energy on the constitutional question, important though it may be, because if we want to renew the confidence of Canadians, we will have to chart a course that will make them feel secure.
It seems to many Canadians that the damage has been done in terms of public confidence in our programs which for many years were the foundation of confidence in this country for those people who were the most vulnerable.
I do not think it serves any useful purpose to simply berate the government or say it should not have done it. Those things have now occurred. I would like the government to address the question directly, rather than indirectly or obtusely, as to what it is going to do. For example, is the government considering a guaranteed annual income? Is it going to scrap a number of support programs and look at innovative, creative new ways to deal with people.
In closing I would say I hope, and I think I speak for many Canadians, that we will hear soon what the new vision of the Conservative government is with respect to medical care in this country, with respect to the Canada Pension Plan and with respect to unemployment insurance, and what kind of generous and caring government and country Canadians from all parts of this great nation can look forward to as we move to the end of this century.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak against Bill C-20 along with the rest of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party because we are concerned that the government has taken the tactic of reducing the national deficit simply by transferring the burden of program cost to the provincial governments. It is very much like somebody who gets into financial trouble and then goes out and robs the grocery store. He simply transfers his financial problems to the owner of a grocery store and so we are not actually reducing the financial problems of Canada or dealing with them.
What the federal government is doing by this legislation is not reducing the problem at all. It is simply transferring the burden of the federal deficit which was caused by federal policies of both the Liberal and Conservative governments over the last several decades to the provincial governments. We are seeing that the provincial governments are transferring those problems down to local governments, as my colleague from Surrey North indicated, or down to individuals in the case of people who are sacked from government jobs and who are seeing their salaries and benefits cut. We are simply transferring the problems which were created by the federal government down to the people who can least afford to bear them in this country.
That is not the way to deal with your problems. What this government should be doing is addressing its own problems head on rather than transferring them to other levels of government.
We are dealing with a bill which extends the worst provisions of Bill C-69, which was passed earlier, by extending the capping of various federal transfer programs for an additional three years and creating even more problems for provinces which have the responsibility to deal with programs such as health care, social services and post-secondary education.
What options do those provinces face? As I said before, they can either absorb the cuts themselves and run into debt or they can pass it on to local governments, which are the creatures of those provincial governments, or to individuals. There have been examples of both which my friend from Surrey North described. He described the Liberal government in Newfoundland which has cut back on health care services as a result of
Government Orders
what this federal government has done, cut back on hospital beds and fired about 10 per cent of the nurses in the province of Newfoundland in order to absorb the cuts that the federal government has passed on to that province.
Who is bearing the burden of the cost of federal deficit cutting? It has been passed through those levels of government and right down to those individual citizens of Newfoundland, the people who can absolutely least afford to bear those costs.
It is interesting to see the different reactions of the Tories when they examine what the Ontario government is attempting to do in order to shield its people from the worst impacts of the recession and when they comment on what is happening in Newfoundland.
They seem to look positively at what is happening in Newfoundland when a government sacks its employees and when the government cuts back on its social, health and education programs. This seems to be a satisfactory method of dealing with that kind of issue for the Tory government.
Ontario says: "We are here to serve the ordinary people of Ontario. We are going to shield these people from the worst impacts of the recession so that when the recession is over and when economic recovery returns, they are going to be better able because they will be better educated and they will have better health care. They will be better able to get back into the work force and begin to live productive and effective lives again." This government attacks that method of dealing with the problem.
What the government of Ontario has done is dealt with the problem head on. It said that the buck stops here. We have to deal with it and we have an obligation to defend our citizens against the worst impact of this recession which, by the way, was a recession that this Tory government created. If it were not for the high interest rate policy, the high dollar policy and the trade policy of this federal government, many of the provinces would not be dealing with the kind of serious economic problems they are dealing with right now.
It is interesting that Ontario has taken the tactic it has, because Ontario feels, very much like Tommy Douglas used to say, that the economy is here to serve the people and that the people are not here to serve the economy. Mr. Douglas used to say that the people were the most

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
important thing the government has to deal with. They were the responsibility of government.
I would like to congratulate Ontario for the way it has dealt with the problem. Once this recession is over and once the economic problems are over, and that will probably come with the end of the Tory government, the people of Ontario are going to be better prepared to go back and create a new and good economy for Canada. I think Bob Rae's government has done what any responsible government would have done in this country. I think he is going to be able to deal with the spending problems when the economy recovers in that province, because his people will be better equipped in every way to deal with those problems.
I think the real tragedy in this whole situation is that social programs are the programs least responsible for our deficit problems. Things like medicare, post-secondary education, unemployment insurance and welfare are the least responsible programs for Canada's deficit.
I would like to refer to a column that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on March 13,1991. It was a column by Frances Russell in which she points out that there are Statistics Canada studies which indicate that the responsibility for the current $400 billion debt can be divided in a number of ways. For example, she says that 44 per cent of that $400 billion debt is due to corporate welfare programs which have been passed by this and by the previous Liberal government, tax forgiveness program which both the Trudeau and the Tory government have passed.
Another 50 per cent of the deficit, she says, quoting the Statistics Canada study, is caused by the interest rates compounding on the interest rates compounding on the original sums which resulted from the problem of those corporate giveaways of the last 20 to 25 years.
Ms. Russell says in her column that only 6 per cent of the deficit can be attributed to, and she has this in quotes, "living beyond our means or out of control government spending which are Tory code words for social programs."
So it is not the social programs in this country that are responsible for the debt which we have accumulated over the last 20 years. What is really responsible for the debt is the corporate giveaway programs which have been
extended to corporations and to the wealthy over the last 10 years by both Liberal and Tory governments during that period.
It is interesting to see how the economy affects different people in Canada. My wife was talking to a hairdresser here in Ottawa just a couple of days ago. That hairdresser is a single parent with a child.
She works eight hours a day. She works hard. She is good at the work she does and she is paid at the absolute minimum wage. Also, because she is a single parent head of a family, she has to budget fairly carefully. She has found out that when her income comes in and she compares it to her expenditures, the expenditures exceed the income by $70 a month. That is careful budgeting when you are budgeting down to $70 a month.
Madam Speaker, you are asking me to wind up. I have a 20-minute speech here and 10 minutes allocated.

If I may ask the House just to conclude my remarks, I would just like to wind up because the impact on this woman is pretty dramatic. She went to the welfare agencies in Ottawa and she was told that in order for her to make up that $70 through welfare she would have to quit her job and then they would give her enough to meet her expenses.
What kind of a country do we have here? What kind of a policy does this Tory government have when people who are good at their work are working hard, have families to raise and are careful with their expenditures, end up having to be told to go on welfare in order to survive in this country? That is the kind of policy that we are dealing with under this Tory government.

Mr. 'Alfonso Gagliano (Saint-Leonard): Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-20, whose purpose is to amend four important Acts of Parliament, namely: the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act, the Parliament of Canada Act, the Public Utilities Income Ikx Transfer Act and, finally, the Unemployment Insurance Act.
June 17, 1991

Madam Speaker, the debate this afternoon arises from the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance on February 26 this year. I thought at the time, and I still do today, that this budget was bad for all Canadians. This budget did nothing to get Canadians out of a recession that was created by the unsound policies of this Tory government. In fact, the same economic policies that were responsible for this recession may be found in the latest Budget, and that is why I object to a bill that implements these policies.
Madam Speaker, I listened carefully to the speech by the Minister of Finance on second reading, and I would like to repeat some of the remarks he made. First of all, the minister said that the government had, and I quote from Hansard, June 11, 1991, "-embarked upon a course that places less reliance upon government and taxpayers' pocket books."
Madam Speaker, the minister has a short memory, because two days earlier, at the meeting of federal and provincial Finance ministers in Charlottetown, he said Canadians were taxed to the hilt. He seems to have forgotten that middle-income Canadians are paying $1,500 more in taxes since the Conservatives came to power in 1984. The course chosen by this government is not one that will lead us to a just society, far from it. Earlier I saw the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) in the House. Bill C-20 which we are discussing this afternoon provides for a 24 per cent increase in premiums to be paid by employees and employers.
Madam Speaker, we know perfectly well that in Canada, at least 75 per cent of our businesses are small and medium-sized businesses. This means that these businesses, which are the foundation of our economy, will have a hidden tax to pay as a result of this 24 per cent increase. That is how the government tries to get us out of a recession that was created by its own policies: an excessively high dollar, high interest rates and, the icing on the cake, the GST, as a result of which the government collected $400 million more after the first three months it was in effect.
So, you can see the kind of position this government has put us in, not only with the May 26 Budget, but with all its economic policies since 1984.
Government Orders
Madam Speaker, before the Free Trade Agreement was signed, the government had promised that training courses would be offered to the workers who would loose their jobs to facilitate their reentry into the labour force. Three years later, we are still waiting for these courses, Madam Speaker. What has this government done since the Free Trade Agreement was implemented to ensure that adjustment programs are available to help the people who lost their jobs because of this agreement and the technology transfers flowing from retrain and find a new job? Nothing yet, Madam Speaker.
At the time Bill C-21 was passed, the government promised that $800 million would be allocated to manpower training. How much of these $800 million were spent, Madam Speaker? They are back today with yet another bill penalizing the workers and the work providers with a 24 percent increase in UI premiums. As we can see, Madam Speaker, there is still no training available and the unemployment rate is still very high, but the government is maintaining its high dollar policy anyway.
It is no wonder, Madam Speaker, considering this high dollar policy, the high interest rates and the GST, that Canadians go cross-border shopping on week-ends. The reason is simple: it is because of these economic policies. Did the government think about that when it came up with the free trade project? Did they think about a monetary policy that would have made it possible for Canadians to live well in their own country instead of moving south, Madam Speaker?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I began briefly a few minutes ago talking about this particular bill, C-20.1 indicated that during my address I would show that the government had a bad attitude toward the governance of Canadians generally. This is demonstrated by some of the things it is trying to do. This is a very sneaky way of going about the business of trying to govern the country. It is also trying to hide the truth.
What is this Bill C-20 all about? It is about transfer payments, and clearly it is about the extension of the freeze on health, education, the Canada Assistance Program. However, it also involves a number of other programs that are particularly important to Canadians
Government Orders
and to provinces: health, education, Canada Assistance Program, equalization, and I could mention several others.
It is also a bill that is extremely mischievous because it uses a stick approach. It is really the law of the jungle.
I want to quote from a research report that has been done on this. In this particular bill, which controls the transfers of massive amounts of moneys to provinces and to territories of Canada, we have a mechanism where, if the government chooses to do so, it could withhold funding in a number of areas. I think it is important to mention all of those areas. The equalization payments total about $8.4 billion. Tferritorial financing totals over a million dollars. Grants in lieu of taxes total $344 million. Public utilities income tax transfer payments total about $280 million. Statutory subsidies total about $36 million in 1991. The Canada Assistance Plan, as I mentioned, totals $6.4 billion. Crop insurance totals $207 million. The Official Languages in Education program totals $243 million. Miscellaneous health and welfare moneys amount to $170 million. Young offenders services amount to $158 million. Justice totals $77 million and transportation totals $69 million.
If the government, with the passage of Bill C-20 chooses to do so, and I quote: "It will be able to withhold transfers to offending provinces and territories" through these programs that I have just mentioned. That is why I have indicated that it is a mischievous piece of legislation that is extremely misleading.
It is also a piece of legislation that goes further in extending the ideological agenda of the government because it penalizes the poor provinces such as Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and the Atlantic provinces. The weak will get weaker, and much, much weaker unless things change and they change quickly.
Let me give an example of where it is particularly brutal.

It is in the field of education. I have talked several times about the administrative rate of 3 per cent that is levied on student loans. Those students are poor, of course, otherwise they would not borrow money if they have any. As far as assistance to students is concerned, I have already mentioned that the criteria have not changed since 1984, even though the inflation rate has gone up 30 per cent and even more. There again, the students have paid a lot more than they should have. It is unfortunate.

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
They also talk about the GST on books and learning material that students need.

With respect to the goods and services tax, I want to bring to the House's attention material I have received from a colleague and friend from my constituency. He brought this to my attention to allow me to share with others a very, very serious repercussion relating to the goods and services tax, and I want to quote from this material. "The effect the goods and services tax has on at least one series of books is as follows", and I am quoting from the material he has received from the publisher, an American publisher. The publisher says that: "Canadian orders will be priced under 'Other countries'"-notice that-"rather than the former pricing under 'the U.S. and Canada'".
The publisher explains that this is the result of high administrative costs connected to compliance with the Canadian GST that became effective January 1, 1991. Canadian members must also pay the 7 per cent GST tax on all orders shipped to Canada.
The publisher says: "We will add this 7 per cent to the invoice we send to the Society, and the Society should instruct members to include the 7 per cent GST in their payment to the Society".
The publisher points to high administrative costs in connection with the goods and services tax and, as a consequence, is raising the prices to Canadian customers. These price increases range from 14 to 19 per cent.
This is an example of not only the 7 per cent goods and services tax on education, quite apart from everything else that has been happening, but another administrative cost that has been added on in order to respond to the additional costs of administering this particular tax.
I find this shocking and I find it most unfortunate because the government has always said that it is simply 7 per cent with very, very slight administrative costs.
I have indicated that this bill attempts to control the transfer of moneys. Education and health has been hit in a massive kind of way.
From 1986, when the government started tampering with the formula, to 1995, the date to which it has
extended the freeze, we are talking about $30 billion less for health and education, $30 billion. That is quite apart from all of the additional costs that I have mentioned, the 3 per cent administrative fee, no change in student aid criteria since 1984, the goods and services tax and those additional fees that have been added on, no increases in training or retraining, and of course, the limitation of growth in research and development. I could go on. I have mentioned that student debt is growing out of sight, tuition fees increasing at an alarming rate. This government has really botched it this time.
It is unfortunate because it could have corrected a number of things. When one looks at what it has done with the economy-the $30 billion deficit, the $400 billion debt, despite the fact that it had a revenue base of $70 billion in 1984, and now it is in excess of $130 billion-you wonder where the money has gone.
It brags about its 3.8 per cent growth limitation. Of course, it has done that. It has off-loaded it to the provinces which off-load it to the municipalities, to the hospitals, to the colleges, to the universities, to the young men and women out there who are trying to train and become educated so that they can contribute fully to Canada, to our competitiveness as a nation.
I am really concerned that the government has stuck it again to the poor, to the poor provinces, to the students, clearly the handicapped, and many, many other Canadians.
Increases in unemployment insurance premiums are another example of a sneaky, sneaky approach to governing because it increased the premium to employees and to employers by over 20 per cent. It is an indirect kind of tax.
We have not looked at that sufficiently, because we would find massive increases to Canadians throughout this country.

I therefore ask the government to do the truly honourable thing and withdraw this bill immediately.
June 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, in this country today, there is a lot of concern over unification. This is a country that seems to have an ongoing debate with respect to the Constitution.
There are other factors besides the Constitution that unify this country. There is some real cement outside the Constitution that keeps us united. Part of that has been a concern by Canadians for all the regions of this country.
We are a country made up of regions and we are a country that is spread out geographically over a large area. This country is a very large nation.
Historically we have found that in order to keep this country together, in order to keep a high standard of living for all Canadians, we have had to implement certain programs and certain policies. Not the least of those programs have been health and education. It is Canada that led the way. Saskatchewan started with the health care program, and the country followed. What we have is a situation where this government is transferring the responsibilities that it has taken in health and education to the provinces.
The reason for national programs in the first place was that certain provinces were unable to provide the same level of health and education that other parts of the country could provide. What we are seeing now is a reversion, a stepping back to that period of time.
When we transfer these responsibilities, we are again going to see certain areas of the country suffering far more than they already suffer. We have already seen health care cuts in Newfoundland. In my province of Saskatchewan, we have seen some major cuts in health and potential cuts in other areas.
Unless a government is going to look after the needs of the poor, the sick and the young, a country will not be healthy. The only government in this country today that has decided to look after those areas of our society has been the government in this province of Ontario under Bob Rae.
The NDP government has received a lot of criticism for its recent budget and for the direction it has taken. It has taken a direction that is different than the federal government and different than any provincial government, but it has decided and it has committed itself to maintaining as high a level of education, of health care and support for those people who need it as it possibly can.
Government Orders
Granted, it is in a better position than many provinces, but it has chosen a different path. It has been the New Democratic Party, over the history of this country, which has chosen a different path. We have chosen a path of committing ourselves to those people who are less fortunate and also to providing opportunities for all Canadians, not just a few.
If this is going to be a country that will stay united, if it is a country that will remain committed to itself, it is essential that we have a viable health care system and a viable educational system. Simply, what we are debating today is a further dismantling of that system.
Unless we proceed to change this attitude, this continued backslide is going to cause more problems with unity in this country than any constitutional change ever did. There are questions this government has to answer that it has been failing to answer. It must justify to Canadians why it is taking this attitude. Why has this government decided to abandon health care? Why has this government decided to cut back on educational transfer payments? Why is it doing these things? Why is it forcing provinces to make some very difficult decisions with respect to hospitals, with respect to nursing care and with respect to education?
The areas that are suffering the most are the areas that can least afford it. We have in this country today large rural areas of Canada which are suffering in many aspects. There are problems with transportation, there are problems with postal services which have been cut. This is a government which has made some vicious cuts in the postal service and is planning to make further drastic cuts. In fact, the government has indicated quite publicly that it wishes to see the postal service privatized. The postal service is now in the business of making money, not providing a service to Canadians. Rural Canadians suffer from that.
In the province of Newfoundland, Memorial University has just recently cut a program that was being sponsored by the university to provide required services to many of the small communities in Newfoundland. It was an extension service of Memorial University which has now been cut. There are something like 700 or 800 small communities in that province. Memorial University, with its extension department, was providing an educational service on a practical basis, where the need had arisen. With the cuts the Clyde Wells government has made, and with its own priorities, which I would suggest are not in the best interests of Newfoundlanders, it has affected that province and those small communities. We see it time and time again.

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
In my province of Saskatchewan, I have spoken many times on the difficulties that rural Canadians are suffering and the effect it is having on communities. It is also having an effect on the urban centres as well. Certainly the city of Moose Jaw is suffering as a result of programs of this government. No place in the province of Saskatchewan is immune.
What we really need is a government that is going to commit itself to providing essential services to Canada, not on a profit-sharing basis, but on a cost per service basis, a basis that is going to guarantee that all Canadians, whether they live in Toronto or whether they live in Watrous, Saskatchewan, or wherever they live, will be guaranteed a level of service. They need to know they can send their children to school and that there will be opportunities for them to attend university, and that the educational system will still remain as a high institution. As well, they need to know that the health care system will remain the vital institution that it still is today, although it is starting to slide.
I want to close by saying that the onus is on this government to stand up and provide its justification for the direction it is taking this country. It should provide answers for the direction in which it wants to see rural Canada develop, because it is making no comment with respect to that.
I think that Canadians would like to see some members on the government side let us know exactly where they stand with respect to this program, with respect to rural Canada and with respect to the regions of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this debate today, because the bill that we are discussing is Bill C-20 which implements the recent budget restrictions on transfers to the provinces and it is an extremely important bill from the point of view of federal-provincial relations. It is also very important from the point of view of the operation of hospitals, medical facilities generally and educational institutions across this country, very particularly in my riding of Kingston and the Islands where the second largest employer is Queen's University at Kingston. There are two universities, the other is the Royal Military College. It will not be affected by these
cuts since it receives its funding directly from the federal government. Kingston's hospitals and Kingston's universities feel the pinch as a result of the proposed changes contemplated in this Bill C-20 and I wish to register my very strong objection to what the government is doing in this case.
I would like to refer to the recent report by the National Council on Welfare which outlined the history of EPF cuts in the last few years, particularly since this government took office. The report is unchallenged by the government. We have had no evidence in any of the speeches given by government members today that would indicate that the report was in any way inaccurate. Perhaps to make clear what is going on, I would like to review some of the items in that report.
In 1986 the government announced that EPF entitlements would no longer grow with the economy as they had done previously but would be held to economic growth minus two percentage points. In 1989 it changed that two to three, so that the EPF entitlements would be held to economic growth minus three percentage points. In the 1990 budget, the government announced a total freeze on EPF entitlements for two years. That is for the two years following that 1990 budget, and after two years the EPF entitlements would increase at the rate of the Gross National Product minus three percentage points, in other words, the old rate.
In the latest budget, and the reason for the bill we have today, the government announced that the freeze on entitlements would continue through to the end of the 1994-95 financial year, and after that the formula of GNP minus three would again apply.
The effect of this freeze that has been imposed is effectively to deprive the provinces of very significant sums of money. I want to look at the chart provided by the National Council on Welfare which indicated the size of the cuts.
I want to point out that in 1986-87, normal EPF entitlement in Canada amounted to $16.8 billion. With the cuts that were imposed in that year, $10 million was given up. By 1991-92, this year, $4 billion a year has been foregone as a result of the changes that the government has introduced. In other words, the provinces are receiving $4 billion less than they would have received had these changes not been introduced.
June 17, 1991

By the financial year ending March 31, 1995, that figure will have more than doubled to $9.2 billion, a very very significant decrease in the federal contribution to provincial programs in education and health.
I suggest that it is becoming a disastrous chain of events.
Now I want to refer to the stealth with which this government has acted in this matter. The hon. member for Mount Royal in her most able speech earlier today indicated how stealthy and sneaky the government was being in its dealings with the public.

The minister answered:
Mr. Speaker, as usual the member for Hamilton East is wrong.

Money given to the provinces this year is more than it was last year, except that the way we provide the money could be different.

I think the record is a disgraceful one. It is a disaster. Surely the purpose of education in our country, post-secondary education in particular, is to equip our talented younger people with the skills they need to carry on effectively in the workplace. We have a pressing need in this country for scientists, for persons with scientific skills of a tremendous variety, and persons with high levels of education in a host of fields. We have ample evidence to support that in the fact that there are job opportunities for these people across our country.
At a time when there is a demand for better training and better educational facilities across Canada, the government is bent on reducing the opportunities for those educational institutions to expand and to provide better services. The effect of the government cutbacks is exactly the opposite.
In my own province of Ontario the significant reductions in the ability of universities to deliver programs has been very marked. I do not have the figures here today but I am sure I am stating the fact when I say that the payments to universities for their operations have not kept up with the rate of inflation. The universities across Ontario have been faced with major cutbacks in all kinds of areas in order to continue to pay a reasonable salary to their employees.

Mr. Speaker, this is another example of the government saying one thing and doing another.
Time and again we have seen the Prime Minister, his ministers and members of his caucus standing up and saying how important post-secondary education is to Canada, how important it is to educate our youth, how important it is for the growth of our economy that we have a well trained and well educated population.
They say it with a very concentrated, serious look into the television camera here in the House of Commons, and give the impression that they really do favour post-secondary education. They then go and introduce bills, such as Bill C-20 which continues the cuts to the provinces for post-secondary education. They are doing this at a time when the universities in the provinces are
increasing their tuition fees. They are doing this at a time when they have cut the moneys available for summer employment for students. They are doing it at a time when jobs are very difficult to obtain, when the rate of unemployment is extremely high.
What will be the result? The result will be, putting all of these policies of the government together, that fewer and fewer people will be able to go to university. The fees will be higher as a result of these cuts that the federal government is dishing out to the provinces. Students will not be able to earn their way to universities with jobs in the private sector or the public sector because the jobs just are not there and the federal government is cutting its support of those programs.
What else is being cut in this bill? Another example of the government saying one thing and doing another. Some people call this sort of politics the politics of rhetoric, the politics of smoke and mirrors where you try to give the impression with that very serious Prime Minister look that you are really in favour of health care and post-secondary education. Then you cut them in another measure another day.
It is the same with health care. The government speaks very highly of its commitment to our health care system-one of the best in the world. It was one of the best in the world, the Canadian medicare system. Here it is, once again, cutting these programs.
If we look at the amounts that the federal government was originally expected to contribute to the provinces under the EPF program-which is the program through which the federal government helps the provinces with respect to post-secondary education and medicare-in 1986 and we look at what in fact it is doing as a result of the bills to cut these contributions starting in 1986, we will see that between 1986 and the year 2000, as a result of this legislation and other similar pieces of legislation, the federal government will have taken away $97.6 billion from the provinces. This is almost $100 billion. Well, $100 billion has to mean a lot to provinces which must find moneys to support their universities, their hospitals, their medical research centres and so on.
For government members to say that this will not mean anything or to give us the impression that they are not really cutting but increasing funding is a fraud on the Canadian population.
June 17, 1991

The government is trying to pretend that because the amounts in dollars are increasing that it is not cutting. In fact, the provinces, the universities and the health care institutions were led to believe that they were going to get a certain amount in the years 1990-91 and 1991-92 and so on. However, because of bills like this they are not going to get those amounts of money. They are going to be left holding the bag, so to speak.
What is also very insidious about this type of legislation is that the more the federal government cuts the more it aggravates the regional disparities in this country. Under the EPF formula when the federal government redistributed money to the provinces for health care and universities, it was assuring by those moves that the Atlantic provinces and other provinces of Canada- Quebec, Saskatchewan and so on-that are not as wealthy as Ontario and B.C. would have equivalent institutions. It was assuring that no matter where you lived in Canada, you could be assured of hospitals, health care and universities that were of a high standard.
If the federal government takes away the money as it is doing in this bill, it is saying that if you live in a rich province like Ontario-and I say that relatively speaking, because Ontario is also suffering a veiy serious recession right now- you have better health care facilities and better universities, because there is a lot of industry and a lot of development in Ontario, but if you live in Newfoundland or Prince Edward Island or Nova Scotia, and you have to rely to a much greater extent on provincial resources, how can you keep up? That is a result of this Bill C-20.
So far I have only spoken about the cuts to health care and to post-secondary education, university education. By the way, post-secondary education also includes the community colleges and the CEGEPs in Quebec, not just universities.
The bill also breaks another promise of the government, and one that I was very closely involved in. That promise concerns the premiums which must be paid for unemployment insurance. When the government introduced its famous Bill C-21 to cut unemployment insurance benefits a few years ago and to transfer some of those benefits into training programs, when it did that the minister made a commitment that unemployment insurance premiums would remain the same for three years, for 1990, 1991, and 1992. At the same time the
Government Orders
government withdrew the federal contribution to the unemployment insurance fund which was a very large amount. Under the law, as it then was, if the rate of unemployment went above a certain percentage-I believe it was 6 per cent-then the federal government was obliged to pay for the benefits as a result of the increased unemployment.
With Bill C-21 the government cut out entirely the federal government's contribution, meaning that the entire unemployment insurance fund would have to be supported by the contributions of employers and employees. At the same time, it said: "We are going to freeze contributions by employers and employees to $2.80 per $100 of income, and that would stay the same". Government Orders
Under the guise of ensuring that the deficit comes under manageable control, the government is abdicating all responsibilities of nation building, bringing people together and ensuring that all Canadians have a stake in this country. They can only ensure this stake, live and materialize it, if they see that all of their hard-earned income, sacrifices, and commitments to their communities, provinces and fellow Canadians result in the kinds of programs that give them access to Canadianism and to a patriotic involvement in medicare, education and those standards that define us, both by our aspirations and by our achievements, those standards that give each and every one of us in this country and elsewhere an indication of what we stand for, both from the point of view of youth and from those who are not as young.
Mr. Speaker, I know that I speak to someone who is more than interested in some of the figures that I draw to your attention. By the end of this decade 14 per cent of our population will be in the area we call seniors. With an aging population, what are we doing? The government says it is going to establish the kinds of cuts and restraints that will ensure that people who fall into that category of seniors, those people who may not be so fortunate as to have access to the kind of jobs that will provide them with a standard of living to which they have become accustomed and through no fault of their own have seen eroded, will not have sufficient funds at their disposal.
We are going to abdicate our responsibility to Canadians who have contributed to this country by sweat of brow, by dint of participation and by a desire to ensure that the political format, the economy and the social structure be such that they take care of each and every one of us, one and all, at a time when we need them the most.
One of the tragedies of today is that the cuts in the EPF financing put at greater risk many of those seniors who rely on their Canada Pension Plan contributions and Old Age Security which combined, assuming that individual Canadians were able to participate fully in the previous program, will give them very little more than $900 a month, on an eroding basis. That $900 a month in the city of Toronto will get them very, very little. The cost of living in a city like Toronto when one takes into account the amount one has to pay for rent and then for a food basket, leaves very little for anyone who falls into the category of seniors.
What are we doing as a country? As I said earlier on, we are turning our backs and abdicating our responsibilities to those people who contributed mightily to the creation of a system upon which they can no longer draw. It is almost criminal that I would have to introduce this example. In Canada we have many Canadians who come from other countries. Fully 8 million Canadians do not have their origins in this country, and they are proud Canadians nonetheless. They have contributed to the wealth of this country. They continue to strengthen its social and cultural fabric, but they still have ties, cultural and spiritual ties elsewhere.
The countries that spawned them still recognize contributions. I might cite one. The country of Italy contributes to former Italian residents. Those citizens represent for us an enormous wealth just by being here, with this infusion of cash that comes in. It allows the government not to give the attention it should to the plight of citizens, because it knows there is a quarter of a billion dollars annually coming from a generous foreign authority. It knows it can draw a further $50 million from such revenues.
It has become even more lax in terms of accepting financial responsibility for the benefits of its citizens. Those citizens, like so many other seniors, are subject to increasing property tax and increasing provincial taxes, and then have to be subjected to a GST of 7 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on the budget bill, Bill C-20.
I participate because I profoundly disagree with the economic and budgetary policies, not only of this govern-
June 17, 1991

ment, but of successive governments, in fact, going back in this country to Confederation.
We happen to live in one of the most privileged comers of the globe. We have a relatively small population, with a relatively high level of technological experience and infrastructure yet, as we look around our country today, we see how we are increasingly squandering our heritage.
I think any budget, including this budget and this bill, must satisfy three tests: first, what does it do about the inequality of wealth in this country? We have a country which, despite our wealth, has one of the worst records in the industrial world for a spread between rich and poor. Over a million Canadians suffer serious chronic poverty, many of them children, most of them women. Over the last six years; in fact, one can reach back into the seventies under successive Liberal and Conservative governments and find that we have increased that spread between rich and poor. This budget, this legislation, fails the test of what it can do for equality of income in Canada.
The second test is how a government, in this case the federal government, uses the power of budget and uses its economic policies to insert progressive social and environmental policies into the marketplace. It now appears that virtually all of us believe that the market has its place, the market is a very efficient tool for the redistribution of certain economic considerations and for developing a certain aspect of our wealth.
But I think all of us agree that the market fails to consider social and environmental factors in its decisionmaking. It is the responsibility of government and of Parliament to insist on certain social and environmental values, for example, the right of collective bargaining, fair standards in the workplace, pay equity, an end to discrimination, environmentally sound policies. This budget erodes the relatively inadequate policies that we already have.
Speaker after speaker has drawn the attention of this House to the abject failure of this government to take its responsibilities seriously for the maintenance of social and environmental standards: the shift of responsibility to the provinces, the erosion of our health care, the inadequate support for poverty groups and for women's programs in this country, the complete failure to take an effective lead in preserving our environment. This budget fails that test.
Government Orders
The third test is whether this budget contributes to the creation of wealth, how we as a country earn our living. We just had the advantage of going to Halifax 10 days ago and visiting the shipyard. I know from my own constituency in Victoria the state of the shipbuilding industry in this country. It has been allowed to collapse under the neglect of Conservative and Liberal policies over the last two decades.
We look at industry after industry. Liberal policies turned the fishing industry over to private companies and this government failed to respond to the disaster in the fishing industry on both coasts. We look at the destruction of the agricultural industry across Canada, the free trade agreement with its destruction of the manufacturing industry. Almost every industry and the way we have to earn our living has been turned over by this government to the marketplace, a marketplace which is increasingly owned by the United States, and other foreign capital, whose interest is not Canadian, whose interest is only in making a dollar for foreign investors.
As a result, our ability to earn our living is fast seeping out of this country. The government in the Speech from the Throne pays lip service to education and research. It says this is critical to make us competitive. Yet where is the money? Where is the leadership? What is the government doing? Zero. This government is failing future generations of Canadians in failing to ensure that education, training, and research in Canada is of first quality. It is a national responsibility that this should happen, that education, training and research should be given top priority. It is the only way in which we can compete in the future, and it will not be enough for the government to make nice statements in the Speech from the Throne. This government, in this bill, and in this budget, has failed Canadians.
Where do we go from here? We look at where the government has spent money. I am the defence/disarma-ment critic for our party and I have the budgetary estimates for defence. But look at some of the things it does spend money on. This year, in my own constituency of Victoria, the estimates provide $1,597 million for a new cadet dining hall at Royal Roads, and nearly $1 million for additional cadet quarters. For projects in other parts it is going to

spend over $16 million for new facilities for Canadian Forces maritime experimental and test ranges, $241,000 for new jetties, $695,000 for a new officers' mess, $3.7 million for programs in Kingston, Ontario, a naval reserve armoury, $1 million for a naval reserve division in London, $4 million for Moose Jaw, and nearly $8 million in Chilliwack, one of the bases that is said to be up for closure.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is probably one of the most aggressive pieces of legislation ever introduced by the Government of Canada.
It should be known as the "bond and gag" provinces bill. That is exactly what it does. If we were to use a nautical metaphor, perhaps they are pushing the provinces to the end of the gang plank with a blindfold over their eyes. It completely restricts and inhibits the provinces for operating programs which people have been used to for years.
I am thinking of programs of not only health and education. The government started by cutting back on Established Programs Financing. What it means in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador is the closing of hospital beds. Provinces such as that depend heavily on federal transfer payments to operate hospital beds and classrooms.
They depend heavily on those transfer payments. When those transfer payments are cut back, one of two things has to happen. Either the province has to increase its costs because it is limited in the amount of tax revenue it can collect or it has to shut down classrooms and hospital beds. That has happened in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador as a result of the regressive and restrictive acts of the Government of Canada.
Beds have been closed and classrooms have been closed in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. I should say too that this comes at a time when this country supposedly is entering what is known as the information economy, in which knowledge and education are more important than ever before.
In a province which has the highest employment rate of anywhere in the country, the young people who want a chance at a job, an occupation and a good way of life are restricted from getting that at the very time when that opportunity means more to them than ever before. That is the effect of the policy of the government. It is not just the last budget. The last several budgets have consistently restricted the growth of Established Programs Financing to the province of Newfoundland and Labrador.
Now the government has said: "If as a result of the cutbacks we have made in transfer payments for health services, you institute additional costs on the people who receive those services, that health care and that education, and if provinces such as Newfoundland and Labrador institute additional costs, you are going to be penalized. How are you going to be penalized? You are going to be penalized in the most severe and restrictive way you can imagine. We can cut any transfer payments to you as a province."
June 17, 1991

Any program that the Government of Canada now enters into with the province of Newfoundland and Labrador as a result of Bill C-20 can be cut. If that government were to try to maintain the level of services that were previously offered by increasing costs, which it would have to do as a result of the cutbacks of Established Programs Financing, it would be penalized by equalization payments being cut.
The province of Newfoundland is trying to increase those equalization payments. Equalization payments can be cut by the Government of Canada if the province of Newfoundland dares to institute costs which simply maintain the level of services that people are getting at the moment.

It is one of those communities which does not have an established, strong private sector. It depends very heavily on the Government of Canada facilities in that town. There is an air force base in Goose Bay and about 2,000 people owe their living directly or indirectly to that. The municipal government depends on that as another community would on Abitibi or the Iron Ore Company of Canada or MacMillan Bloedel.
The Government of Canada in Goose Bay is in exactly the same position as a major corporate taxpayer and the Government of Canada transfers every year to the municipality of Goose Bay a great deal of its budget, the budget it, at the municipal level, uses to provide normal services to the people who live in that community.
If Bill C-20 goes through, grants in lieu of taxes can be cut. If the province of Newfoundland dares to increase costs to maintain a level of services, the Government of Canada can now cut out the grants in lieu of taxes to Goose Bay and every other similar community in Canada.
What else can they cut?
Native people, the Inuit, the Innu who live in Labrador depend for their education, their health services, their post-secondary education and for many of the services in their community on federal-provincial agreements between the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador because the Government of Canada transfers to the province of Newfoundland an amount equal to what it pays per capita on average to a native person anywhere else in this country. It transfers every year to the province of Newfoundland that amount for providing services to native people.
