If Bill C-20 goes through and if the province of Newfoundland and Labrador has the temerity to increase costs in order to maintain a decent level of services, grants for native funding to Newfoundland and Labrador can be cut.
What else can be cut?
Many women who want to enter the work force are single mothers. Seventy per cent of all post-secondary education students, part time, are women. Many of those, probably the majority, are single mothers. Why do they want an education? They want an education because it is the only passport they have to success.
What happens to their children while they go after that passport? They must have day care.
If Bill C-20 goes through, the Canada Assistance Plan, which is the main vehicle for providing day care to those who have children and who yet want to take advantage of post-secondary education, can be cut automatically and arbitrarily by the Government of Canada if the province of Newfoundland and Labrador dares to increase its costs in order to maintain services because of the cutbacks of the Government of Canada in Established Programs Financing and other budgetary items. If it does that the Government of Canada has the right under C-20 to cut back the Canada Assistance Plan.
This is bad enough anywhere in the country. It is doubly worse in rural areas or in single industry towns and which are well away from urban centres, but in northern Canada it can be even more disastrous.
I have just cited the example of Goose Bay, a community of about 8,000 people which could be severely affected if grants in lieu of taxes are cut.
I thought that the Government of Canada had realized that it simply cannot treat everybody in this country equally. There are some who are stronger and there are some who are weaker, there are some who have a strong private sector and some who have a weak private sector. There are some who have well developed economies and there are some who have less well developed economies. If you treat everybody the same across the board, then those who are far away and remote suffer more than others do.
I thought the Government of Canada had realized that because in its policy on the taxation of northern benefits it showed some understanding. I would say that the policy now of this present government is more generous and more comprehensive than the policy under the previous administration. All we were able to do was maintain the lack of taxation of northern benefits. The present government has instituted a wider and more

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
generous program. I thought it understood the special needs of northern Canada, but it obviously does not.
Under this particular bill, under this most regressive piece of legislation we have ever seen, it has the right to cut payments to native peoples, payments to students, payments to patients in hospital, payments to single mothers and payments to all those who are disadvantaged wherever they live in Canada, in cities but more particularly I am thinking of those in remote areas.
This bill cannot be allowed to pass. Those of us in this Chamber must do everything possible to stop it. We must say now, to all those Canadians who are listening across the country that it is time we had a revolution like the one we had on gray power when the government tried to tamper with pension payments. We saw a movement among the people in this country which forced the government to cancel that particular initiative. The same force must be used here, the same political power must be used here.
If this legislation goes through, it will give the government an ironclad grip, unmercifully bearing down on the economic future of young and old alike, all Canadians no matter where they live, in urban or in rural communities.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-20 is part of the continuing and sorry saga of Tory cutbacks in federal transfer payments to the provinces. If there were no cutbacks at all, there would be no need for this bill, no need whatsoever. It would be business as usual. The government would continue as a full partner in medicare.
According to this government, the purpose of the bill is to provide the government with the power to enforce provisions of the Canada Health Act. With the government getting out of medicare in just a few years down the road, it would soon have no say in the operations of our national health scheme.
The Tories, and this is their line, have brought in this bill ostensibly designed to punish provinces which do not
live up to the Canada Health Act. This is the Tory way of saying that we care about medicare. Do not believe it. Do not believe it for a minute. Do not believe it because there is a good chance that this bill, if it ever became law, would be thrown out by the courts.
Under our Constitution, the administration of health care is the sole prerogative of the provinces, and the provinces certainly will not let go unchallenged any law that would punish them for the way they run their health schemes.
The federal Tories have had a say in medicare since they assumed power in 1984, but only because they provided cash. Once the cash is gone, so goes the say in running medicare, Bill C-20 or no Bill C-20; it is as simple as that. In other words, this bill is a sham and it is a fraud. If the government really cares about medicare the way it says it does, then I say this: fund medicare. It is the proper thing to do. It is the only thing to do. It is exactly what the Canadian people want this government to do. Fund medicare and fund it properly. Medicare is a source of pride for all Canadians. It is one of the high points of our civilization. It provides us with one of those wonderful differences between ourselves and Americans. The Americans are deeply jealous of our system, deeply jealous of medicare. They wish they had it, and they wish they had responsible politicians who would give it to them.
Canadians were shocked when they heard a report from the National Council of Welfare the other day. The report said: "Soon medicare will be effectively dead as a national health insurance system." This does not come from a partisan political party, it comes from an advisory group to the federal government itself, and a highly respected group at that.
According to the welfare council, if the current trend continues, these cash payments to the provinces will first disappear in the province of Quebec just five years from now. The last payment, according to the current trend, will occur in the fiscal year 2009-2010, and that would be to the territory of Yukon.

If this happens, what would be the result? According to the Welfare Council-we will pick a group which is not partisan on this issue-it says, and I quote: "Without substantial federal cash payments, regional disparities would be magnified and people in poorer provinces would have to make do with health care services which are inferior to the services enjoyed by Canadians who happen to live in richer provinces".
The people of my province, Manitoba, understand that. They know that if they are left to finance medicare on their own, they would not be able to afford the kind of health care scheme that richer Ontario could sustain. If that were to happen, in a sense Manitobans would be turned into second-class citizens. That, to me, is totally unacceptable. To me there is only one kind of Canadian citizen, and that is a first-class Canadian citizen.
I believe, to my very core, that Canadians will punish any political party that does not give its full support to medicare and that is why I believe that they will defeat this government at the first opportunity. Canadians also have this warning. They warn anyone to beware of politicians who advocate putting medicare in the hands of the provinces. It is a warning because it is just a code word for getting rid of medicare. Those politicians know very well that the smaller provinces cannot afford the kind of medicare that we have become accustomed to.
What have we become accustomed to? Have we become accustomed to a scheme, to a national program that we really cannot afford? Not on your life. On a comparative basis medicare is a bargain. It is a bargain, particularly compared to what is available in our big neighbouring country of the United States of America. We Canadians spend only 9 per cent of our wealth on medicare, and from that 9 per cent of our wealth we receive full coverage.
What is the case in the United States? It spends 12 per cent of its wealth on its national health scheme. Under its scheme almost 40 million Americans have no health coverage at all, and another 100 million Americans have only spotty coverage. Think of it. We spend 9 per cent for full coverage while Americans spend 12 per cent of their wealth and they have poor coverage.
Government Orders
One other thing, and this should always be driven home, we spend no more as a percentage of our wealth on medicare today than we did 10 years ago. That is an absolute fact.
I want to say a few words about post-secondary education. I want to mention post-secondary education because these cutbacks in transfer payments to the provinces also affect federal support of our colleges and universities. Federal funding has made it possible for huge numbers of Canadians to go to college and university without having to pay exorbitantly high tuition fees. That is another of those wonderful differences between ourselves and Americans. Any cuts in the area of post-secondary education are very worrisome to me, and I would say very worrisome to most Canadians. I say that because of the real link between poverty and the level of education.
The Welfare Council printed a graph which shows very clearly the link between poverty and the level of education. This graph shows that almost 20 per cent of family heads with an elementary education live below the poverty line and 60 per cent of Canadian individuals with elementary education live below the poverty line. How does that compare with those who have gone to university? About four per cent of family heads with university education live below the poverty line and about 12 to 13 per cent of those with university education live below the poverty line. That is the link between post-secondary education and poverty and it is something that we should not tolerate.
The Tories talk about increasing competition around the world. How are we going to compete in this global environment if we cut back on education?
This bill should be defeated and it should be defeated now because it is simply a continuation of the erosion of federal support of medicare and post-secondary education.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to rise tonight to discuss this bill. It is a bill which furthers the off-loading of federal responsibilities on to the backs of the provinces and, as in the case of other matters, the backs of municipalities as well.

Government Orders
In Saskatchewan we are only too aware of the results of the off-loading of federal programs on to provinces and municipalities. In fact, thanks to the efforts of members of the Saskatchewan Urban Municipalities Association the matter of RCMP funding was reviewed and readdressed by this government. RCMP funding is something that would devastate the funding base of Saskatchewan's smaller communities. Thanks to Mayor Carlson in Melfort, who headed up the Saskatchewan Urban Municipalities Association negotiation team, and representations by numerous members of Parliament in this House the issue was readdressed by this government.
We can only hope that the government will also be reconsidering the moves that it is making in terms of off-loading for education and health care spending as well.
Certainly, the off-loading restricts the provinces in their ability to do other things. Those other things are within their own area of responsibility, such as funding infrastructures within the provincial boundaries to ensure that we have good quality facilities for the delivering of education and health care, and also the structure of sewer and water systems in the provinces, highway systems in the provinces, and the other structures that we rely on for improving our quality of life.
A province like Saskatchewan, significantly rural in nature, relies heavily on that collective support base from the province and the federal government. The support base helped, during the CCF years in Saskatchewan, to deliver the electrification period to the rural areas. Without that we could not fly over Saskatchewan today and witness the bright dots of light all over that province.
It also means that if the province has good funding for education and health care it can support the other areas of economic concern which are the direct responsibility of the provincial governments.
I speak specifically here, coming from Saskatchewan, of agricultural issues. I personally would like to see the federal government take more responsibility for agricultural matters. I do not believe that the provinces should have the level of responsibility that they are being forced to accept for agricultural issues. Certainly if the funds were available to adequately finance education and health care then the provinces would be freer to fund
such programs as the crop insurance and income insurance programs which have been developed recently. I am also quite critical about the agricultural support program that exists today.
I am very proud of the work done by New Democrats at our recent convention in Halifax, held just a weekend ago. Party members from all across Canada attended a national convention in Atlantic Canada. One of the main resolutions coming out of that convention was one dealing with farm policy on the prairies. It was very pleasing to me to recognize the unanimous support of Canadians from across the country for our agricultural policy.
I would like to bring parts of it to the attention of the House, because I think there is nothing more important than communication, sharing information and understanding. One of the things that impressed me about our convention in Halifax was that Canadians from broad, diverse backgrounds got together to discuss issues, the Constitution among them. This agricultural policy was developed by people who have an interest in shipbuilding, mining, real estate, teaching, small and medium sized businesses, and people who just have an interest in people in general.
The delegates to the convention recognized that GRIP, the Gross Revenue Insurance Program, a joint program supported by the federal government and negotiated with the provinces, did not return the cost of production to the farmers. They felt that it was very important for the government to develop programs that would do that. The delegates looked very closely at the way the GRIP was being administered and said: "This certainly off-loads federal responsibilities on to the provinces". It was another one of those programs which was tying the hands of the provinces for funds which they should not have had the responsibility for.
The federal government funds a piece of the program, but the producers, the farmers within that province, do not have access to those funds unless the provinces agree to support the program as well and kick in a certain amount of funding for it.
In Saskatchewan we are now seeing the provincial Conservative government being forced to harmonize the provincial tax system with the federal government's GST. They are saying it is because they have to support this federal government agriculture program financially.

Therefore, off-loading has really hurt the people of Saskatchewan. I do not have to tell them, but I tell members of the Conservative Party here in the House that the people who just a few months ago were not paying any tax on restaurant meals or children's clothing are now finding that they have the 7 per cent GST and now a brand new provincial 7 per cent tax being added on to those items and in the near future to all services-mechanics fees', accountants' fees, lawyers' fees and those sorts of thing which were not previously taxed either by provincial or federal government.
When this group of people looked at the agricultural policy, they felt that there were some very important things that had to be dealt with. The New Democratic Party has now developed a support program for agriculture, supported by members of the party from Newfoundland to Vancouver Island.
The resolution of the party is very specific. It asks that any agricultural program not down-load the costs to the territorial or provincial governments and to the farmers. It also asks that any program be based on the cost of production and not some artificial numbers that the government or someone else comes up with. It has pay-out levels capped at a reasonable level. In other words, in order to prevent the large farmers from getting the lion's share of any dollars available on support programs, they are evenly distributed to ensure that the small and medium sized producers get more, I would say in this case, than their fair share of the support dollars available. More important, the policy supports the marketing of all grains and oilseeds through the Canadian Wheat Board and would like the name of the Canadian Wheat Board changed to the Canadian Grains Board, indicating that the export marketing of grain would include oilseeds as well as grains.
Certainly the policy supports the reinstatement of a two-price wheat policy in Canada, the policy that this government implemented in order to help lower the price of breads in Canada because we would be able to bring in lower priced wheat for milling. In fact anyone who has bought bread in Canada knows that the change in the two-price wheat system has only been to the detriment of the farmer and not to the benefit of the consumer.
Government Orders
Our policy also suggests and demands that we continue the interest-free, cash advance program on a permanent basis and that it establishes a market assurance program in which farmers would be paid for unsold grain at the end of the crop year and storage would also be paid for that grain. Finally, the program would have to be sensitive to environmental concerns and to the need for sustainable production.
There is a great need for strong agricultural policy in provinces like Saskatchewan. We cannot deliver those types of programs if the hands of the provinces are restricted by federal policies tied to the off-loading of funding.
It is time this government and its supporters rethink the way in which they are looking at this type of government control over spending and develop much fairer programs that are much more inclusive for the Canadian population.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity tonight to express my views on Bill C-20, an act which extends the government's cap on Established Programs Financing.
As members know, this bill already reduces the federal government's commitment to the federal cash payments that go to the provinces for education and health. It also invokes the increase in unemployment insurance premiums which were announced in the last budget among other things.
This government has been talking for some time about the need for Canada to be internationally competitive. I do not think anyone quarrels with that objective, but certainly a government is judged or should be judged on its deed and its policies, not on its words and on its rhetoric.
In 1991 the former finance minister said that the world economy continued to grow more fiercely competitive. I want to quote what he said. He said that the fundamental problem is that our underlying ability to compete in the world marketplace has been falling behind that of our trading partners.
I commend the government for recognizing the problem, but I certainly condemn it for doing nothing about it. In fact, this government continues to bring in policies that have a negative effect on the institutions which train, educate and prepare our future work force for the challenges of international competition.

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
How are we going to compete in this fiercely competitive, international, economic environment if our work force is not equipped to compete?
This legislation that we have before us this evening continues the cap on the federal transfer payments for health and education. Right now universities are already feeling intense pressure from the federal government's cutbacks to date. We should be encouraging Canadians to attend post-secondary institutions. Instead this government is making policies that have a detrimental effect not only on the quality of the education experience, but on the financial capability of young Canadians to afford this necessary education.
I look at my own province of Prince Edward Island where just recently the University of Prince Edward Island announced that it would have to raise tuition fees 15 per cent. Student loans have not increased since 1984. Students are also feeling the effects of the GST. They even have to pay the GST on books. They have also been inflicted with a 3 per cent administration fee on student loans. These policies are all detrimental.
To tell you how it affects these students, I want to quote what one student has to say. A 21-year old honours physics student from the University of Prince Edward Island was quoted in an Island newspaper to have said: "I blame it on Mulroney. He really put a damper on higher education. He has been cutting grants left and right, freezing funding to the provinces. It is no wonder".
This government's policies are causing a deterioration of our education system both in quality and accessibility. It is not just the students, the educators, and the opposition members of Parliament who are concerned about this government's lack of support for education. The report by the National Council of Welfare released earlier this month expressed concern about the ability of the less prosperous provinces in our country to shoulder this increased debt that the federal government is pushing on to them.
Another report concluded saying that their continuing fear is that economically disadvantaged people in all areas of this country, as well as Canadians from the less
prosperous regions of our country, will be denied equality of opportunity if the federal government continues the present trend.
If one looks at the per cent of the Gross National Product that each of the provinces contributes to health and education spending one sees very quickly that the eastern provinces will be at a distinct disadvantage as the federal government reduces its commitment to education and health.
In my province of Prince Edward Island health and education spending is equivalent to 10.5 per cent of the GNP, whereas the average in Canada is a little over 7 per cent. What it means when we pay 10.5 per cent of the GNP as compared to the average of 7 per cent is that the burden of educational funding is much greater for provinces like Prince Edward Island. The impact of the decrease in the federal financial commitments is much more on this region than on any others.
In other words, what I am saying is that provinces with larger and stronger economies will have less difficulty raising that tax revenue than those with smaller economies.
If this type of government policy continues, there is no doubt that it will lead to regional discrepancies in education quality and inaffordability. It will mean that students in a more prosperous province which can afford to maintain and increase its level of educational funding will have a greater opportunity to succeed than students in a less prosperous region.
The long and short of this is that many of our young people will not receive the training, the education or the skills that will be required to compete in a highly competitive global market.
I have talked about the future, but I want to speak for a couple of minutes about what this bill will do to our present ability to compete. Certainly small business today is considered the engine of the economy. Roughly three out of four new jobs are created by small business. You would think that if a government wanted to put people back to work and stimulate the economy, it would bring in policies to help small business.
June 17, 1991

This government does not do that. In fact, it brings in policies that hinder small business. In this bill before us tonight, we have unemployment insurance premiums that will be increased 24 per cent. This increase becomes effective July 1 and this extra expenditure follows a record of bankruptcies of approximately 77 per cent last spring.
I think that one of the most frustrating aspects of this government's lack of policies for small business is watching as the government afflicts its attack on small business, knowing that small business is not the corporate elite. We are not talking here about the jet set, the executive lifestyles, the Bay Street society, the private clubs or the yachts in the harbour. We are talking about the farmer, the fishermen, the tourist operator, the comer bakery and the antique dealer.
Many of these people live in my riding, and they spend a lot of time, effort and energy in their work. Yet, this government continues to inflict more taxes, more paperwork and more reasons to reduce its work force than to expand it.
I want to conclude by asking this government to withdraw this bill. By doing that, it will help to ensure that our work force will receive the education, the skills and the abilities to compete in this very fast-changing, global economy. Also, it will help to ensure that we build a strong, competitive, Canadian economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak to Bill C-20. As you' know, Mr. Speaker, this legislation deals with federal-provincial fiscal arrangements and federal post-secondary education and health contributions.
Since 1977, the federal government makes contributions to health care and post-secondary education through the transfer of tax points and cash payments. Federal support for health and post-secondary education was supposed to keep pace each year with overall economic growth. Unfortunately, since 1986, support has been reduced as result of a series of decisions made by the Tory government, ostensibly to reduce the deficit. If this trend continues, according to the latest report by the National Welfare Council, the entire amount transferred in cash for health and post-secondary education under the 1977 fiscal arrangements would disappear in a matter of years.
Government Orders
Furthermore, if federal support continues to be cut, Canada will be faced with 12 different provincial and territorial systems instead of the national medicare system we have now, which varies very little from one end of the country to the other. If balkanization occurs, we will probably see a return, in many regions, to extra billing and hospital user fees, something the 1984 Canada Health Act had practically wiped out.

Bill C-20, the Budget Implementation Act, is to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act, Parliament of Canada Act, Public Utilities Income Thx Transfer Act and the Unemployment Insurance Act.
This is a very regressive bill. It will affect the fiscal arrangements between the provinces and the federal government, all provinces and the territories and the federal government.
It can affect areas of health care, child care, welfare payments, taxes, grants in lieu of taxes to municipalities, aboriginal grants.
It will affect farmers in the sense that they can cut back on crop insurance. It will affect students in post-secondary education especially and an area that has not been mentioned too much today, listening to the debate off and on, official languages and education. It will affect the young offenders services by the possibility of those transfers being cut to provinces.
It could affect legal aid programs and last, but not least, it could also affect transportation grants to provinces and municipalities.
That is one area that I am very concerned with also, seeing that it could very well affect moneys that are destined to airports for their operations. I have the Shilo airport in my riding which is in much need of funding at all times and cannot afford to be cut.
When we talk about Bill C-20,1 mention that it does affect the UIC and the unemployment insurance provisions within this legislation reverse the government's promise to help finance the program in difficult times.
If we go back a little bit and we look at the 1989 budget, the then finance minister pledged and I quote: "The government will continue to contribute to the financing of the program in difficult economic times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums and prudent to allow deficits to build up in the unemployment insurance account."

Government Orders
Given the extremely difficult economic times now faced by Canadians, the need for the government to contribute to the fund is quite obvious. I find that very amazing. I guess down east we would not use the words "broken promises". We will be very outright and use another word which is not allowed in this House, but we are very concerned with the way and the direction that this government is going in at this point in time.
When we look at the bill in its entirety, I guess the biggest chunk of it has to do with cash payments from medicare and higher education. One of the areas that we should look at is the report recently published by the National Council of Welfare. They they seem to substantiate their information. I will just read a quote here from one of their press releases. It says here and I quote: "federal cash payments from medicare and post-secondary education will disappear within a few years unless new fiscal arrangements are negotiated with the provinces and territories."
Looking at that report, and I notice that a number of my colleagues used that report for the basis of their speeches today, I should point out to those who are listening that the National Council of Welfare is not a Liberal organization. It is not a Conservative organization. It is non-partisan. It is a group of individuals mandated to advise the minister on matters pertaining to welfare, to the Health and Welfare Act and whatever. It is a group that is there to advise the minister. What are they actually saying? One of the things they are saying is that if the cuts continue, we could end up with 12 vastly different provincial and territorial medicare systems; we could end up with extra billing; we could end up with hospital user fees-we saw that in the past; we could end up with wholesale closures of hospital beds. In fact one of the statistics that is mentioned indicates that with these cuts there are going to be about 10,000 hospital beds closed across Canada.
Coming from Atlantic Canada, there is certainly an issue down home, and that is the question of regional disparities. According to the National Council of Welfare, regional disparities are going to be increased. So it
certainly is a concern for me and for members from Atlantic Canada.
If I could quote from this document, Mr. Speaker, on page 6 it says: "Without federal support, poorer provinces would be left with essentially two options, neither of them appealing; they could either raise provincial taxes to intolerable levels to support health and higher education as they now stand, or they could eliminate all but the barest of medical and educational services."
What we are going to end up with and what the council is trying to warn us of is a system for the rich and system for the poor. We could be going back in history, back to medieval days, if we want to use those terms.
On the weekend I had occasion to meet with a number of my constituents off and on, and at that time one of the questions they posed-and I have been getting this question quite often-is: What is going on up there in Ottawa; what is wrong with this government; can it not see the light up there? This bill is a continuance of that. They cannot understand how a government could be so cold and callous in introducing these types of bills.
This bill in itself, this Bill C-20, is a blatant attack on rural Canada, it is a blatant attack on all of Canada and it is certainly not acceptable to most citizens in Canada. It is going to force provinces such as mine, New Brunswick, to make some tough decisions, and they have already been forced to make tough decisions. The people of New Brunswick recognize that the province of New Brunswick, the government that is in power at the present moment, is forced to take these decisions because of the government in Ottawa cutting back on these fiscal arrangements.

Mr. Speaker, at a time when Canada is going through a critical period in its history, the government must take steps to promote national unity and reduce regional disparity. However, if the federal government keeps reducing cash payments, regional disparity will only get worst. Residents of provinces that are less well off will then have to make do with health services and post-secondary education that are lesser in quality than the kind enjoyed by Canadians in the richer provinces.
June 17, 1991



Mr. Speaker, I would urge all members to vote against this bill.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to associate myself with a number of remarks that were made in this House on a very similar issue, and I would like to read them into the record because this previous speaker in this House dealt with the issue of how the federal government funds health care and post-secondary education in co-operation with the provinces.
These remarks were given in the context of changes in those arrangements that were being proposed by the federal government of the day.
The government had large revenues in earlier years; it established a number of programs and forced its will on provinces; it invaded the provincial fields of education and medical care. But now it does not have the money nor the will to control its spending so that it can continue to finance its obligations and responsibilities to these programs. It now wants to shift the problem over to the provinces, it wants to shift the deficit problem which has built up to such enormous proportions at the federal level down to the provincial level.
He goes on:
Government Orders
This is no time for confrontation and it is no time for unilateral action. This is a time when we need co-operation to nurse the tender relationship which exists between the two levels of government.
These remarks were made on March 23, 1982 by the member for Etobicoke Centre, currently the Minister for International Trade. He goes on to say a few other things to which I would like to refer:
We have a problem here which is partly financial, the government has a major deficit problem. This has been building up over the past 10 years and I think the government must deal with the problem. However, there is a very clear question as to how it should be addressing it. Should it be addressing that problem from the standpoint of unilateral cuts, throwing the problem of the deficit onto another level of government, or should the government be addressing the problem in its own house?
He goes on:
The government does not seem to realize that there is only one taxpayer who pays the taxes for the federal government, for the provincial governments, as well as for the municipal governments. That taxpayer does not care where the service comes from, he wants the service. That taxpayer wants to see the service provided to meet his needs. This is why we have such a cynical attitude toward government today. This government is showing utter contempt for the taxpayer by doing that sort of thing. Therefore, we must rethink this whole system, this system of federal-provincial relationships, so that we do not have such unseemly squabbling between the two levels of government over which one gets credit and which one pays at the end of the day. Governments must get together.
That is the end of the quotation, but the member for Etobicoke Centre, currently the Minister of International Trade, the former Minister of Finance who brought in the budget which contained these changes to the EPF arrangements, was exactly right. He was exactly right. It was not the time then, it is not the time now, it is never the time in a federation like Canada for governments to act unilaterally on fundamental matters that go to the relationship between governments.
The problem that we have today which this bill tries to address is only partly a financial problem. I think we would be wrong not to recognize that there is a financial problem and that it needs to be dealt with. The fundamental problem we have here goes beyond that. What are the basic things that Canada consists of? What is the nature of the social contract that exists which binds us together as Canadians? Why is it that we have a nation stretching from east to west against the normal pull of geography, with a very unlikely combination of people, which has managed to stay together for almost 125 years?

Government Orders
What are the kinds of commitments that we make to one another each time we pay our taxes, each time we go to the polls and vote? What is it that we are saying to one another? I suggest that we are saying something not just about where we were bom or what our citizenship is, we are saying something about the nature of the relationship we expect between ourselves as individuals and our governments.
I want to look for a moment at the provisions that have been introduced in this budget relating to unemployment insurance. Again, I would like to quote the member for Etobicoke Centre, who presented the 1989 budget in which the concept of changing the unemployment insurance fund so that it was entirely funded by employers and employees was introduced.
He said: "The government will continue to contribute to the financing of the program in difficult economic times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums and prudent to allow deficits to build in the unemployment insurance account".
I am not sure that anyone has noticed, but we were in a recession from the second quarter of 1990 which continued until the time this budget was presented. Surely to goodness this is when it is inappropriate to raise premiums, to use the minister's words.
Look at what was done six days prior to the 1988 election when, of all things, the economy was not in recession. In 1988 the economy grew almost at 5 per cent. What did the employment minister at that time do? On November 15, 1988, six days before the election, she announced that employer and employee premiums were to be cut and weekly benefits were to be increased. That, at a time when the economy was in a period of rapid growth, was absolutely disgraceful.
What happened a few short months after that? An overheated economy had to be cooled down by a policy of high interest rates, following a year not only in which unemployment insurance premiums had been reduced, but in which income taxes had been reduced and in which monetary policy according to the governor of the bank himself was perhaps unduly relaxed just before an election. We go into 1989 and interest rates have to be increased. What was the effect of that? By the second quarter of 1990 we were in a recession.
The Minister of Finance, as he soon became and as he was not yet back in 1982 when he gave those remarks which I began with, was talking about a cynical attitude toward government. He had seen nothing at that time. Cynicism is now the order of the day in Canada. I suggest that the kinds of things that this government has done with tax policy, with unemployment insurance and with transfer payments, are at the heart and root of much of the cynicism we have in Canada today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to mention a few facts because I think some of the statements made tonight are not necessarily factual.
Let me just talk a little bit about some comments I have heard just in the past few days. Most people or certainly a good number, when we talk about transfers to the provinces, seem convinced that we are reducing the dollar amount. Let me make it very clear that we are not. The dollar amount over the years since we have been in government has gone up by billions and billions. Our plans are that the dollars will continue to go up. Let the record show that dollars are being increased. The percentage increase is less, but it is still up.
Thanks to perhaps the media and the opposition parties one would think we were slashing the CBC by several hundred million dollars. Not so. Our total subsidies to the CBC will be between $800 million and $900 million this year, and they are going up.
I think our record on restraint has been, in all honesty, quite remarkable. Our average increase in spending for almost seven years is about 3.6 per cent or 3.7 per cent. Compare that to the provinces over the same period. Their average increase is about 7.2 per cent. Regrettably Ontario is leading the pack. Under the Liberals the average increase was a little over 10 per cent. Now we have a new government there and the increase planned by the NDP government is something over 14 per cent, if you can believe that.
We have taken moves on privatization: Air Canada, Petro-Canada and de Havilland. These were all moves which neither of the other parties would ever have supported. We have made some very difficult decisions quite recently in terms of much needed restraint. The public servants' level will be frozen this year. There is a commitment to reduce the layers of management in the bureaucracy. The commitment includes the termination of 10 per cent or at least 475 executive jobs.
June 17, 1991

Rather than me as a member of the government party going on and on about a number of these accomplishments, I would like perhaps to take a different route to get this in a better perspective.
I would like to make some quotes from an article in The Ottawa Citizen last June 13 written by Marjorie Nichols of The Ottawa Citizen staff. This is clearly an impartial reporter and a woman very respected, certainly on Parliament Hill. I will start with some of her quotes:
Historians in pursuit of causes for the calamitous decline in popularity of the federal Conservatives need look no further than the public relations disasters of their fiscal policies.
Instead of distributing the fiscal facts to their taxpayers, the Tbries succumbed to their fatal weakness: the need to put a "spin" on reality.
The facts are that this country has its debt under control and its spending under the most stringent restraint in the western world.
This is not Bill Attewell speaking; this is Maijorie Nichols. She continues:
Yet, the perception persists of a nation managed by a gang of irresponsible spenders in a nation teetering on the edge of bankruptcy.
In truth, the Conservatives have succeeded in their seven years at the helm in reversing the countiy's fiscal direction.
The Government of Canada is now running a program surplus of $13 billion. Next year's surplus is expected to be $20 billion.
To put it another way, if it were not for interest payments on the national debt, this country would be running a huge cash surplus.
Program spending is all government spending except for payments on the accumulated debt, which now totals about $400 billion.
The Tories have literally reversed the country's fiscal picture by adding $30 billion annually to the credit side of the country's ledger.
The Liberals during their last years in office were borrowing to pay for government programs, a situation that can be likened to a taxpayer using a Visa card to pay for groceries and rent.
The Ibries have turned around the entire fiscal mess that they inherited. Instead of borrowing to buy the groceries, they are now paying off their Visa card.
The budgetary deficit numbers actually distort the fiscal truth. In fiscal 1984-85, the Liberal budget deficit was $38.3 billion, of which $16 billion went to pay for "groceries" -federal programs and salaries.
Government Orders
In fiscal 1991-92, by contrast, the Conservative deficit will be $30.5 billion, all of which is interest charges on the national debt.
Instead of bragging about its fiscal management, the Mulroney government decided immediately after the November 1988 budget to try to persuade Canadians that the national debt was about to make the sky fall all over Canada.
Then-finance minister Michael Wilson kicked off his doomsday campaign in his February 1989 budget speech.
"We, as Canadians, have a serious problem," Wilson told the Commons-"our large and growing public debt. In the time it takes to present my budget, that debt will grow by $3 billion."
The Tories also exaggerated the national debt by including nearly $100 billion in bookkeeping accounts that bear no interest debt. Things like future public service pensions.
It was scary stuff. And the government's sales campaign was a rip-roaring success. Every Tbry with access to a microphone stoked the fires of fiscal doom with verbal kindling.
A major attraction of the Reform party-perhaps its major attraction-is its pledge of fiscal frugality. Leader Preston Manning runs around the country promising to cut 15 per cent of all federal public service middle managers.
The marvel is that Manning is attracting crowds with such absurdities. There are 50,000 fewer public sector jobs in this country than when the Tbries took over. And federal spending has increased by an annual average rate of only 3.7 per cent, an achievement unmatched anywhere.
Common sense has now overcome the Tbries, who have begun telling the unvarnished truth about the state of the nation's fiscal affairs.
Like others, I was skeptical when the prime minister appointed Don Mazankowski to serve as finance minister. Mazankowski is a former small-town businessman with no economic expertise.
It appears, though, that the Mazankowski appointment may turn out to be a brilliant stroke. The opposition has not been able to lay a mitt on the straight-talking, straight-dealing former car dealer from Vegreville, Alberta.
Hying to pin "Maz" to the carpet in the Commons is a task akin to pinning jello on a bulletin board.
Canada's fiscal future is bright. Trouble is, Canadians do not know it because of the Tbty spin doctors.
I have laid it all out there. That is the end of her quotes. Clearly, we have a big communications job ahead

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
of us. We have taken more difficult decisions in the past three years than any government took in the past 50 years. Making decisions for the long-term good of Canadians has its price. It is easy to make short-term decisions, handing out money here and there. I am very proud to have been a member of this government. We expect to go onward and upwards as we get that message out.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to know why it took the member 15 or 20 minutes to prepare to read a column by Marjorie Nichols. If he did anything more in his talk than that, I did not catch it.
Ms. Nichols has many good qualities, especially the fact that she was bom and raised in Alberta. I do not think she has ever passed herself off as a financial analyst.
The "ungetaroundable" fact for the member is that during six good years in the economy those opposite have added, I think, $210 billion to the national debt of the children, the parents and the grandparents of this country. Paragons of fiscal responsibility they are not. I know the members think that compound interest only began in 1984. It did not. It began way back in the never, never land when unfortunately deficits began to creep into our national practices.
That has to stop. On that I fully agree with the member and those opposite who talk about fighting the deficit. Every time one of them gets up they tell us: "We have been fighting the deficit". As I say, the facts are that the former Minister of Finance has added more red ink to the ledgers of Canadians than all of the other finance ministers in Canadian history, during six good years of the economy.
Mr. Speaker, before you say I am not speaking about Bill C-20, I would ask members to reject this bill for, among others, the following reasons.
It will effectively limit the access to a post-secondary education for many people. It maintains the freeze on the growth of the Established Programs Financing transfer payments until 1995. I am sure that many members have already dealt with those issues and I will not reiterate what has been said.
The Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act of 1977 provides for federal support for health care and post-secondary education in two ways: transfers and
federal grants based on domestic productivity. In an attempt, albeit not a very good one, to make those EPF transfers equitable to all regions the value of the tax transfers was fully equalized.
It is estimated that the EPF entitlements for 1991-92 will top $20.4 billion, according to the National Council of Welfare. It seems like a lot, an awful lot. However, if we look at the amount the federal government actually contributed to those programs in 1977-78, in 1991 dollars total EPF spending came to $16.4 billion. The 1990 budget froze all EPF entitlements for two years. After that the funding formula for federal grants was set at gross GNP minus 3 percentage points beginning in fiscal year 1992-93.
Now if that was not enough, the 1991 budget told us that the EPF freeze will remain in effect until 1994-95. This brings me to Bill C-20, a bill which legalizes this form of financial terrorism against the provinces and the ordinary people of Canada, the people who do not live in Markham-at least as far as I understand the incomes of the people who live in Markham.
If the bill is passed and its provisions implemented, the federal government will be denying Canadians $97.6 billion worth of services and resources provided by health and post-secondary institutions until the year 2000.
This would have been paid out to the provinces if the growth rate had averaged 7.5 per cent a year and the Tory government had not decided to stick it to the provinces. Even more disturbing to health and educational groups such as the Canadian Federation of Students, the National Council of Welfare, and the Canadian Association of University Teachers is the value of the tax points turned over to the provinces. The value of those tax points will likely increase by 8 per cent a year since the Tory assault on the EPF began.
As cash transfers rise, federal contributions gradually become an afterthought, so much of an afterthought that by the year 2005 the federal government will no longer fund EPF programs directly, only through tax transfers. I say: "Shame".
The effect on post-secondary education has been staggering. Anybody who has attended university recently or helped pay for the higher education of a son or daughter knows that both the federal and most provincial governments have abdicated responsibilities in that regard.
June 17, 1991

Let me mention somebody who graduated from university only a year ago. When he enrolled as a freshman he paid roughly $1,500 for tuition and books. Four years later in 1990 he paid over $2,000 just to walk on campus in the final year. At the ripe age of 23 this person is in debt to Canada Student Loans for $11,000. That is just for a bachelor's degree. He, like the vast majority of other students, would not mind paying a higher price for higher education in Canada. The tuition hikes would ease over-crowding of classes, purchase more academic resources and personnel and pay for capital initiatives.
However, as we all know, the provinces have not seemed to take a very active interest in post-secondary education, a responsibility granted to them under the BNA act of 1867. Tuition hikes have by and large only covered the losses on annual provincial operating grant cuts.
Under the mandate of the tax transfers agreement the money raised is not ear-marked for post-secondary education. If the provinces had been spending what they were supposed to on higher education we would not have the situation today where so many universities and community colleges are understaffed and inadequately equipped.
We have had several commissions of inquiry including the McDonald inquiry and they have all called for the federal government to play a more active role to ensure a national standard of post-secondary education is met. Indeed, did not the throne speech speak about national standards.
In the age of globalization a renewed commitment to quality higher education has never been more important. Constitutionally the federal government could be well within its rights to undertake this because we are substantial contributors to the operating grants of postsecondary institutions and are therefore entrusted to ensure that the national interest and common good be served.
In my view post-secondary education is not merely another service to be paid for mostly out of tax dollars. It is about as important an investment as society can make. We only have to look at the economic miracles of the Pacific Rim where countries have invested enormous
Government Orders
sums of money in education and R and D. Those countries did not become economic powerhouses by accident. They made the initial investment and now it is paying off for them handsomely.
I say this for the benefit of my friends opposite who hold people on this side of the House in disdain for our supposedly irresponsible spending habits. It is well known that any economist can tell you that a society is only as good as its ability to compete. Look at Singapore. Look at Taiwan. Look at Japan. If there is anything that is going to get us out of this recession and out of this mundane cycle of booms and busts and into the realm of a truly prosperous society it will be a solid commitment to higher education with emphasis on quality and accessibility.
Recently I have been attending high school graduations in Edmonton. I have been asking myself where these young men and women, full of ability, energy and brains, are going to find the jobs, the careers that we need, they need, and the whole country needs. I hope it is clear that the federal government must not abdicate its responsibility for education and training.
What has this government opposite and its provincial counterparts done instead? They have cut, they have slashed, and-to speak figuratively-they have burned. In 1977 dollars general operating grants to universities and colleges have averaged $5,426 per a full-time student in 1978. In 1988 those grants averaged $4,492, in 1977 dollars, per full-time student according to Statistics Canada.
Why is it so hard for those opposite to understand why we cannot compete with many other global economies? Post-secondary education cannot be described only as a better future for our children. It is the key for a better future for our entire population. If we cannot have a strong economy, we cannot afford our social programs.
How do we get it across to those opposite that it is essential to have a strong economy before our pensioners, disabled communities and others will be able to get the social benefits they need. However, the Tories want to fritter away this responsibility just like they frittered away so many others.

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
Bill C-20 will ensure that the federal government has no way of maintaining national standards in higher education such as the Canada Health Act ensures that certain health standards are met. The quality of education will not remain the same in every region, I am sorry to say. In fact it is a sure bet, as the member for P.E.I. indicated earlier, that some provinces will have better standards than others; the wealthy provinces will have better standards than the poorer ones.
The provinces are ill-equipped to take on that responsibility with their current taxation bases and powers. If there were ever an attempt to destroy co-operative federalism, Bill C-20 will certainly help to get the job done. The former finance minister is not doing our country any favours with this bill. He is simply ensuring that Canada is reduced to a collection of 10 little fiefdoms to hog tax credits.
I would like to close with a scenario for those opposite. It is estimated that under the EPF funding formula this bill will usher in, health care and higher education will gradually become things of the past to the federal government.
According to the National Council of Welfare per capita EPF federal payments to the provinces will actually be below the initial amount paid out in 1978. By 1995, the federal transfers to provinces will equal $689 per person. In 1978 dollars, it equals $705. In short, it seems to me that this bill is an exercise in nation busting and harmful to Confederation.
I wish that some of those opposite would get up and defend the bill. How can our children be proud of a nation that does not care enough to provide satisfactory training and resources to help catapult our country into the big leagues of competitiveness. If the government insists on making higher education inaccessible to those without high income, so be it. Let us have the $15,000 annual tuition fees we see in the United States.
At the very least, quit the charade that the federal government is actually participating in a national strategy on post-secondary education.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate today and to put on record some of the views of my party and I, but not a pleasure because of the subject matter we have to speak on tonight.
We are debating Bill C-20, legislation to implement some of the budget items tabled in this House on
February 26. We are just now getting around to the legislation actually to implement some of those measures.
It is remarkable for people at home who are perhaps watching on television to see what a government can do with six pages. This legislation has six pages. It is remarkable just exactly how much a government can do to attempt to destroy what has been done to date and to tear apart much of what we have come to see in the country in terms of how our federal government has worked with the provinces in trying to develop both our post-secondary education and our health care systems which are major parts of this bill.
Part of the legislation amends another piece of legislation with a very lengthy title, but essentially it is legislation that lays out the fiscal arrangements by which the federal Government of Canada transfers funds to the provinces for both health and post-secondary education.
What we have learned through the budget and obviously the legislation to implement those measures is an ongoing withdrawal by this government from the field of helping Canadians in terms of health and education. It is clear that our universities, our colleges and our health care institutions are threatened by this government.
Why is it doing that? It is my belief-and I believe that a lot of Canadians feel this-that this government does not believe in health care. It does not believe in education in this country. The way we have attempted to achieve this has been through legislation by which the federal government shares with the provinces the funding for many of these important measures.
It is clear, if we take a look at any of the advanced economies in the world today, that those economies which have developed are those that have invested funds in education, post-secondary education, and have developed health care standards as a right.
It is clear that this legislation will give this government more of an opportunity to withdraw from that field than it has ever had before.
I ask why. Frankly it was a relief last week, I believe it was, when the finance ministers met in Charlottetown. I hope they had an opportunity to visit Province House, as I did once before, to see where Canada started. Maybe the Prime Minister, if he has not visited Province House, should go there and get a little dose of nation building. It is very sobering to be there and recognize where the
June 17, 1991

fathers and now the mothers of Confederation really started to talk about our country. It was a relief to hear for the first time in some time a finance minister-and I am talking about the finance minister from the great province of Ontario-speaking out for average Canadians, for people who need protection, for Canadians who need the health care and post-secondary education we are talking about to build a better Canada.
It was a relief because of the legions of Tory and Liberal finance ministers we have had to put up and listen to for the past number of years display their litany of ways in which to trash government, to trash some of the innovative programs that have been developed in this country. It was a relief to hear a finance minister talking about people and the kind of services that a government can deliver to people.
All we have to do is to look at that litany and that record, that tragic record we have had from previous governments, both Conservative and Liberal. I think in particular about the legislation we are dealing with right now, the legislation that talks about the transfer of funds to provinces for health and education.
I am thinking primarily of changes that were made in 1977 when we went to a block funding formula where the federal government in essence gave a blank cheque to the provinces to spend those transfer payments as they wished.
In my province-and I have mentioned this before in the House-there are many who alleged that Socreds paved highways with health and education dollars.
What is important is what should have been in this bill, what should have been part of Bill C-20, an amendment to the previous legislation that would have compelled the federal government to show clearly to Canadians that when it transfers its tax funds, our tax funds, Canadians' tax funds, to provinces to spend on health and education, that is where those funds are spent.
That is an important principle missing from this bill. It should have been in there. I would hope, certainly in the future, that whatever government it is will consider introducing legislation to that effect. That is the vehicle by which a federal government speaking for the nation, for the country, for all of its people, sits down and works with its provincial colleagues to develop the kind of
Government Orders
education and training programs that can ensure in our country we are a leader and we are entering the competitive world the new trade minister talks about and that we can have a revolution in the health care from the cradle to the grave. We need a cradle to the grave system of health care now more than we have ever needed it before. With this kind of legislation we are not going to have the opportunity to do that, be it this party that forms the government or obviously government members opposite who have no interest in doing this. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, if there is one piece of legislation that is the plank in the Tory destruction of Canada's social programs it is these six pages that we are debating tonight. It is frightening what this government can do in six quick pages.
I hope that the government members will see the light of day, vote against this legislation, and help us build good education and good health care in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last election Liberals attempted to warn Canadians of what they could expect from another four years of Tory rule. Those predictions seem now rather prophetic as we have seen this government's decision manifest into the hardships that are being suffered by Canadians in 1991.
Before the House today is Bill C-20, the latest chapter in the Tory guide to social Darwinism. Medicare, postsecondary education and unemployment insurance were sources of hope for the poor and security for the middle class. Bill C-20 marks the end of that hope and security for so many Canadians.
Ironically, Canada is regarded as the last hope for medical refugees from the United States. We have all seen recently the U.S. congressional hearings which depicted the tragic circumstances of people whose children will die because they have been cut off by their insurance company and cannot afford the treatment their children need to stay alive. Canadians to date have been spared that kind of tragedy by a more humane system of health care that was established and improved upon by a series of Liberal governments over several decades.

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
This government has been relentless in its assault on the institutions that have benefited all Canadians and have in the past attracted so many people from around the world.
Recent ministers of health and welfare have tried to defend this government's underfunding of medicare by accusing the opposition of trying to frighten the elderly, the sick and the poor. It is the elderly who will have to worry about whether or not their local medical establishments will have the funds to provide the constant care they need. It is the sick who have to spend several days on stretchers waiting for one of the few beds not already closed for lack of funds, it is the poor who cannot escape the waiting list for cardiac surgery by travelling to the United States and paying for treatment out of their own pockets.
For many of these people it is too late to be frightened. They put their trust in this government only to find that their trust has fuelled their own misfortune. Many of these Canadians now feel that in 1988 when they buried their ballots in the box they put medicare on death row.
The ministers of this government have tried to relate their financial decisions to those of ordinary homemakers. I know, however, of few homemakers who would not spend whatever money was necessary to buy medicine for their children. I know of few parents who would not take time off work to take their child to hospital. I suspect that few, if any, homemakers would cancel their health insurance, disability insurance or dental plan to take out frivolous ads in newspapers. This government will underfund medicare by another $338 million this year, but it is determined to spend $3 billion on advertising, public relations and consulting.
This government is spending money on cosmetics to hide the scars of budget cuts. Canadians know that if it is a choice between your health and this government's image, the ad agencies always win out.
This is hardly, as this regime claims, putting Canada's finances in order. The excuse for cuts is always the deficit. But the deficit never goes down. It is $12 billion higher this year than the former Tory finance minister predicted in 1985.
If you are looking for answers, look no further then the unemployment rate. We have 1.5 million unemployed. This government's response to high unemployment is to put an even greater burden on employers and workers by increasing the UI premiums. They have made it even more difficult for small business to maintain their work forces.
We all remember the Prime Minister saying in the last election that the best social program is a job. Canadians now realize that their best social program is taking away the Prime Minister's job. For those who are looking to universities and colleges to improve their job opportunities, this government has erected new financial barriers. Tuition fees are being propelled upwards by Tory cuts to transfer payments. There is a new student loan surtax and the GST was slapped on to books, perhaps to discourage Canadian students from reading about our inefficient tax collection system that squanders billions of dollars year after year.
If the Tory student loan surtax remains and Canadian tuition fees continue to rise at their current rate, it will not be long before the poor and middle-class Canadians will face the same despair as the millions of Americans who cannot afford to become qualified and employable.
Indeed, this government's concept of order has bankrupted countless Canadians. These Canadians are financially bankrupt because this government is morally bankrupt. It would rather spend public money on its image than on the essential needs of ordinary people.
Nearly every institution that is distinctively Canadian has been under attack by this government, from the pillars of our social structure, medicare, education, unemployment insurance, to Via Rail, CBC, Air Canada, Petro Canada and Canada Post. Everything is up for sale.
Bill C-20 is not a defence of the Canada Health Act. With each passing moment, the federal government's commitment to health, education and jobs continues to dwindle under the guise of fiscal restraint and economic impetus. The Tories are meticulously plotting a course set forth by the free trade agreement. Bill C-20 is simply another example of how the Tories' sacred trust has been foreclosed.

It is rather like a cruel parent, starving the child and then discussing punishment when the child shows signs of malnutrition. Canadians now realize that if the institutions of medicare, post-secondary education and unemployment insurance are to be salvaged, this government must not survive.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, I am grateful this evening for the opportunity to say a few words about Bill C-20 which, as others before me have explained, is a bill to amend certain statutes in order to implement the February 26 budget.
The bill extends the limits of federal transfers to the provinces under the Established Programs Financing Act introduced in last year's budget for another three years to fiscal 1994-95. The bill amends the Public Utilities Income Tkx Transfer Act in order to restrict payments to provinces for certain privately-owned public utilities. And the bill amends the Unemployment Insurance Act to provide for an increase in premium rates. It is easy to be confused by the technical language in the statutes cited, unless one strips away the legalese to get down to the bare bones of what this government is actually doing with this legislation.
What this government is doing with Bill C-21, and with its misguided February budget, is asking the poor, the sick, the unemployed, the university students, the weaker regions of this country to pay for its colossal fiscal mismanagement.
Bill C-20 is a betrayal. It is a betrayal to the commitment by this government to workers and employers not to increase UI premiums until 1992 and to assist with the cost of the UI program in difficult economic times. This commitment was made as recently as the budget of 1989 and the legislation Bill C-21, which modified the UI program.
Instead, with this bill, the Minister of Finance jacks up UI premiums a full 24 per cent, in the middle of its own made-in-Canada recession. This premium increase is a direct tax on jobs and will increase the already too high unemployment rate.
Bill C-20, is a betrayal of this government's commitment to higher education, a commitment that was made as recently as the last throne speech, a commitment it
Government Orders
says is vital to making Canada internationally competitive in a global economy.
This bill is a betrayal to universal medicare and national health standards. It is a betrayal to the form of co-operative federalism that has made our national health care system work.
What the government is doing with Bill C-20 is withdrawing large sums of federal support to provincial governments for post-secondary education and health. The minister of health earlier today claimed that the government was only slowing down the increase in these payments over the next three years.
Schedule VI of the recent Nova Scotia budget tells a different story. Estimated federal transfers under the Established Programs Financing component of the Nova Scotia budget are expected to fall from $351.9 million in
1989-90 to $331.3 million in 1991-92, a decline of nearly $21 million.
From fiscal 1982 to fiscal 1994-95, the cumulative impact of these transfers is expected to reach $1.5 billion. The provincial budget states, and I quote:
Declining financial support from the federal government for
programs and services in Nova Scotia has placed increasing pressure
on provincial own-source revenues to make up the shortfall.
As a consequence, this year's budget has continued the practice begun last year of cutting back on basic health services to Nova Scotians, limited growth in programs, including health education and social services to 2 per cent; lowering the age limit on dental insurance for children; reducing the permitted frequency of eye examination coverage; closing and consolidating schools; raising the cost of seniors' drugs from $3 to 20 per cent on each prescription.
We can and we do argue with the government of Nova Scotia about its spending priorities. We can disagree and we do with its targets for lowering its own deficit. We know that the provincial government in the last 10 years has mismanaged its own finances. But we cannot argue with the fact that the cutbacks in provincial transfers which this bill will authorize will translate into lower basic services for those who need them most.
Indeed, the National Council of Welfare in its report on funding for health and higher education, appropriately called Danger Looming, has suggested that the federal government's plan to extend the freeze on Established Programs Financing could mean the end of medicare as a national program within five or six years. As the govern-

June 17, 1991
Government Orders
ment withdraws its financial commitment to national health care standards under the National Health Act, it reduces its coverage, it reduces its leverage on provinces to encourage compliance with the basic medical principles of accessibility, comprehensiveness and portability. It undermines the very foundation of a program which has been a source of pride for all Canadians: our universal health care system.
The government says not to fear. Although it is taking away the carrot of federal transfers to provincial governments to encourage their compliance with the National Health Act, with Bill C-20 it is giving itself a big stick. This bill will allow the government to punish a province which attempts to resolve its fiscal difficulties by eroding its own health care services, difficulties which in the poor provinces such as Nova Scotia are being caused by the cutbacks in the federal transfers by this government. What this bill will do is to punish that province by withdrawing federal payments under any act of Parliament or agreement with that province undertaken before or after this legislation. That is what section 23.(2) of Bill C-20 authorizes.
This astonishing provision will mean that the government will be able to attack transfer programs to provincial governments under the equalization payments formula, under territorial financing, under grants in lieu of taxes paid to provincial and municipal governments by the federal government instead of paying taxes on federal or diplomatic property. It will be able to cut into statutory subsidies, into federal-provincial agreements, into programs not related to national health care in order to impose its standards on provincial governments for programs which it is unwilling to finance itself.
At a time when we are facing increasing tensions between the federal and provincial governments, a provision such as this is a red flag, it is an act of federal-provincial war by the federal government on provinces. It is absolutely incompatible with any attempt by a provincial government to try to provide a comprehensive or co-operative federalism in an age in which we need co-operation between federal and provincial governments on basic services.
What it will also mean is that the poor will pay twice. They will pay through the reduction in the federal transfers to provincial governments designed to pay for
the services that they consume and they will pay through the discipline which the federal government will impose on those provincial governments which cannot pay for these services out of their own resources.
This is a terrible bill. It is a bill which all members of this House should denounce, including those on the government side, and which should begin a correction in a wrong-headed fiscal stance by this government and a restoration of sanity and co-operation in the management of our nation's finances.
