Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak today on Bill C-20, although there is not much pleasure in the bill itself. As I stop and think about it, it is a bill that is going to very much restrict funding and post-secondary education by the federal government, it will have drastic effects on health care, again by contributions of the federal government, and it certainly is bringing a burden on the unemployed and increased premiums to employers here in Canada.
I have to stop and think, how did we really get where we are at today?
The Conservative government was elected in 1984 with all kinds of promises. We heard promises to reduce the deficit and promises to bring our financial picture in line. Seven budgets later, we are in a position where, basically, we have increased taxes 81 per cent plus the GST. We have increased expenditures almost 50 per cent. We have a deficit that is well over 100 per cent greater today than seven budgets before. We have some 30-odd tax increases plus the GST.
I heard members on the other side of the House say: "It was because of the Liberal government". There is a time when some people must accept responsibility. Eight years of Tory reign and no responsibility is pretty sad in this country. But we have arrived because of a supposed group that has abilities in business. They have really come down to the point of, financially, putting this country in very difficult straits.
When the government talks about 40 cents out of every dollar being used to pay the debt, it is the debt that it built. It is the debt that it has incurred over the seven budgets. Mr. Wilson is so far away from his projected targets he gave in 1984, it is absolutely ridiculous in this country.

However, it is interesting to look at Bill C-20 today under that light because it is the first time, the second time, the third or maybe the fifth, well, numerous times this government has not been able to deal with reality. It has, this time, totally abdicated responsibility in health care, responsibility in post-secondary education and responsibility in unemployment. It is now turning it over to other people to manage. It increased taxes by 80 per cent and it is now turning over everything to the provinces, to businesses and to individuals to pay those debts.
What does Bill C-20 mean to the people from my riding in Essex-Kent? Well, certainly, it means on the surface that many students who really desire to go on to higher levels of education will not be able to do so. I think of my children, I think of the children of every member in this House, I think of the children of every person in Canada, their opportunities at post-secondary education are restricted drastically by this bill.
What it means to universities is that, unless the provinces pick up extra payments, there is absolutely no way they will be able to continue the service that they are presently giving.
What does it mean to health care? It is going to separate a society of those with funds to be able to pay the health care system and not worry about the extra cost to the doctor, and the weaker part of our society.
This government supposedly presents itself as a caring group who is running a very caring society. Well this is just exactly opposite to what that caring society means.
Post-secondary education, health care and unemployment have traditionally in this country been strong, Liberal policies and the Tory government have tom them down.
As I stop and think, my colleagues from the New Democratic Party have criticized the Liberal Party, however, they never once said or brought the real point forward, that these are Liberal policies, policies which Liberal government after Liberal government after Lib-

eral government have encouraged in this country so that we can be a successful society.
The problem that I see right now is that we are on a course in which there really is no solution if we continue downstream.

Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you that there is no doubt in my mind that when this bill comes up for my vote it is not going to get it, in case there is any doubt in anybody's mind.
I will tell you why. I have had very little difficulty in making up my mind on this. I want to explain to people just what is this disgusting, despicable Bill C-20 that everybody is talking about tonight? What does it do? How can one bill do so much damage to upset so many people? How can it?
It is very inoffensive. To describe it, it says: "Bill C-20, an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in Parliament on February 26, 1991". Aha, the budget of February 26, 1991.
It says it is going to amend certain statutes. There are two statutes which bother me, and I want to talk to them this evening.
The first one is the statute entitled the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act and the second one is the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I want to take a mythical couple in my riding. I can either put them at one end of the riding in Old Perlican, Grates Cove or Bay de Verde, beautiful little fishing villages in one end of my riding, or I can put them in the other end of my riding, the north end of my riding, up in Wesleyville, Valleyfield, Brookfield, Lumsden, Newtown, Templeman. I can put them in any of these places.
Let us take a couple and apply Bill C-20 to them and see how it is going to affect them. I want to say at the very beginning these are the people who in 1988, when I was going around campaigning with my opponents and other members of other parties, were listening to what we had to say. They were hearing the then sitting member from the party across the floor, the government party, saying: "Don't worry, be happy. Do not worry about all of this free trade business, this fear-mongering that Mifflin and his crowd are doing because nothing is going to happen to unemployment insurance. Mr. Cros-bie and the Prime Minister have given their word that nothing is going to happen. It is in the newspapers. Do not worry about that. Do not listen to those scare-mongers. When they say if you vote for this government and this free trade business, you are going to find yourself in a position where your credit card will be checked before your pulse is checked".
I never said that myself but that term was being used. I thought it was rather scary. Some people were saying that it would never happen, that it was scare-mongering and that no government would ever do that to its people. They said: "We have a system that if it was not there we would try to invent it. So because we have it we would not dare, even contemplate, getting rid of it".
The cost of education came up. There was no direct relationship between what was happening and the present cost of education but I think people, even then in 1988, knew that the cost of education would certainly not decrease and in all likelihood, as everything else had in the past four years, it would probably go up.
I want to mention the couples again in either end of my riding, put them in their mid-40s, give them three or four children, they are a working couple. Here is how I think it will affect them. I have to go back now and describe what this means in terms of money to the province I represent, the province of Newfoundland.
We do not have a very large budget in Newfoundland. The point is that half of that budget comes from the federal transfer payments in one way or another. We are very grateful to the government for that, I am not suggesting that we are ungrateful people. However, when practically half your budget comes from a certain source and that source has been cut dramatically then you are in trouble, particularly as it affects the three areas of unemployment insurance, post-secondary education-university education in other words-and health.
What can be more important to people of all ages?
In 1990 there was an announcement in the budget of that particular year that there would be a two-year freeze in federal transfer payments and that this freeze would cost Newfoundland $19 million in 1990 and $34 million in 1991-1992. That announcement was just last year. Nothing else had happened. That is what it would cost the province of Newfoundland.
In the last federal budget-and this is what we are talking about now, the effect that Bill C-20 has-the freeze was extended for another three years. If you take this freeze plus the freeze before, plus all the other freezes of the federal transfer payments and all the other various transfers to the province of Newfoundland, in the past six years since this government has been in power it will have cost Newfoundland a half a billion dollars by the end of 1992. In 1991-1992, this fiscal year alone, it will cost Newfoundland about $150 million. That is shameful. This is a very serious matter.

I have talked in general terms about the cost of education. What is our future in this country if we cannot afford to educate our children? What is the future? We know now we are behind the eight ball. We are behind the curve when it comes to the Europeans and the Japanese. We do not have our people educated properly. We are not going to improve the situation by increasing the cost of tuition, which is one of the results of Bill C-20, which we are going to effect this evening.
Let me talk about health right now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank you for the opportunity to raise a very important matter on behalf of not only people in Winnipeg and Manitoba, but across this country.
Last week I had the opportunity to raise in this House the question of federal funding for the Mother Earth's People's International Pow-Wow. It may appear at first glance as being just another opposition politician looking for money for another group in his constituency. However, we are going through a transformation right now in the aboriginal community which is very, very important for all Canadians to understand, particularly all members of this House. They have come in times of desperate need and, in many ways because of poverty, unemployment, housing and welfare issues, are still in times of tremendous need.
There is a transformation among the leadership which is permeating the youth of this country, making them a much more positive force in our society than any of us would have seen five years ago.
Last week we saw the election of a new Chief of the Grand Council for Canada for the Assembly of First Nations, a chief who will represent the aboriginal peoples of this country in a fine fashion. He will negotiate in good honour on behalf of his people.
Immediately after that, the aboriginal cultural society held the pow-wow which I was very proud to attend. It was held at the Convention Centre in Winnipeg over the weekend and it attracted thousands of participants from across North America and some other continents. It was also an event attended by thousands of people from around Manitoba.
In seeking funding, and the Assembly of First Nations was very modest in its proposals, not only does the federal government not fund it, which is the choice of any government, but the federal government refused to meet it. The only response it received from the Department of the Secretary of State was a curt letter which said in part: "A project such as this would normally be eligible for funding under the social and cultural development component of the Native Citizen's Program. Unfortunately, as you probably know, this particular component was adversely affected by the budget and it was terminated as of April 1, 1990."
In other words, the sad fact is that the federal government no longer has space in its programming for the needs of aboriginal peoples in our cities.
Public servants, if they are so inclined cannot even find a method of supporting groups such as this. So here we have the sad spectre of the largest gathering in the city for a pow-wow, perhaps one of the largest pow-wows in the history of this country. We have a new minister responsible for constitutional negotiations in this country speaking in this House sometimes in eloquent terms about the need for greater aboriginal participation, and at the very moment when those two interests could have been brought together, the interest in favour of aboriginal peoples and the Constitution, and a chance to have participants get together, have a great time and share a culture, many of whom were sharing it for the first time, the federal government turned away from them and refused to even meet.
I rise here today to call upon the House to review the position of the federal government. I ask that the cabinet consider its position of not funding programs such as the Mother Earth's People's International Pow-wow and meet with it as soon as possible to arrange financing.
June 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, further to a question asked on May 29, the National Parole Board and the Correctional Services of Canada have embarked on what many people believe is a very dangerous experiment by allowing a convicted serial rapist out into society on an escorted temporary absence.
Larry Takahashi is no ordinary criminal. He was once considered a model citizen until police came to question him in 1983. He had to be subdued with tear gas before the officers could arrest him.
Edmonton police estimated that during his trial in 1984 he was responsible for well over 100 sexual assaults. He was charged with 138 counts of sexual assault but after evidence was called on only 14 cases, the other victims were sent home and their cases were, in effect, dropped. He was sentenced to three consecutive life sentences on the 14 charges, plus an additional 73 years in prison.
Correctional Services of Canada and the National Parole Board are not as convinced of his threat to the public as are his victims, the judges and a battery of psychiatrists which has him pronounced a danger.
He has been granted escorted temporary absences from Mountain Prison in Aggasiz, B.C., on a monthly basis since July 1989,1 understand. On several occasions he and a convicted murderer played a nine-hole round of golf at a nearby country club with only one unarmed escort in tow, more of a caddy than an escort.
Because the Solicitor General appears to be more committed to rehabilitating criminals, and we all believe in that, he seemed to dissociate himself from his responsibilities as Canada's top law enforcement officer.


Adjournment Debate
It was not until May 31 that he agreed to an immediate review of Mr. Thkahashi's pass privileges. The National Parole Board issues absence permits for those serving life or indeterminate sentences, the violent career criminals. In 1988-89, the Solicitor General's department's annual report revealed the National Parole Board received 311 applications for temporary absences from these types of convicts. A total of 277, or 89.1 per cent of the applications were approved.
Absence permits are officially granted on three grounds: compassionate leave, the funeral of a family member; family contact for special events and occasional exposure to the community; and administrative leave, court appearances. I do not believe a round of golf would meet any of those criteria. Does anyone?
Any review of Takahashi's absence privileges should include a psychiatric assessment by the same team of doctors that examined him prior to sentencing in 1984. In the team was Dr. Herbert Pascoe, a renowned psychiatrist who has helped set standards in the assessment of criminal minds. He described Mr. Takahashi as a unique sex offender: "Cunning, calculating, highly intelligent who terrorized women for sport where most rapists are motivated by vengeance or primordial satisfaction."
If Dr. Pascoe concludes that Thkahashi's criminal disorder has subsided to the point where he does not pose an unreasonable threat to women, people might be convinced that he should receive strictly controlled pass privileges. Until then, public safety is unreasonably at risk with Takahashi on the loose for whatever reason.
There are instances when a violent offender has convinced the entire judicial establishment dealing with his case that he is a dangerous person with little hope rehabilitation. In dealing with these people, the Solicitor General is primarily responsible for protecting law-abiding citizens from convicted offenders. In the case of Larry Takahashi, it would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, and I think to your constituents and to all of our constituents, the Solicitor General has ignored that responsibility.
Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic
Canada Opportunities Agency): Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member opposite for Edmonton Southeast, I also share his concern about the inmate that we have been talking about because he is housed in my riding at present and has resided there for I am not just sure how many years and the escorted leave that he was on was in my riding as well.
I might add that the protection of Canadian society is the highest priority of the Solicitor General, the Commissioner and staff of Corrections Canada. However, in Canada, as in most western countries, judges' sentences lead to an eventual return to society for the majority of inmates.
To facilitate this inevitable return, the Correctional Service of Canada and the National Parole Board have developed a gradual, controlled and supervised release program for releasing inmates into the community. Risk is the prime criteria in any decision they make concerning the release of offenders. After discussions with the Solicitor General, the Commissioner of Corrections Canada directed that an independent review of Mr. Takahashi's case be conducted by an independent forensic psychiatrist. The result of this review will be provided to the National Parole Board for consideration in any subsequent Parole Board reviews.
At the present time, I am advised that Mr. Tikahashi is not receiving further escorted temporary absences.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to a question I raised with the Minister of National Revenue on June 4, 1991, referring to the minister's admission that Canadians were grossly overtaxed, I just wanted to add a few more items perhaps for comment from the parliamentary secretary.
From 1984 to 1989, to bear witness and evidence to the fact that Canadians are being over-taxed, the government collected 66 per cent more on income taxes for a grand total of $25,457 billion while personal incomes during the first four years increased by only 36.5 per cent. In fact the amount of disposable income increased by only an average of 7.2 per cent per annum over those years.
June 17, 1991

At the same time, from 1984 to 1989, the government collected 34 per cent less in corporate taxes in 1989 than it did in 1984, while the corporate profits before taxes increased during the first four years to 41.2 per cent and, after taxes, by 54.4 per cent.
What those figures tell us is that from the point of view of competitiveness, corporate Canada should at least have been able to absorb the government's strategy or stated economic policies designed for greater competitiveness. Instead, what happened is that we saw the taxation increased and increased and, in fact, under this 1991 budget the government has indicated that it will raise an additional $1.4 billion in 1991-92 in tobacco taxes alone, a further $1.14 billion in 1992-93, a further $1.03 billion in 1993-94 and a further $980 million in 1994-95.
For all that kind of collection of taxes on that one item, tobacco, we do not have a government that has given us an indication of any kinds of programs that are going to deal with the health problems associated with greater tobacco consumption.
Yet, we have a government that says that what we need to do is to become more competitive. That same government, from 1984 to 1989, increased income taxes as a share of federal revenue by 9.03 per cent and it decreased corporate taxation by 34 per cent.
The minister responsible for that, former finance minister Michael Wilson, acknowledged that the tax reforms initiated in 1987 were "the wrong policy for the wrong time because what they did they did stimulate the economy" when the economy was already strong, thereby encouraging higher interest rates. The net impact of those interest rates, according to the member for Mississauga South, then chairman of the finance committee, was: "climbing interest rates represent a cash transfer by the government from the relatively poor to the relatively well off."
Yet, the government insists on shifting the burden of taxation, the burden of the deficit, the burden of the public debt and the burden of government expenditures on to the backs of ordinary Canadians' personal income. It should be looking for other solutions.
Adjournment Debate
The GST was not a solution. It is even a greater burden. The minister admitted as much. His department indicated that it grossed more than $400 million more than anticipated.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to respond to the hon. member opposite for Eglinton-Lawrence.
According to figures available from the OECD, Canada's total tax revenues of all levels of government represent about a third of the country's Gross Domestic Product, less than that in France, Germany, the United Kingdom and Italy.
Tkxes on corporations at 2.6 per cent of the GDP, and consumption and direct taxes at 13 per cent of GDP are roughly equivalent to those of the other G-7 countries.
The study by Global Economics gives the government high marks on its corporate tax changes. Specifically, it notes that: "On balance, the Tory corporate changes have tended to improve the efficiency of the tax system." As pointed out in the study, this has led to a "pattern of investment and economic activity that is more productive and conducive to economic growth and employment creation".
Furthermore, as the study notes, corporate income tax revenues have grown more slowly than those from other taxes, due to the decline in corporate profits which are
8.4	per cent lower in 1991-92 than they were in 1984-85. Despite this decline, corporate tax revenues have increased over this period by 17.3 per cent.
This increased revenue is a direct consequence of discretionary actions taken by this government to ensure that corporations contribute to our deficit-reduction efforts. These include the base broadening measures of tax reform and the imposition of the large corporation tax.
The Global Economics report also gave the government high marks for its sales tax reform initiatives, lb quote: "Over-all, however, on efficiency grounds, the government deserves high marks for finally getting rid of the outmoded manufacturing sales tax and introducing a modem consumption tax."

June 17, 1991
Adjournment Debate
An integral part of the introduction of the goods and services tax was the enrichment of the sales tax credit to ensure that lower-income Canadians were better off as a result of the reform.
While this has meant an increase in revenues, this has been done in a fair and equitable way. Measures such as the surtax on high-income earners and the alternative minimum tax ensure that high-income Canadians pay their fair share.

Mr. Speaker, once more I rise to speak on the incredibly important and incredibly crucial matter of assistance from the federal government to the port of Halifax.
I am delighted to see the hon. member for Calgary Southeast who I presume is going to respond to this. Perhaps, I may be overly anticipating the hon. member in his reply, but I would like to put paid to the rumour here and now that the problems in the port of Halifax with most particular reference to the problems of container traffic and the weighing anchor of container companies away from Halifax to Montreal and other points is due to increased tonnage in the area.
This is something that I suspect was invented first by the Minister of Fisheries, has been picked up by the Minister of Transport, by the Associate Minister of Transport and most lately, by the Deputy Prime Minister in response to a question last week.
The president of the last container company to leave Halifax said explicitly and directly when asked: "Why are you going?", "The reasons are twofold: The first and foremost reason was the problem of freight rates between Halifax and Montreal. They were just not competitive." Consequently, we were losing business either to Montreal, within Canada or to the eastern ports of the United States, most of which interestingly enough are serviced by a railroad owned by Canadian Pacific which is, in itself, heavily subsidized and has been over the years by the federal government. The second problem cited by the president of that container company was the unfair tax structure yet again.
We do not ask for a great deal. We do ask for some action. We have asked for years that something be done
about the freight rates that are charged between Halifax and central Canada. We have asked again and again and again. What response have we received? One of the responses that we received is Bill C-ll, and in its former incarnation Bill C-26, the cancellation of the At and East grain subsidy. This is not the response that Haligonians and Nova Scotians are looking for. We are looking for some true action on the part of this government.
Four-and-a-half weeks ago in this House, the Minister of Transport told me, and I quote, as I quoted before, that he would: "do everything in his power to help the port of Halifax". On Friday last, the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada said: "We take this seriously. We take it as seriously as the member from Halifax does, and we are going to do something".
Several weeks ago I questioned the Associate Minister of Transport, and she, too, said something will be done. Sadly, what those comments remind me of, and what they remind Haligonians who have a sense of history of, were the words of the then King of England, Edward VIII, when he visited the coal fields in Wales and saw the unemployment. He said: "Something must be done".
What he did two weeks later was abdicate his responsibility. This government is abdicating its responsibility in and to the people of Halifax. Something has to be done, not mere words, not fine phrases. Assistance is needed and assistance is needed now for the Port of Halifax and for the people of Halifax.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of TVansport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank again the member from Halifax, who has been most diligent in the pressing of this issue before the House.
As we have said before, the present difficulty facing the port of Halifax is the product of a host of economic factors, most of which are international in scope and largely beyond the power of any Canadian entity to solve. The focus for the majority of the problems lies within the international container shipping sphere, which has excess capacity everywhere. Reductions in importations have precipitated an excess of transportation supply over demand of over 30 per cent in some trades, the most prominent being the European-Canadian sector.
International shipping lines have had to cut operational costs and to make other commercial adjustments in an extremely tight market. It must be remembered, howev-
June 17, 1991

er, that such ebbs and flows are part of the normal cycle of international business and reflect the market economy of world shipping. What is more difficult to accept is the degree to which these business cycles impact upon the interface operations, in this case, Canadian ports and railways.
It has been estimated that the portending departure of Hapag Lloyd from the port of Halifax will cause a short-term loss to the port of between 40,000 and 50,000 20-foot equivalent units, which is a standard container measurement. While this level, which represents some 12 per cent of the port's container tonnage, must be seen as significant, it should be recalled that, between the years of 1980 and 1982, an even larger amount was lost to the port, only to be quickly regained and increased during the recovery period which followed.
This government knows that all those with interest in the port and the Canadian routes must work together to produce a long-term, system-wide approach to intermodal traffic so as to keep our ports competitive. What is needed is the help of all parties to produce a comprehensive and efficient package of intermodal services.
In the longer term, in order to ensure the continued competitiveness of our Canadian ports and routes in a dynamic and difficult market, all parties may need to develop strategic alliances in order to create a competitive position for Canadian ports, and for Halifax in particular. The department is currently listening to what those interested parties have to say and I can assure you that full consideration will be given toward identifying and implementing an appropriate long-term response.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 3,1 rose in the House and asked a question of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans regarding the need for a full environmental assessment of the Alcan project, as ordered on May 16 by the Federal Court of Canada. On that day, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans suggested that the matter was under review and that an announcement would be made within a reasonable time as to what kind of action the government was going to propose.
The details and concerns that people have had over this project have been fairly well documented, in particular by reports now coming out from retired Department
Adjournment Debate
of Fisheries and Oceans scientists whose reports and information that had been released show there is considerable concern over the fish habitat of the Nechako and eventually the Fraser River and many other concerns related thereto, the main problem being the reduced flows due to the Alcan project. I would like to quote from the decision on May 16 in the Federal Court because I think it says most clearly what this government should do and what we hope the parliamentary secretary will be able to announce tonight. I am quoting from the decision:
I conclude that the Kemano II Completion Project requires an assessment by virtue of the Environmental Assessment Review Process and that the Ministers involved and specifically the Minister of the Environment were under an obligation to arrange for it and not frustrate this by the Settlement Agreement signed in 1987 and finally by the Order of the Minister, confirmed by Order in Council-
That was passed late last year. Most important:
It is not sufficient to be satisfied with the review, however extensive, performed by the Proponent of a proposal, even in co-operation with the Ministers involved, without a public assessment by an independent panel at which all interested parties may be heard.
It is very clear in the decision what the judge in this case was suggesting. He has thrown out the original Nechako settlement agreement and in particular makes reference to the Order in Council exempting this project from an environmental assessment.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will announce two things tonight: notwithstanding the company's decision on Friday to appeal this decision, an announcement as to the government's intention in that regard and, regarding that, a decision by this government to announce a full environmental assessment of the Alcan project.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member opposite from Prince George-Bulkley Valley and in reply also to a similar question that was asked on June 3,1991,1 am pleased to provide additional historical information on this matter.
By the late 1970s, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans had become concerned that reduced flows being released by Alcan from the first Kemano Project built in the 1950s could endanger the Chinook and sockeye salmon populations in the Nechako and Stuart Rivers in British Columbia. The department therefore obtained an injunction requiring Alcan to release more water than

June 17, 1991
Adjournment Debate
it was obligated to do under the 1950 British Columbia Water licence.
When Alcan proposed the second project, the Kema-no Completion Project in the early 1980s, and also sought relief in court from the injunction, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans entered into a settlement agreement with British Columbia and Alcan in order to secure longer term protection for the fish stocks. The agreement formalized the release of flows to protect fisheries and required Alcan to provide measures to mitigate the potential impacts on fish and fish habitat.
Before the minister entered into the agreement the department conducted considerable analysis of the potential impacts of the proposed Kemano completion project. The agreement was reached after an independent review panel chaired by the president of the University of British Columbia advised that fisheries experts agreed that impacts on the fisheries could be mitigated. The department applied the principles of its policy for the management of fish habitat providing for no net loss of fish habitat and responsible resource
management. In particular the agreement called for a mechanism to ensure that impacts on fish and fish habitat could be mitigated on an ongoing basis. Therefore, if an issue arises that was not initially thought to be a problem, there is a process in place designed specifically to deal with it.
We can see that the settlement agreement was entered into with consideration for potential impact. They were in fact considered extensively. In the understanding of the day when the settlement agreement was signed, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans took what he believed to be the-necessary and appropriate steps to ensure that the protection necessary for fish and fish habitat was provided.
